article_content: The ongoing Ukraine-Russia conflict has escalated into cyberwarfare, with hackers from both nations causing service outages, data breaches, and website defacements. Modern cyber operations, including Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, website defacement, and network breaches, echo historic acts of resistance but are now executed online. Groups associated with Anonymous—like OpRussia and Russian CyberCommand—have focused their attacks on Russian governmental and business sites in objection to President Putin's actions toward Ukraine. At the same time, pro-Russian groups such as Anonymous Ukraine and CyberBerkut have targeted Ukrainian and NATO-linked online resources. The interconnectedness of today's globe creates both a rich ground for information sharing and an inherent insecurity, leaving even the most advanced countries exposed to skilled hackers. Many of the most impactful hackers operate independently of any state, at times surpassing official cyberwarfare capabilities. Following the November 2013 suppression of 'Euromaidan' demonstrators, Ukrainian cybersecurity experts began forming volunteer cyber defense groups. By March 2014, cyberattacks by both sides increased, with OpRussia issuing warnings to Putin while regularly disrupting Russian online platforms. The Russian CyberCommand, another group aligning with Anonymous and opposing the Crimea annexation, has continually hit Russian agencies and leading cybersecurity firms. In contrast, pro-Russia groups like Anonymous Ukraine and CyberBerkut—suspected to have ties to former security officials—have assaulted hundreds of Ukrainian state and commercial websites, as well as NATO sites, during pivotal events. Unlike previous cyber conflicts such as those in Estonia (2007) and Georgia (2008), there is little concrete evidence indicating direct involvement by the Russian government in today's attacks. Notably, some Russian hackers now oppose Kremlin policies. Despite heavy investment in cyber and information warfare by Russia and other countries, including the creation of dual-use tools for both defense and potential offense, the expertise and initiative of independent hackers continue to exploit vulnerabilities, posing a constant challenge for digital security everywhere.

article_content: Renana Jacob was not at home when Hamas launched its deadly attack on her kibbutz in southern Israel on 7 October, but she was able to reach her two sons by phone. "The boys told me they heard gunshots outside. I tried to reassure them, saying it was the army coming to save them," she said, referring to Yagel, 12, and Or, 16. However, it was not Israeli soldiers outside, but Hamas gunmen, who killed about 1,400 people, mainly civilians, and took more than 200 hostages during those attacks. A few hours after the attack began, Ms Jacob said Yagel whispered over the phone that people had broken into the house. "They were terrified," she recalled. "The last thing I heard my youngest son say a month ago... he begged not to be taken. He said, 'I'm too young. Please don't take me. I'm too young.' But they took him." She has had no contact with her children since that day. Yagel and Or are believed to be among the 242 people, according to the Israeli military, whom Hamas is holding hostage in the Gaza Strip. The World Health Organization (WHO) says it is 'gravely concerned' about the hostages, especially children, the elderly, and those in poor health, and has called for their immediate release. Ms Jacob spoke to the BBC's 'The Context' in an emotional interview with two other Israeli mothers, Batshema Yahalomi and Hadas Kalderon, whose children were also kidnapped by Hamas. The three mothers traveled from Israel to the UK to raise awareness, giving media interviews and meeting with the Qatari ambassador to the UK. Qatar is acting as a mediator between Israel and Hamas—designated as a terrorist organization in the UK—in efforts to secure the hostages' release. Ms Jacob said the ambassador conveyed that Qatar is making every effort to help, and she believes him. Ms Yahalomi also experienced a terrifying ordeal when gunmen entered her family's home on 7 October. She managed to escape with her two daughters, including a baby, after Israeli soldiers intercepted the attackers near the Gaza border. Her husband Ohad, whom she says was shot by Hamas gunmen, and her 12-year-old son, Eitan, were taken to Gaza on motorbikes; she has not heard from them since. "That was the last time I saw my son. I haven't had any contact or news from him," she said. Ms Kalderon had five family members taken hostage, including her children Erez, 12, Sahar, 16, and their father, Ofer. Her elderly mother and niece were killed by Hamas. "I don't even have time to grieve. I couldn't attend the funeral because I have to fight for those still alive," she said, emphasizing the urgent need to prioritize the release of hostages. "We know nothing about them. They're being held in tunnels underground. They can't see the sky or sunlight, and I'm sure they are terrified," she added. Ms Jacob said that 32 children are currently held by Hamas and urged for their immediate release. Since the 7 October attacks, Israel has launched near-constant air strikes on the Gaza Strip. According to the Hamas-run health ministry in Gaza, over 10,300 people have been killed, including more than 4,100 children. While some politicians have questioned these figures, the WHO considers them reliable. Ms Jacob called for a 'pause' to allow children in Gaza to escape to safety. "There's so much violence. My heart goes out to every child and mother affected," she said. "Let’s pause and have a time-out for children—get ours out and allow Gaza’s children to get out too," she added. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces both international criticism for the bombing campaign and anger at home over the security lapses that allowed the Hamas attack and slow progress on freeing hostages. So far, only five hostages are known to have been released. Mark Regev, a senior adviser to Prime Minister Netanyahu, also appeared on 'The Context' and acknowledged a 'terrible failure' in the security response. He said a special directorate has been established to communicate with families of the hostages. "We can only feel their pain and suffering, and we're making every effort to retrieve their loved ones," he said. Ms Jacob, Ms Yahalomi, and Ms Kalderon are focusing on ensuring the release of their family members as soon as possible. "They disappeared from our lives. We don’t know if or when we’ll see them again," Ms Kalderon said.

article_content: Andrew Brannan, a 66-year-old Vietnam veteran, is set to be executed this week in Georgia for the 1998 shooting of Deputy Kyle Dinkheller. Brannan’s defense claims his actions were heavily influenced by severe mental health issues, specifically post-traumatic stress disorder and bipolar disorder that originated from his war service. They argue that executing a veteran whose criminal actions stem from service-related mental illness violates constitutional rights and are requesting his sentence be reduced to life in prison. His lawyers have appealed, maintaining that the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments—as well as the Georgia Constitution—bar the execution of veterans whose psychological injuries contributed to their offenses. The legal team has also petitioned the state parole board for clemency, stating the death penalty should only be applied in the most severe cases. Footage from Deputy Dinkheller’s dashboard camera reveals Brannan acting irrationally and confrontationally after being stopped for speeding near Dublin, Georgia. The video shows Brannan escalating the situation, ending in him shooting and killing Dinkheller before fleeing the scene. Brannan, with no prior criminal record, was convicted of the murder in 2000. His defense argues that the trial did not fully consider medical expert testimony about his mental health. A judge’s order for a new sentencing trial was later overturned by the state Supreme Court. Deputy Dinkheller’s family has stated that, while nothing can bring back their loved one, the execution represents some measure of justice. Brannan’s execution by lethal injection is set for 7:00 p.m. on January 13, 2015.

article_content: Convicted armed robber John Killick has lost his NSW Supreme Court battle against extradition to Queensland. Justice Carolyn Simpson upheld the order to send Killick north. 'I left myself open for this, but you have to face what you’ve done in the past,' Killick told reporters on Thursday. Killick, 72, could now be required to serve the remaining two and a half years of a sentence imposed in 1983 for armed robbery. He will be extradited to Queensland over an alleged breach of bail from 21 years ago. Killick must report to Queensland Police by June 27, and may have to serve out his outstanding sentence. Killick became internationally known after a daring escape from Sydney’s Silverwater prison in 1999, when his then-girlfriend Lucy Dudko hijacked a helicopter to break him out. Killick’s lawyer, Eidan Havas, said he is considering options for appeal and is working with a Queensland solicitor to seek a judicial review of the cancellation of Killick’s parole. 'Although we were optimistic and hopeful, we weren’t surprised by today’s decision,' Mr Havas said. 'He’s been prepared for this and is ready to go to Queensland and serve time if required.' Killick remains on bail with an electronic ankle bracelet and must report daily to NSW Police. 'The longer I’m out, the more I feel human again after all that time,' he said. 'My wife was hoping for the best, but we know this ordeal will be over soon.' At the time of his helicopter escape, Killick was serving his sentence for armed robbery. He spent 45 days on the run after Dudko hijacked the helicopter at gunpoint and landed it in Silverwater prison’s exercise yard. Killick climbed in and escaped as prison guards fired warning shots. After being captured, he returned to prison and was released on parole in April this year. Immediately after Killick’s release, Queensland authorities issued a warrant for his arrest and requested his extradition, alleging he breached parole back in 1993 after an offence involving a dangerous weapon. Killick’s legal team argues the warrant is an abuse of process.

Delhi continues to grapple with hazardous air quality, as pollution levels remain far above safe standards. On Sunday, Delhi Environment Minister Gopal Rai said that farm fires in Haryana and Uttar Pradesh are currently contributing more significantly to Delhi’s poor air than those in Punjab. Citing Central government data, Rai stated that Punjab has burned less stubble this year compared to the previous year, and due to stagnant wind conditions, smoke from Punjab is not reaching Delhi as much as smoke from Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

For the fourth day in a row, Delhi’s air quality remained in the ‘Severe’ category. According to SAFAR-India, the Air Quality Index (AQI) at Lodhi Road was recorded at 385 (Very Poor), while the Delhi University area registered an AQI of 456 (Severe). Drone footage over the Qutub Minar showed thick haze blanketing the city. Residents describe the worsening conditions: one morning walker at Lodhi Garden noted a sharp decline in visitors due to difficulty breathing, while another reported a burning sensation in the eyes attributed to pollution.

Neighboring cities are experiencing similar problems. Noida’s AQI dropped to 466 (Severe), and Gurugram’s was at 392 (Very Poor), per SAFAR-India figures. Health experts caution that healthy AQI levels should remain below 50. With many AQI readings above 400, the health risks—particularly for those with respiratory problems—are severe, including an increased likelihood of lung cancer.

In response, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) has required the Chief Secretaries of affected states to take immediate steps to bring pollution under control and provide a report on their actions. The NGT emphasizes that swift action is crucial to prevent further harm and to improve air quality in cities with AQI levels in the ‘Severe,’ ‘Very Poor,’ and ‘Poor’ categories.

Other recent news includes: India’s first 100% foreign direct investment (FDI) in the defense sector, with Sweden’s Saab approved to set up a rocket manufacturing facility; the State Bank of India (SBI) posted an 8% rise in net profit due to steady loan growth and reduced provisions; and edtech company Byju’s reported delayed audited results for FY22, showing revenue growth yet continued operational losses.

article_content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has updated its website, removing statements that suggested Ebola can, in rare cases, spread from person to person through coughing and sneezing. The current guidance states there is 'no evidence' Ebola spreads in this manner. According to the New York Post, the CDC also took down a poster on Thursday indicating that Ebola could be transmitted via 'droplets' from coughing or sneezing that land on hard surfaces, such as doorknobs. An undated CDC handout photo shows a kit given to travelers from Ebola-affected West African countries, which contains informational cards and a thermometer. Previously, the CDC suggested rare person-to-person spread through coughing and sneezing, but now reports there is 'no evidence' supporting this claim. The Huffington Post reported the language change, although the CDC has not provided an explanation for the update. The change occurred a day after the New York Post reported on the poster's existence. A former CDC fact sheet stated: 'Droplet spread happens when germs traveling inside droplets that are coughed or sneezed from a sick person enter the eyes, nose, or mouth of another person.' The current webpage says: 'The What’s the difference between infections spread through air or by droplets? Fact sheet is being updated and is currently unavailable. Please visit cdc.gov/Ebola for up-to-date information on Ebola.' The removal of the previous information follows a public campaign by Republican Senator Rand Paul, who called for the CDC to be more transparent about how Ebola spreads. Previously, the CDC's frequently asked questions page indicated that fluids like saliva or mucus from a symptomatic Ebola patient could be a source of transmission if they contacted another person’s eyes, nose, or mouth. Senator Paul has cited CDC statements as evidence that Ebola could, in theory, spread if a person is close to someone infected. He has commented on the CDC's definition of 'direct contact,' describing it as being within three feet of an infected individual. Paul has criticized the CDC for, in his view, downplaying the risks and not being precise enough in its disease description. Following these criticisms, the CDC has updated at least one page to say: 'There is no evidence indicating that Ebola virus is spread by coughing or sneezing. Ebola virus is transmitted through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a person who is sick with Ebola; the virus is not transmitted through the air (like measles virus).' However, the agency also clarifies that droplets (for example, splashes or sprays) from a sick person could be infectious, so standard, contact, and droplet precautions are still recommended in healthcare settings. Senator Paul was not immediately available for comment regarding the CDC's updated guidance.

According to William Hill, Alistair is one of their top three all-time payouts for weight loss bets and is the only person to win such a bet on Christmas Day. The company typically receives about 100 weight loss bets per year. William Hill spokesperson Rupert Adams commended Alistair’s achievement, calling it 'an amazing accomplishment.' Alistair’s transformation surprised friends and family, with some not recognizing him after his significant weight loss. He has expressed gratitude for the support he received, emphasizing that his life has changed positively as a result of his efforts and the bet.

Kyle Vogt, the CEO of General Motors' autonomous vehicle division Cruise, has resigned following a safety review of the company’s U.S. fleet. Vogt, 38, announced his departure through an email to staff, providing no detailed explanation. In his message, he wrote, "The last 10 years have been amazing, and I'm grateful to everyone who helped Cruise along the way."

His resignation follows recent challenges for Cruise, which temporarily suspended all U.S. testing after an October 2 incident where a self-driving Cruise vehicle was involved in an accident that resulted in a pedestrian being dragged. On Saturday, Vogt took responsibility for the situation, stating in an internal email, "As CEO, I take responsibility for the situation Cruise is in today. There are no excuses, and there is no sugar coating what has happened. We need to double down on safety, transparency, and community engagement."

Cruise, a competitor to Alphabet’s Waymo, had been testing hundreds of autonomous vehicles in several U.S. cities, especially San Francisco. However, in November, the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) ordered Cruise to remove its driverless cars from state roads, citing public safety concerns and allegations that the company misrepresented the safety of its technology.

This series of events marks a setback for both Cruise and the broader autonomous vehicle industry, which depends heavily on public trust and regulatory approval.

article_content: In the aftermath of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 being shot down, Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko urged the United Nations to designate the Donetsk and Luhansk separatist groups as terrorists. Poroshenko emphasized to CNN that the world must take a stand, choosing either to support terrorist groups or to align with the civilized global community. From a legal standpoint, only the UN Security Council—rather than the secretary-general or other bodies—can make such a designation. This is largely due to the ongoing absence of a globally agreed-upon definition of terrorism, an issue debated at the UN for over twenty years as member states struggle to distinguish terrorism from legitimate self-determination movements. Despite this, certain international treaties like the 1971 Civil Aviation convention do define specific acts of terror, particularly those targeting planes, such as the Flight 17 incident if proven intentional. Poroshenko maintains that the Donetsk and Luhansk rebels are terrorists with or without direct evidence linking them to Flight 17. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin sees these groups as self-defense and independence seekers. Notably, while Putin brands all anti-government fighters in Syria as terrorists, he supports the opposite narrative regarding Ukraine—highlighting the selective use of the term. Such labeling often seeks to attract international condemnation, but also clouds the line between legitimate political action and violent extremism. Since 9/11, what constitutes terrorism has evolved. Organizations like ISIS, Boko Haram, and Al-Shabaab now control extensive regions, blurring the boundaries between insurgencies and traditional terrorist groups—unlike older examples such as the IRA or ETA. The Ukrainian scenario also prompts questions about Russia’s role. If the separatist fighters are deemed terrorists, this suggests implications for potential state support, even though the prominence of state-sponsored terrorism diminished after the rise of non-state actors like al Qaeda. Today’s conflicts are marked by combinations of terrorism, armed uprisings, and obscure proxy fights, all fueling confusion and suffering. As seen with Flight 17, civilians are too often the ones who pay the highest price. Regardless of political or legal labels, no justification excuses such tragedies.

article_content: Irish author Paul Lynch has won this year's Booker Prize for his dystopian novel 'Prophet Song.' The book, set in a reimagined Dublin experiencing totalitarian rule and upheaval, follows a woman's struggle to safeguard her family during a national crisis. Awarded at a ceremony in London, the £50,000 Booker Prize recognizes exceptional fiction. Judges, led by Canadian writer Esi Edugyan, commended Lynch's writing for its emotional resonance and powerful narrative, describing the work as a significant literary feat. Aged 46, Lynch had been a leading candidate for the prize, which is known to propel writers to wider recognition. His novel emerged as the winner among six shortlisted titles authored by writers from Ireland, the UK, the US, and Canada. In his remarks, Lynch noted the personal challenges he faced in writing the novel, sharing concerns that the subject matter might jeopardize his career but feeling compelled to bring the story to life. He described 'Prophet Song' as an exercise in radical empathy, immersing readers in the experience of life in a failing society. Lynch explained that current unrest in Western countries, as well as crises like Syria's conflict and refugee situation, inspired his work. His goal was to elicit a deeper, more personal response from readers. He clarified the novel is a counterfactual narrative and not a forecast. Although judging occurred shortly after violence in Dublin following a stabbing incident, Edugyan assured the decision was independent of those events. Reacting to the riots, Lynch expressed both surprise and recognition that such volatility can exist beneath societal surfaces. The other finalists were Paul Murray ('The Bee Sting'), Paul Harding ('This Other Eden'), Sarah Bernstein ('Study for Obedience'), Jonathan Escoffery ('If I Survive You'), and Chetna Maroo ('Western Lane'). While not unanimous at first, the panel ultimately agreed on Lynch's book for its outstanding quality. Since its inception in 1969, the Booker Prize has celebrated excellence in English-language fiction published in the UK and Ireland, often giving winners a major career boost. Previous recipients include Margaret Atwood and Salman Rushdie. Lynch expressed pride in winning for Ireland and said the prize money would help cover increased mortgage costs. The ceremony also featured Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, who recounted how literature, especially Margaret Atwood's 'The Handmaid's Tale,' comforted her during her imprisonment in Iran, serving as a tool for psychological escape.

article_content: Protesters held placards in Kathmandu, Nepal, on November 18, 2023, rallying against the country's recent ban on TikTok. Nepali TikTok creator Manjita Manandhar was surprised by the sudden decision, which the government justified as protecting 'social harmony and goodwill.' Manandhar, who typically earns around $1,500 a month by creating content for businesses and sharing it on TikTok, said, 'I was shocked as the decision came suddenly.' She shared that her earnings have halved since the ban, and income from platforms like Instagram and YouTube is insufficient to cover the loss. She also supports a videographer and a manager from her earnings. Nepal's centre-left coalition government is the latest to ban TikTok. The platform, owned by China-based ByteDance, has faced criticism in multiple countries over its ties to the Chinese government and concerns about data privacy. India banned TikTok and other Chinese apps in June 2020, citing threats to national security and integrity. Many in Nepal say the ban has taken away a significant income source and restricted a space for free speech. Protests erupted in Kathmandu, and some citizens have filed petitions in the Supreme Court, which has requested the government to provide written justification for the ban before a hearing scheduled for December 5. Cybersecurity expert Rajib Subba highlighted that many Nepalis relied on TikTok for livelihood, creativity, innovation, entrepreneurship, and advocacy. Sudhir Parajuli, president of the Internet Service Providers' Association of Nepal, estimates there are around 2.2 million TikTok users in the country. TikTok stated in a letter to Nepal's telecommunications regulator that it addresses violations of its community guidelines but did not give specifics. According to local reports, over 1,600 cyber crime cases in Nepal in the past four years have been linked to TikTok. Sushila Pokharel, a regular user who shares dancing and singing videos, believes, 'It's wrong to ban the app entirely. Instead, address harmful content.'

SYDNEY: Operations have resumed at Australia’s key ports, which account for about 40 percent of the nation’s freight trade, after a cyberattack caused significant disruption, according to port operator DP World. The company disconnected its systems from the internet immediately after detecting the breach last Friday, preventing trucks from loading or unloading cargo at the affected ports in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, and Fremantle.

“DP World Australia is pleased to announce that operations have resumed at its ports nationwide,” the company said in a statement. DP World reported that key systems underwent successful overnight testing before operations restarted. The company expects to move 5,000 containers through its four terminals today, close to its normal daily volume.

Nevertheless, investigations and ongoing efforts to secure systems could cause occasional, temporary disruptions to port services in the coming days. DP World cautioned that the investigation and remediation process may take some time. Alastair MacGibbon, the company’s advisor on the cyberattack response, confirmed to Nine Network television that there had been ‘unauthorised activity in the system’ and that data had been accessed by a malicious or unauthorised party, though he did not specify what information was taken.

article_content: European Union scientists have indicated that 2023 is on track to be the hottest year in at least 125,000 years. In October, global temperatures broke records, exceeding the previous high from 2019 by an unprecedented 0.4°C, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). Samantha Burgess, deputy director at C3S, described the temperature difference as 'very extreme.' This warming is mainly attributed to ongoing greenhouse gas emissions resulting from human activities, compounded by the return of the El Nino weather event, which heats up Pacific Ocean waters. On average, the globe in October this year was 1.7°C warmer than the pre-industrial benchmark of 1850-1900 used by Copernicus. Breaking multiple recent records all but ensures 2023 will surpass previous record years—including 2016, another El Nino year—for the warmest year based on data from Copernicus (dating to 1940). Combining with findings from the IPCC, which pulls from sources like tree rings and ice cores, scientists estimate this is the highest global temperature in more than 125,000 years. The dramatic difference in October follows a major September heat record, a pattern that suggests the climate is shifting more rapidly than previously thought, according to Burgess. Climate expert Michael Mann (University of Pennsylvania) said El Nino years now frequently coincide with record-breaking warmth, as the additional heating from El Nino layers onto ongoing human-driven climate change. Piers Forster (University of Leeds) warned against normalizing this year's destructive floods, wildfires, extreme storms, and heatwaves, urging countries to drastically curb emissions now to significantly limit further warming. Despite ambitious climate goals, global carbon dioxide emissions reached a record high in 2022, underlining the urgent need for more decisive action.

article_content: Infosys founder Narayana Murthy recently sparked a national discussion after suggesting that Indians should work 70 hours a week. However, data from staffing firms shows that employees in India's software companies already work, on average, 45-50 hours per week—around 10 hours a day over five days. This exceeds the industry standard of 40 hours weekly, with many compelled to work longer to meet project deadlines. Experts believe the focus on hours worked instead of output, lengthy commutes, infrastructure issues, and elevated work stress hinder productivity in India's IT sector. Over the past five fiscal years, the productivity per rupee spent on employee compensation has remained largely flat. Xpheno data reveals that since April-June 2020, for every rupee spent on talent, revenue returns stayed around Rs 1.8-1.9. This is supported by annual report data from top IT firms such as TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro, TechMahindra, LTIMindtree, and Mphasis. According to Prasadh MS, head of workforce research at Xpheno, 'Per-person productivity at Indian IT companies, measured by the cost-to-revenue ratio, has barely changed over four fiscal periods. There’s been no significant productivity growth despite digitalization, AI, and automation investments.' Productivity in IT is often measured as 'revenue per employee.' Aditya, a 27-year-old developer at a major IT firm, commented, 'In Indian culture, hard work is valued and hours are equated with success. But not all those hours are productive. When people work 10-hour days on tasks that could be automated or are repetitive, fatigue sets in, making problem-solving slower.' For FY23, aggregate revenue per employee at TCS, Wipro, and HCLTech dropped 3.8-11% (five-year CAGR), while Infosys and TechMahindra saw increases of 2.6% and 5.6%, respectively. Krishna Vij, business head of IT staffing at TeamLease Digital, acknowledged that productivity levels are lower due to high employee costs but noted recent improvements: 'Despite a slowdown and cautious spending, higher employee utilization has driven overall revenues up, increasing productivity per employee. In 2023, average revenue per employee rose 13% while employee costs grew 9%, signaling a positive trend.' IT firms also have subcontracting and outsourcing costs. Salary expenses accounted for about 50-54% of total expenses at major companies in 2023, which is 3-4% higher compared to previous years according to staffing firm officials. The Indian IT industry, valued at $245 billion, also faces work-life balance challenges: 58% of the workforce report average to poor work-life balance, compared to the global average of 40%, as per TeamLease Digital data. This comes during one of the sector's slowest growth periods, with hiring down and pay increases modest. Much of the productivity lift is linked to increased demand for IT services since the pandemic. Measuring individual productivity is complex and varies by job function, says Manu Saigal, director at Adecco. Some roles, like business analysts, are moving to more flexible schedules, sometimes working as little as four hours a day, reflecting a desire for better work-life balance and remote work. For real progress, experts suggest IT companies should move away from simply counting hours and foster a culture valuing productivity and balance. Changing this mindset, argues TeamLease Digital’s Vij, is vital for a more effective workforce.

Actor and activist Cynthia Nixon has joined state legislators and Palestinian rights supporters in a five-day hunger strike outside the White House, calling for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza. At a press conference Monday, the demonstrators condemned President Joe Biden's unwavering support for Israel's military actions in Gaza and the recent pledge of more than $14 billion in additional U.S. aid to Israel. Organizers pointed to public opinion polls indicating most Americans support a ceasefire and highlighted the severe humanitarian toll in Gaza, where more than 14,800 Palestinians have died. UN experts have warned that Palestinians 'are at grave risk of genocide.'

The hunger strike comes as Israel and Hamas extend a temporary truce for an additional two days to facilitate further hostage and prisoner exchanges. Hunger strikers asserted that the pause demonstrates diplomacy's potential to resolve the crisis. However, Israeli officials have signaled that fighting may intensify once the truce ends, and they have advised northern Gaza residents not to return home.

The protest was organized by a coalition including Palestine solidarity groups, progressive Jewish organizations, and Arab and Palestinian-American advocates. Cynthia Nixon, known for her role in 'Sex and the City' and her 2018 run for New York governor, used her speech to stress the destruction in Gaza and the deaths of journalists and aid workers. She implored President Biden, who has endured personal loss, to empathize with the civilians in Gaza and commit to lasting peace.

Delaware legislator Wilson-Anton, a Muslim American, expressed anxiety about fasting but said her focus remains on the suffering in Gaza. She echoed the protesters' frustration with government inaction, noting, 'The majority of Americans are for a permanent ceasefire.'

Protester Zohran Mamdani welcomed the release of hostages and prisoners during the truce, emphasizing that only negotiations, not warfare, can bring families together. He said the hunger strike is a response to American foreign policy and the erasure of Palestinian experiences.

New York organizer Abdelhamid connected the violence in Gaza with increased prejudice and hate crimes against Arabs and Muslims in the U.S., referencing the recent shooting of three Palestinian students in Vermont as an example. She argued that inflammatory rhetoric from leaders contributes to such incidents.

Sumaya Awad, another hunger striker, stressed America's complicity in the conflict and described her action as a 'fragment of what Palestinians are enduring' daily. She argued the events in Gaza have real repercussions for Americans, urging continued advocacy for a permanent ceasefire.

article_content: Getting to cancer treatment is a huge challenge for many families. For instance, two-year-old Sisi Johnson has neuroblastoma and needs to make frequent trips—sometimes up to six per week—to Rady Children's Hospital in San Diego. Because her mother, Silvia, doesn’t have a car and Sisi’s weakened immune system prohibits using public transit, transportation becomes a critical issue. Helping fill this gap is Richard Nares, who started the 'Ride With Emilio' program after losing his own son, Emilio, to cancer in 2000. Richard’s mission is simple: No child should miss treatment because they can’t get a ride. His foundation now gives free, clean, and organized rides to children like Sisi and their families, serving hundreds each year. Silvia Johnson, a single mom with two kids, depends on the program for eight to ten rides a week. She describes the service as lifeline, praising the cleanliness, punctuality, and care they provide. Richard Nares understands these struggles firsthand. When his son Emilio was diagnosed with leukemia in 1998, the family had a strong support system—including family, flexible jobs, and friends—to help with daily burdens. However, during Emilio’s treatment, Nares saw many families lacking such help, facing emotional and financial strain, with some even unable to afford food. After Emilio passed away, Nares asked the hospital how he could support families like those he’d met. When they identified transportation as a major barrier, he began giving rides himself. As needs grew, he formalized his efforts into the Emilio Nares Foundation in 2003, collaborating with hospital staff, hiring drivers, and developing a schedule. The organization’s first clients included a young boy whose mother endured an exhausting four-hour bus journey each way to chemotherapy appointments. The foundation’s free rides drastically reduced travel times, bringing vital relief. Today, the Emilio Nares Foundation provides over 2,500 rides each year, traveling more than 70,000 miles. Operating through Rady and Orange County Children’s Hospitals, the program also helps families overcome additional obstacles by offering translation services and guidance on navigating healthcare systems and insurance. Most families served by ENF live in poverty and often face language barriers. To further support children battling cancer, Richard Nares is about to embark on his 'Richard Runs California' fundraiser—running 700 miles in 30 days from San Francisco to San Diego. Nares says his work honors his son’s memory and that Emilio continues to inspire the foundation’s mission. Those interested in helping can learn more at the Emilio Nares Foundation website: www.enfhope.org.

He lost his son, Emilio, to cancer in 2000 and launched the 'Ride With Emilio' program so that no child misses treatment because of transportation problems. Now, his foundation arranges hundreds of free, clean, and reliable rides for families like Sisi’s. Silvia, a single mother of two, relies on these rides for her daughter, often needing eight to ten trips a week. She calls the service a lifeline, commending their organization and care. Nares knows these difficulties personally. During his own son's leukemia treatment in 1998, he and his wife benefited from a strong support network and job flexibility. But he saw many families who struggled alone, dealing with financial and emotional stress—sometimes even lacking money for meals. After Emilio’s passing, Nares asked the hospital how he could support other families. When they said transportation was a huge hurdle, he started giving rides himself. As demand grew, he formalized his efforts into the Emilio Nares Foundation in 2003, working with hospital staff and hiring drivers. One early family they helped had to take a four-hour bus trip to get a young boy to his chemotherapy sessions. Free rides from the foundation shortened these exhausting commutes dramatically. Today, the Emilio Nares Foundation gives over 2,500 rides each year, covering more than 70,000 miles. Based at Rady and Orange County Children’s Hospitals, ENF also offers translation help and support with health systems and insurance. Most of the families ENF serves live in poverty, often facing language barriers. Aiming to raise funds and awareness, Richard Nares is about to run 700 miles in 30 days—'Richard Runs California'—from San Francisco to San Diego. Richard says his son’s memory is the driving force behind his work. For anyone wanting to help, information is available at the Emilio Nares Foundation website: www.enfhope.org.

article_content: The Texas legislature has passed a new bill empowering state police to arrest anyone suspected of unlawfully crossing the U.S.-Mexico border. Once Governor Greg Abbott signs it, as expected, local judges may order deportation of those arrested, placing Texas at the forefront of strict state-level immigration enforcement. Mexico's government quickly condemned the legislation, arguing it risks racial profiling and could separate families. The Texas House approved the bill mainly along party lines after extensive debate, with notable resistance not only from Democrats but also from Republican Senator Brian Birdwell, who said it oversteps state authority. Texas already enacts aggressive immigration measures: busing migrants, arresting for trespass, and putting up border barriers. This new law extends the power to arrest undocumented migrants to all police statewide, not just those near the border. Offenders face misdemeanor charges and possible judicial orders for removal. Proponents contend the law is focused on border protection and contains adequate safeguards, aiming to avoid targeting long-term residents. Republican Rep. David Spiller emphasized its limited scope, while critics fear wrongful arrests, diminished trust in law enforcement, and constitutional violations—since managing immigration is usually a federal function. Legal experts and advocates highlight potential conflicts with the Supreme Court's 2012 Arizona v. United States ruling, which reaffirmed the federal government’s primary role in immigration regulation. Mexico reiterated that U.S. states cannot legally deport foreign nationals. Meanwhile, Governor Abbott’s administration plans further border wall construction and is battling federal agencies in court over border security measures. Despite these initiatives, migrant crossings remain high. A brief drop in October provided little relief to the Biden administration, which continues to face bipartisan criticism for its border policies.

article_content: Patrick McMahon, a former transplant coordinator, is suing the New York Organ Donor Network, alleging he was fired for raising concerns about the organization’s practices. The lawsuit claims that some New York hospitals, under pressure from the donor network, may be prematurely declaring patients brain dead to harvest organs. McMahon, 50, alleges that approximately 20% of patients declared brain dead still show signs of brain activity when their organs are removed. He details accounts in which doctors were allegedly pressured to declare patients dead and describes incidents where patients reportedly exhibited movement or brain function during organ procurement. The lawsuit, filed in Manhattan Supreme Court, cites specific cases, including a 19-year-old car crash victim at Nassau University Medical Center, who was reportedly still showing signs of brain activity and struggling to breathe when declared brain dead. McMahon also describes cases at Kings County Hospital and Staten Island University Hospital where similar concerns are raised. McMahon claims that the donor network operates a quota system, employs coaches to help staff persuade families to consent to donation, and awards bonuses to staff who secure the most organs. He alleges that the organization’s focus on increasing the number of organs collected may compromise proper patient assessment. Network CEO Helen Irving and director Michael Goldstein are named in the lawsuit. McMahon asserts that staff who question these practices may risk losing their jobs, as he claims happened to him. When asked about the allegations, spokesperson Julia Rivera told The New York Post that claims of a quota system are 'ridiculous.' The New York Organ Donor Network provided no additional comment, according to media reports.

article_content: Malala Yousafzai, the Pakistani teenager who survived a Taliban assassination attempt for campaigning for girls’ education, delivered her first official public address at the United Nations on her 16th birthday. In her speech to an audience including Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and hundreds of children from around the world, Malala wore a pink shawl that once belonged to Benazir Bhutto, Pakistan’s former prime minister who was assassinated in 2007. Expressing gratitude for the outpouring of support she received after the attack, Malala addressed the audience warmly, thanking God and all who prayed for her recovery. Malala recounted the 2012 attack, where Taliban gunmen shot her and wounded two classmates after boarding their school bus in Swat Valley. She told the UN that the attack failed to silence her advocacy, inspiring 'thousands of voices.' Demonstrating her commitment to nonviolence, Malala stated she holds no hatred or desire for revenge against the Taliban, emphasizing that her mission is to promote education for every child, including sons and daughters of extremists. Drawing inspiration from leaders like Martin Luther King Jr., Jesus Christ, Nelson Mandela, and Mother Teresa, Malala stressed forgiveness and peace. Malala began her activism at age 11, secretly blogging for the BBC about life under Taliban rule, which banned girls from attending school. Her father operated a school defying this edict, and Malala’s courage brought her international attention. In her 2011 CNN interview and again at the UN, she asserted the fundamental rights to education, play, and self-expression. During her UN speech, Malala highlighted recent attacks on schools and educators in Pakistan, including killings and bombings targeting teachers and female students. Malala called on world leaders to guarantee free and compulsory education for all children, presenting a petition backed by nearly 4 million signatures in support of the 57 million children worldwide denied education. Authorities previously arrested six men in connection with the attack on Malala and her schoolmates, but all were released due to insufficient evidence. The primary suspect, Atta Ullah Khan, remains at large.

article_content: A law student’s career prospects were seriously damaged after he admitted to sending racist messages on Twitter to former England footballer Stan Collymore. Joshua Cryer, 21, was arrested in January after Collymore, who is now a radio pundit, contacted police. Cryer, the son of a company director, at first denied sending the messages, claiming his account had been hacked. However, he later confessed to sending offensive tweets, aiming to provoke Collymore. Cryer, in his final year at Newcastle University’s Law School, was sentenced at Newcastle Magistrates’ Court to a two-year community order and required to complete 240 hours of unpaid work. District Judge Stephen Earl told Cryer his actions would have a dramatic effect on his future career, adding: 'You put yourself here and have to accept the consequences. I find it difficult to understand your reasoning. It was foolish, and you should have known better.' The court heard Cryer sent the messages to get a reaction from Collymore, who works for talkSPORT and campaigns against racism. One message from the law school football team captain’s Twitter account (@joshuacryer1) read, 'Has anyone ever called you Stan ****ymore.' Another said, 'Has anyone ever referred to you as semi pro as in a semi pro ****.' Collymore, who was capped three times for England and is now a presenter, shared the posts with his 230,000 followers and responded, 'Not having this anymore. Joshua, I see you’ve deleted your tweets. I haven’t. Not having it any more; it’s happening nearly every day now. Two officers from Staffordshire Police have taken a statement and evidence. I am in the process of reporting you to Newcastle Police for racist abuse, which contravenes UK law. See you in court.' After the tweets, the @joshuacryer1 account was deleted, and Cryer’s personal details were posted on football forums. At Newcastle Crown Court, prosecutor Veronica Jordan said that Cryer’s tweets were racist in nature and were sent repeatedly over several days. She described Cryer as boastful, quoting, 'I have found a new hobby.' She explained that Cryer tried to cover up his actions by falsely claiming his account had been hacked, but upon arrest, he admitted the offense and appeared remorseful. Cryer’s sentencing comes shortly after biology student Liam Stacey admitted to writing racist tweets after Bolton player Fabrice Muamba collapsed during a match. Stacey, a Swansea University student, will soon be sentenced for inciting racial hatred. Meanwhile, police in Strathclyde investigated racist Tweets sent to two Rangers FC players, and two teenagers were previously released on bail after Newcastle player Sammy Ameobi claimed he faced online racist abuse. Collymore has stated that he regularly receives racist abuse on Twitter and called for clearer legal guidance regarding online comments. 'Some people believe freedom of speech means you can say anything to anyone,' he wrote. 'You can't.'

article_content: Nigeria's election schedule has been repeatedly disrupted by court rulings, unexpected events, and litigation after general elections, leading to off-cycle (off-season) gubernatorial polls. These elections deviate from the standard four-year timetable, mainly because of prolonged legal disputes or sudden vacancies caused by impeachment, death, or resignation. Currently, states like Anambra, Bayelsa, Kogi, Edo, Ondo, Ekiti, Osun, and Imo hold these off-cycle elections. The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is responsible for organizing these polls, often rescheduled due to judicial outcomes. One major example is Peter Obi’s 2006 victory in Anambra, which pulled the state out of Nigeria’s unified election timetable. More recently, off-cycle elections in Imo, Bayelsa, and Kogi on November 11, 2023, reinforced the trend of incumbents holding significant advantages—Hope Uzodimma (Imo), Douye Diri (Bayelsa), and Usman Ododo (Kogi) all secured victories, some by substantial leads. These unsynchronized elections are expensive, with Nigeria holding the world’s second-costliest elections according to The Election Network. Many believe that the proliferation of extra elections puts major pressure on both finances and human capital. Notable figures like ex-President Goodluck Jonathan and retired diplomat Ogbole Amedu-Ode have urged for amendments to the constitution, so all election disputes are resolved before officials are inaugurated. They argue this would restore regularity, lower costs, and bolster public trust. Commentators such as Busari Dauda and Williams Akanbi blame judicial sluggishness and political gamesmanship for the current pattern, calling for legal reforms to ensure all cases conclude before inaugurations. However, they also note that unforeseen circumstances will always present exceptions. Nevertheless, proponents like Youth Hub’s Rotimi Olawale see advantages in off-cycle elections, arguing they allow INEC to better focus resources, which could translate to improved election management. The issue remains unsettled, but unless Nigeria addresses delays in resolving legal battles and the tendency toward election-related litigation, off-cycle elections will likely continue—with both positive and negative implications for the nation’s democracy.

article_content: A dispute is intensifying over whether major technology companies should pay for using copyrighted materials to train artificial intelligence systems. This issue has become more personal after Ed Newton-Rex, the head of audio at Stability AI, resigned on Wednesday and criticized the company for its stance against compensating creators. Stability AI contends, in line with other tech giants, that the financial burden of paying for such data could severely impact the rapidly growing AI sector. Generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion rely on massive datasets collected from the internet, which frequently include copyrighted works such as artwork, music lyrics, and books. Many creators argue their work is being used without permission or compensation and have launched legal action against companies including Stability AI and OpenAI. Newton-Rex, whose work at Stability AI included developing an AI music generator using licensed music, echoed these concerns in a public statement announcing his departure. He argued that companies worth billions are exploiting creators by training AI on their work without permission and that he could only support generative AI that respects creators' rights. Regulators are taking notice, with the US Copyright Office currently considering new rules for how generative AI can use copyrighted content. Still, tech companies—including Meta and Google—have pushed back, warning that requiring payment for training data would create a ‘crushing liability’ for AI developers. Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz similarly cautioned that enforcing such payments could destabilize the industry. Computer scientist Giorgio Franceschelli, commenting to Business Insider, suggested that while some see training AI on copyrighted works as falling under fair use (like humans learning from art they see online), the rationale given by tech companies doesn’t fully align with fair use’s underlying principles. Franceschelli argued that, regardless of legality, the practice is ethically questionable because it allows companies to profit while potentially threatening creators’ livelihoods. With critics of the tech industry’s approach now emerging from within its own ranks—including Newton-Rex—this latest resignation could signal a significant turning point for AI development. Newton-Rex encouraged others in the field who share similar concerns to voice their opinions both internally and publicly. Stability AI did not respond to requests for comment at the time of publication.

article_content: Massachusetts-based Altaeros Energies has partnered with the Alaska Energy Authority to bring a new renewable energy solution to remote communities: the Buoyant Airborne Turbine (BAT). These innovative wind generators are designed to float at altitudes of 1,000 feet (305 meters), where winds are significantly stronger and steadier than at ground level. The BAT employs a helium-filled, inflatable shell for lift, drawing on technology adapted from aerostats—industrial relatives of the blimp. High-strength cables anchor the system and transfer the generated electricity back to the ground. According to Altaeros, utilizing stronger high-altitude winds enables BAT units to cut energy costs by as much as 65% and reduces installation times from weeks to just days. The technology is also touted as having minimal environmental or noise impact and requiring little maintenance compared to traditional tower-mounted turbines. The first commercial BAT deployment, partnered with Alaska Energy Authority, will serve as a pilot to evaluate the turbine’s effectiveness and cost. Potential applications extend to remote and island communities, industrial operations, disaster relief efforts, and military bases—areas where access to reliable and affordable electricity is often lacking. Altaeros successfully tested its automated, airborne wind turbine at 350 feet in Limestone, Maine, and reported more than twice the power production at high altitude compared to conventional tower height. The unit was launched and recovered automatically from a trailer, demonstrating rapid deployment. Ultimately, Altaeros aims to scale its airborne technology to reduce the cost of offshore wind energy. 'For decades, wind turbines have required cranes and tall towers to access stronger winds,' said Ben Glass, CEO of Altaeros Energies. 'We are excited to demonstrate that modern inflatable materials can lift wind turbines into more powerful winds almost anywhere, providing a cost-competitive and easy-to-deploy platform.' The BAT project aims to displace the expensive diesel fuel typically used to power generators in isolated industrial, military, and village locations, promoting sustainable energy solutions.

To return to form, Honda will need to deliver competitive engine performance, especially against teams like Mercedes. Jenson Button highlighted both the challenge of competing with top teams and his confidence in the team's motivation, while looking forward to working with Alonso. Fernando Alonso, returning to McLaren after his stint at Ferrari, emphasized his strong motivation for the season and readiness for the challenges ahead. He stressed McLaren-Honda’s commitment to learning and development, expressing excitement about the new partnership and teamwork with Button.

article_content: Concerns about Kenya's human rights record have overshadowed a recent UN decision authorizing Kenya to lead a multinational armed force in Haiti to combat rampant gang violence. The operation, planned for one year, will involve about 1,000 Kenyan police officers deployed to Haiti, where criminal gangs are responsible for widespread killings, kidnappings, and sexual violence. Human rights groups argue that Kenya's past abuses must be closely examined before such a deployment. On Tuesday, Amnesty International Kenya urged UN member states, human rights organizations, and citizens to scrutinize the potential 'human rights and humanitarian implications' of sending an armed multinational force to Haiti. The UN Security Council approved the deployment, despite longstanding criticism of the Kenyan police for their violent responses to public demonstrations. In July, over twenty civilians were reportedly killed during anti-government protests in Kenya. The UN expressed concerns about police brutality and estimated up to 23 protestors may have been killed. Kenya's Foreign Minister Alfred Mutua dismissed these UN concerns as 'inaccurate,' but did not provide alternative figures. The Kenya National Civil Society Center also opposes the deployment, accusing the Kenyan police of 'extrajudicial killings' in recent protests. The organization described the police force as 'notorious for excessive use of force and responsible for numerous extrajudicial executions,' according to Citizen Digital. President William Ruto of Kenya welcomed Monday's UN vote, calling it 'overdue' and a pivotal moment in global efforts to support Haiti. In a statement, Ruto expressed his satisfaction with the Security Council's decision, citing his recent UN General Assembly speech advocating a multinational force for Haiti. He described the mission as a reflection of Kenya's moral responsibility to support its global partners, drawing parallels to Kenya's own history of struggle and support from international allies. Kenya has previously contributed to UN peacekeeping and African Union missions. A senior Biden administration official noted Kenya's past capacity to lead international security operations and its commitment to UN human rights standards. The US has pledged $100 million to support the force in Haiti. Despite this, some Kenyans remain doubtful. Political analyst Herman Manyora told CNN that many see the mission as an 'unnecessary risk' motivated by President Ruto's desire to curry favor with international powers. Manyora also highlighted practical concerns, including the language barrier—Haiti's official language is French—and the dangerous, unfamiliar environment Kenyan forces will encounter.

article_content: Investigators are examining why a Jet Airways Boeing 777-300, carrying approximately 280 passengers from Mumbai to Brussels, abruptly descended more than 5,000 feet while in Turkish airspace during August. According to reports, the captain was taking a scheduled nap (known in aviation as ‘controlled rest’) in the cockpit when the incident occurred, leaving the co-pilot responsible for the flight. The co-pilot told investigators she was occupied with her electronic flight bag (a tablet with aircraft documents) and failed to notice the significant loss in altitude. A report by Boeing, which analyzed data from the plane's digital flight recorder, concluded that the co-pilot had interacted with the aircraft’s controls prior to the altitude drop. Air traffic controllers in Ankara contacted the cockpit after noticing the aircraft had descended from its assigned altitude of 34,000 feet. Other planes were flying at the lower altitude, raising safety concerns due to crowded airspace as routes over Iraq and Ukraine are currently being avoided. Upon being contacted, the co-pilot woke the captain and the crew returned the plane to a safer altitude. However, the crew did not mention the incident in their post-flight report. India’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) was alerted only after receiving an anonymous tip regarding the descent. The DGCA has suspended both pilots while it investigates, working in coordination with Jet Airways and reviewing the Boeing report. Jet Airways stated it is conducting an internal inquiry and will cooperate fully with the investigation, reiterating its commitment to passenger and crew safety. Authorities are also examining whether the captain's period of controlled rest was permitted under the airline's regulations.

Sony Pictures Classics has finalized the release schedule for 'Freud’s Last Session,' a drama starring Anthony Hopkins and Matthew Goode that explores the relationship between psychoanalyst Sigmund Freud and author C.S. Lewis. The film is based on the stage play by Mark St. Germain, who also wrote the screenplay. Directed by Matt Brown, the movie will premiere in theaters in New York and Los Angeles on December 22, followed by a wider release in January. It will open alongside A24’s 'The Iron Claw,' Searchlight’s 'All of Us Strangers,' MGM’s 'American Fiction,' and Universal/Illumination’s 'Migration.'

Lewis (Goode) for a thought-provoking debate about the existence of God. The film also examines Freud’s relationship with his daughter Anna and Lewis’s unconventional romance with his best friend’s mother. 

Producers include Alan Greisman, Rick Nicita, Meg Thomson, and Hannah Leader. Sony Pictures Classics has previously collaborated successfully with Anthony Hopkins and Westend Films, notably on 'The Father.' International distribution rights have also been secured in Australia (Sharmill Films), Italy (Adler), Portugal (NOS), Israel (United King), and Greece (Spentzos).

article_content: The risk posed by Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) has increased significantly according to the World Health Organization (WHO), but it has not reached the threshold of a global health emergency. WHO officials state that—based on current information—there is still no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. MERS, first detected in Saudi Arabia in 2012, is related to SARS and can cause symptoms such as cough, fever, breathing difficulties, severe pneumonia, and rapid kidney failure. No vaccine or specific antiviral medication exists, and the fatality rate is approximately 30%. According to the WHO, since September 2012 there have been 496 confirmed cases worldwide, with 463 recorded in Saudi Arabia. A total of 126 deaths have been reported in the region. Experts believe camels may be the source of the initial transmission to humans. Though most cases are in Saudi Arabia, isolated infections have also been confirmed in neighboring countries, as well as in Europe, the US, the Philippines, and Malaysia. After reviewing the latest data, WHO’s emergency committee concluded there are insufficient grounds to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) at this point. Dr. Ben Neuman, a virologist at the University of Reading, described the WHO response as measured and suitable for the evolving crisis. He pointed out that while MERS is very dangerous for those infected, the general public’s risk of contracting it—even in Saudi Arabia—remains low. Global collaboration among healthcare professionals, scientists, and agencies continues to monitor and combat the spread of MERS.

A fishing trip off the Florida coast ended in disaster in late February when a 21-foot boat with four men aboard—including NFL players—overturned about 35 miles from St. Petersburg. Nick Schuyler survived by holding onto the capsized craft, while Marquis Cooper, Corey Smith, and William Bleakley went missing and have not been found.

Investigators from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission determined the accident was caused by incorrect anchoring techniques; the anchor was attached to a portside bracket, and an attempt to free it by moving the boat forward in rough Gulf waters led to the capsizing. As a storm rolled in, all four men initially held onto the vessel, but eventually became separated in the water.

Their journey started at the Seminole Boat Ramp near Clearwater Pass early in the morning of February 28.

article_content:
Reports of suicide are increasingly frequent across Nigeria, intensifying nationwide concern. Notably, Toluige Olokoobi of Edo State, known for a viral video with her son, died by suicide—reportedly in the presence of her one-year-old child—after experiencing depression and leaving behind three children.

Other recent suicides include Nigerian Army Captain Alphonsus Bazza in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, who left behind a wife and child; Terver Orfega in Abuja, 29, who ingested a lethal substance after business failure and debt; and Betwom Bitrus, 17, in Bauchi State, who hanged himself last month. In July, 72-year-old Kareem Aderemi of Osun State shot himself, reportedly after facing partial blindness and depression, while young Anambra pastor Prosper Igboke allegedly died by jumping from a building after a failed romance.

In August, bystanders intervened to prevent Lagos socialite Fareeda Abdulkabir from jumping into the lagoon off Third Mainland Bridge as she expressed distress over her marriage. The PUNCH reported 79 suicides across Nigeria in 2022, with Lagos recording the highest number; however, experts warn the real count is likely higher due to underreporting.

According to mental health experts, factors such as poverty, unemployment, hunger, insecurity, and social change are contributing to increasing mental health challenges. Social workers point to family breakdown, substance abuse, cultism, bullying, and untreated mental illness. The Association of Psychiatrists in Nigeria estimates over 60 million Nigerians are affected by mental health issues, yet only about 200 mental health professionals are available nationwide.

The World Health Organization (WHO) states suicide is the fourth leading cause of death for those aged 15-29 globally, with over 703,000 such deaths per year. In Nigeria, the ease of access to lethal means—including pesticides, hanging, and firearms—has led to government interventions like a temporary restriction of Sniper pesticide sales.

Experts emphasize that anyone, regardless of age, gender, or background, can struggle with suicidal thoughts—often signaled by hopelessness and withdrawal—highlighting the need for vigilance from loved ones and communities. WHO and advocacy groups recommend steps such as restricting access to means, sensitive media coverage, and decriminalizing attempted suicide. Ultimately, coordinated efforts among government, communities, families, and faith leaders are vital to reducing suicide rates.

article_content: Russian authorities have added Ukrainian singer and Eurovision winner Jamala, whose real name is Susana Jamaladinova, to their wanted list for allegedly spreading false information about the Russian armed forces, according to state media. The Kremlin frequently presses such charges against individuals who share details of its invasion of Ukraine that contradict the official narrative. Jamala has been openly critical of Russia’s invasion. According to the independent Russian human rights website Mediazona, she was placed on the wanted list last month, though details surfaced only on Monday. The Russian news Telegram channel Shot claims Jamala was listed for posting so-called 'fakes' about atrocities committed in the Ukrainian town of Bucha in 2022. While there is substantial evidence implicating Russian forces in the massacre during their occupation of the Kyiv suburb, the Kremlin denies responsibility. Jamala, currently in Australia, responded by sharing a photo of herself outside the Sydney Opera House, linking to coverage of the news along with a facepalm emoji. The 40-year-old fled Ukraine with her family after Russia's invasion in February 2022. She won the Eurovision Song Contest in 2016 with '1944', a song inspired by the forced deportation of her ethnic group, the Crimean Tatars, by Soviet authorities. The song sparked controversy for its perceived political message but was ultimately accepted, beating Russia to the title. Many interpreted the song as an indirect reference to Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea. Jamala continues to emphasize the importance of giving a voice to her homeland. Speaking to the BBC earlier this year about her folk album, Qirim, she said her work aims to share the truths and stories of Crimea, in response to long-standing Russian propaganda intended to silence Crimean Tatars.

article_content: Shaun Solomon, a 23-year-old retail worker from Northampton and avid Ed Sheeran fan, recently shot to internet fame after a parody video he created went viral. After sharing the video on his personal YouTube channel, it was picked up by LadBible and UniLad, two popular Facebook pages. LadBible's post drew about nine million views, while UniLad's amassed over 13 million. Alongside more than 180,000 views on Solomon's own YouTube, the combined total surpassed a staggering 22 million views in just two days. Despite enduring gentle teasing about his distinctive goatee for years, Solomon now jokes that if he shaved it off, he would be in 'deep trouble.'

article_content: European Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) have a currently known inventory of about 11,000 species and are generally considered well-researched. However, a newly described genus and species from the Geometrid moth family, published in the journal ZooKeys, presents a different perspective. The moth, named Mirlatia arcuata by a team from Germany, Austria, and the United Kingdom, represents one of the most remarkable Lepidoptera discoveries in recent decades. In the early 1980s, Austrian amateur entomologist Robert Hentscholek collected three specimens of an unidentified moth in southern Dalmatia, Croatia. These specimens were either kept in his collection or given to colleagues. Decades later, the collection was sold to Austrian hobbyist Toni Mayr, who noticed the unusual insect, which stood out from all known European species and could not be assigned to any known genus. Further investigation revealed that two specimens, a male and a female, had been given to another collector who had since passed away. The female specimen was rediscovered in 2015 at the Natural History Museum in Vienna, while the location of the other remains unknown. The unique male was later donated to the Tyrolean Federal State Museums by Toni Mayr. In 2022, a research team was formed to examine the mysterious moth, leading to its official description as a new genus and species in November 2023. It was named Mirlatia arcuata, with 'Mirlatia' derived from two Latin roots meaning 'bringing a surprise,' alluding to the unexpected nature of the find. Discovering such a large and distinctive moth in a well-studied area like southern Croatia may seem unlikely. However, as researcher Peter Huemer from the Tyrolean State Museums noted, surprisingly little research had been conducted in this region during the moth’s flight season in March. He suggests Mirlatia arcuata could be a cold-adapted, winter-active species, which might be best sought in the heart of winter. The hypothesis that the moth was introduced from other continents was rejected for several reasons. Axel Hausmann from the Zoological State Collection in Munich examined global moth records and found no similar species in cold regions of either hemisphere. Additionally, Podgora, the collection site, is not close to a major port, and maritime traffic was limited during the Yugoslavian era. Split and other Croatian ports rarely received intercontinental ships during the communist period, and Hentscholek had never collected in the tropics, eliminating confusion due to labeling errors. Despite these efforts, the evolutionary relationships of the new genus and species remain unresolved. Even its placement within the subfamily Larentiinae is tentative, supported by traits such as wing venation. Early genetic data and characteristics of its tympanal organ suggest Mirlatia arcuata holds an independent systematic position, and further whole-genome studies may clarify its classification. Biological knowledge about the species is minimal, beyond its presence in coastal rock habitats with Mediterranean vegetation. A thorough search led by Slovenian lepidopterologist Stane Gomboc in March 2022 was unsuccessful, possibly because the moth’s flight season already ended due to climate warming.

article_content: Syria’s conflict erupted in March 2011 after President Bashar al-Assad’s government—dominated by the Alawite minority—responded with a harsh crackdown against largely Sunni-led protests, which soon developed into an armed uprising. The initial spark occurred in the city of Daraa, where at least 15 children were arrested for painting anti-government graffiti. Public outrage over both the arrests and the authorities’ forceful reaction spread quickly, fueling demonstrations across the country by mid-March. The government's response included a siege on Daraa starting April 25, followed by similar crackdowns in other cities like Homs. Reports of mass arrests and torture circulated widely, strengthening the protest movement. According to Paul Salem of the Carnegie Middle East Center, the events in Daraa were pivotal, but the underlying political and economic grievances meant unrest was likely inevitable. Initially, protesters sought basic reforms, increased freedoms, a multi-party political system, and an end to emergency rule. The government attempted some reforms, but many saw these as insufficient and overdue. Calls for Assad’s resignation and demands for democratic elections soon followed. Bashar al-Assad has been in power since 2000, after his father Hafez ruled for three decades. Twelve months into the conflict, violence shows no signs of abating. The UN estimated in March 2012 that over 8,000 people—including many women and children—had been killed; opposition activists put the death toll above 9,000. Thousands more have been detained, disappeared, or fled to neighboring countries as refugees. Independent verification of events on the ground is difficult due to restrictions on international journalists. Government officials consistently blame 'armed terrorist groups' for the violence, but opposition sources accuse the regime of targeting and killing civilians. There are signs that some rebel tactics are becoming more militant, with videos showing attacks on government forces that resemble those used by jihadist groups. Many analysts underestimated Assad’s resilience. Fawaz Gerges (London School of Economics) notes that Assad has 'weathered offensives and absorbed shocks,' maintaining control with support from key military and security leaders. Unlike Egypt and Libya—whose leaders were ousted—Assad’s regime has not experienced significant defections. External actors play a major role. article_content: Sasha and Malia Obama are fans of Beyonce and Jay Z, though neither has shown an interest in politics, their parents recently revealed. In a joint interview for People Magazine, Michelle Obama shared, 'They love Jay Z. They love Beyonce. Sasha is still a One Direction fan, although Malia seems to have grown out of boy bands.' Barack Obama added, 'They've gotten to know Beyonce, and she's always been very sweet to them.' Michelle Obama recounted that sometimes their daughters hesitate to introduce their friends to their father, worried he might be too formal or ask too many questions. The girls themselves were not present for the interview, but when President Obama was asked whether he'd prefer to spend a day with the Duck Dynasty cast or with Kim Kardashian and Kanye West, he remained diplomatic. He noted, 'The Duck Dynasty family seems like a fun bunch. Kanye's music is outstanding—I have a lot of his music on my iPad. If it's a concert, I wouldn't mind listening to him.' President Obama has previously criticized Keeping Up With the Kardashians and referred to Kanye West using an expletive after West interrupted Taylor Swift at an award ceremony. Despite those past remarks, Obama avoided controversy in this interview. However, the timing was awkward for Duck Dynasty, whose patriarch Phil Robertson recently made comments criticized as anti-gay, prompting calls for an apology from GLAAD. While the Obamas' celebrity connections are popular among their daughters' friends, the President doesn't always get the same reception. Michelle Obama recalled, 'Malia had friends over, and she wondered whether to introduce them to her dad, because sometimes he gets a little formal, asking about school and their interests. She said, "I don’t know if my friends can handle that." But ultimately, she said he did well.' Barack Obama joked, 'I acquitted myself well. I did not embarrass her.' The whole family shares in lighthearted teasing of the President: 'I've got three opinionated, strong, tall women, and if they get together, they enjoy teasing me about my ears, my volume, or my fashion sense.' He credited his daughters with introducing him to Instagram and Vine: 'Technology is something they still help us older folks with. Instagram, Vine, those are things I first heard about from them.' The interview, part of People Magazine's Most Intriguing issue, briefly touched on heavier subjects such as the NSA surveillance program and the troubled healthcare rollout. President Obama expressed frustration over the Snowden disclosures—which required him to call German Chancellor Angela Merkel after it was revealed that her phone records had been collected—and admitted that the healthcare.gov signup problems were also frustrating. Looking ahead, Obama seemed hopeful about having better news to share in the future. However, current tensions persist between the White House Press Corps and the administration over restrictive access guidelines, which limit regular interviews and bar photographers from covering events formerly accessible to them. Santiago Lyon of the Associated Press criticized the policy in The New York Times, saying, 'These so-called private events include meetings with world leaders and other visitors of major public interest—just the sorts of activities photojournalists should, and used to, have access to.'

article_content: Ivory Coast entered their Africa Cup of Nations opener amid high expectations, regarded by many as strong title contenders. However, their performance against Guinea suggested they are still struggling to handle the pressure. Guinea, whose players have dedicated their efforts to a nation affected by the Ebola outbreak, exploited Ivory Coast’s familiar weaknesses despite the presence of stars like Yaya Toure, Wilfried Bony, and Gervinho. Lacking cohesion in attack and defense, the Ivorian side allowed Guinea, who had scored six goals in their final two qualifiers held in Morocco due to the Ebola crisis, to take the initiative. Mohamed Yattara delivered a powerful volley to give Guinea a 1-0 lead after 36 minutes. After halftime, the situation worsened for Ivory Coast when Gervinho—one of their more purposeful players—was sent off for an altercation with Naby Keita. Seydou Doumbia provided a lifeline, finishing a well-constructed move to equalize in the 72nd minute following Wilfried Bony’s skillful setup. Despite the 1-1 draw, coach Herve Renard, who succeeded Sabri Lamouchi after last summer’s World Cup, faces many unresolved issues. Renard, aiming to secure Ivory Coast’s first Africa Cup title since 1992, made bold decisions, notably substituting Yaya Toure late in the game. The team showed flashes of their potential even with ten men, but failed to consistently play as a cohesive unit. With matches against Cameroon and Mali ahead, Renard will urgently seek to unlock his squad’s full capabilities—a familiar challenge for coaches of this talented Ivorian side.
