article_content: Elon Musk visited Kfar Aza, an area in Israel that was attacked by Hamas militants on October 7. The visit, which took place weeks after Musk faced accusations of antisemitism, was conducted on Monday morning alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Video footage released by the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office shows Musk wearing protective clothing while touring the devastated community. Kfar Aza, located about three miles east of Gaza, was infiltrated by Hamas fighters during the October 7 attacks, resulting in the deaths of more than 100 civilians. These attacks were part of a broader offensive that left about 1,200 people dead in Israel. Israeli retaliatory strikes have since killed over 14,500 people in Gaza, according to Palestinian authorities. During the tour, Musk received explanations from an Israel Defense Forces spokesperson and other officials about the extent of the destruction, including numerous burned-out homes. Musk and Netanyahu also visited the home of Ofir Libstein, a former regional council head who was killed during the attack, as reported by The Times of Israel. The officials further visited the site where 4-year-old Avigail Idan was abducted after her parents were killed on October 7. Idan was taken hostage by Hamas but released on Sunday. Musk’s visit follows a previous meeting with Netanyahu in California in September, where the two discussed antisemitism on X, Musk’s social media platform formerly known as Twitter. Musk is also expected to meet with Israeli President Isaac Herzog, with plans to address antisemitism online. Earlier this month, Musk drew widespread criticism after referring to an antisemitic post on X as 'the actual truth.' The White House condemned the post as an 'abhorrent promotion of antisemitic and racist hate.' President Herzog’s office stated that during their meeting, the president would emphasize the importance of combating rising antisemitism online. Musk also angered Israeli officials in November by stating he planned to offer Starlink internet access to Palestinians in Gaza. Following discussions with Netanyahu’s office and Ronen Bar, head of Israel’s Shin Bet security agency, Musk clarified that he was not in a hurry to activate satellite communications in Gaza, according to N12. After visiting Kfar Aza, Musk posted on X: 'Actions speak louder than words.'

article_content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has announced new measures to phase out the use of certain antibiotics in livestock, aiming to curb the rise of dangerous antibiotic-resistant bacteria. On Wednesday, the FDA emphasized that these powerful drugs should only be used when medically necessary, noting that antimicrobial resistance is a serious global public health threat.

Many antibiotics used in animal agriculture are also critical in human medicine. The overuse of these drugs in animals can make bacterial illnesses more difficult—and sometimes more deadly—to treat in people, according to the FDA. A report released in April found that 81% of raw ground turkey tested by the agency contained antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Similar contamination rates were observed in 69% of pork chops, 55% of ground beef, and 39% of chicken samples.

Antibiotics are routinely used in livestock not only to prevent disease but also as a growth enhancer and a safeguard against unsanitary conditions. In 2011, 29.9 million pounds of antibiotics were sold for use in meat and poultry production—significantly more than the 7.7 million pounds sold for human use, according to the Pew Charitable Trusts. Dr. Gail Hansen, a veterinarian and senior officer with the Pew Campaign on Human Health and Industrial Farming, voiced concern about these practices, stating, "Feeding antibiotics to sick animals is appropriate, but routinely adding them to feed and water to promote growth or to compensate for poor conditions is not. If drugs are necessary just to keep animals healthy, it’s time to reevaluate the system."

The FDA’s new plan will address how farmers use antibiotics to promote animal growth and reduce feed costs. It also provides guidance for animal pharmaceutical companies to voluntarily change drug labels, eliminating animal production as an approved use. This step effectively makes it illegal to use these drugs solely for growth promotion. Therapeutic use to treat, prevent, or control disease will require veterinary oversight, meaning antibiotics can only be administered with a veterinarian’s prescription. Companies have 90 days to indicate their willingness to comply and up to three years to implement the changes.

Industry groups, such as the Animal Health Institute and the American Meat Institute, have expressed support for the FDA’s plan, highlighting the continued importance of antibiotics for disease treatment, control, and prevention under veterinary supervision. They believe these steps will strengthen consumer confidence and uphold animal welfare.

Conversely, critics like the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) argue the FDA’s voluntary, industry-led approach is inadequate, as similar methods have shown little progress over decades. "FDA’s policy is a hollow gesture that does little to tackle a widely recognized threat to human health," said NRDC health attorney Avinash Kar. The Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI) added that the onus is on drug companies to initiate changes, but welcomed the FDA’s pledge to monitor compliance and offer updates after the initial 90-day window. CSPI emphasized that while treating sick animals is necessary, antibiotics should only be given based on veterinary assessment, to preserve these drugs’ effectiveness for people and animals in the future.

Currently, federal tracking only monitors antibiotic sales, not actual usage in animals, making it difficult to determine where and how much antibiotics are used. The FDA retains the authority to take regulatory action if needed to protect public health. This latest step follows other recent FDA initiatives to enhance food safety, such as efforts to reduce trans fats in the food supply.

article_content: In American boxing, rematches are often seen as less exciting than original bouts, with notable exceptions. British fighters Nigel Benn and Chris Eubank nearly filled Old Trafford for their historic rematch, but the fight did not meet fans' high expectations. This Saturday, Carl Froch and George Groves will meet again at Wembley Stadium in a much-anticipated rematch, following their controversial first fight five months ago. Froch previously secured a thrilling win against Mikkel Kessler in a rematch, and expects the Wembley crowd will see an even better contest. Historically, rematches in boxing can either be letdowns or classics. The public often demands them, and Groves was vocal about wanting another shot at Froch after his TKO loss in November. The IBF ordered the rematch, and Froch noted that Groves removed a clause for a possible third fight from the contract, adding an extra layer of tension. Froch commented on Groves not granting past opponents, like Kenny Anderson, a rematch after their 2010 Commonwealth super-middleweight title bout, where Anderson, coming in as a late replacement, lost in the sixth round after an early knockdown. While Groves can point out Anderson's issues outside the ring, their rematch never happened, though Anderson went on to win the British title. Still, no rivalry captured public interest like Froch-Groves II. Both fighters are confident: Groves predicts a knockout in the third round, while Froch expects to stop Groves in the mid-to-late rounds. Looking back, some rematches have disappointed: — Benn vs. Eubank II (1993 at Old Trafford) ended in a draw after a lackluster fight. — Henry Cooper vs. Muhammad Ali II (1966 at Highbury), where Ali was cautious and won after Cooper suffered an eye cut. — Lennox Lewis vs. Oliver McCall II (1997 in Las Vegas); McCall suffered an emotional breakdown, causing the referee to stop the fight. — Ali vs. Frazier II (1974 in New York) lacked the drama of their first encounter. — Tyson vs. Bruno II (1996 in Las Vegas) saw a declining Bruno lose decisively to Tyson in his retirement fight. There have also been legendary rematches: — Ali vs. Frazier III ('The Thrilla in Manila,' 1975) is remembered as an epic, with both fighters enduring severe punishment before Frazier's corner stopped the fight. — Evander Holyfield vs. Riddick Bowe II (1993) included a memorable 21-minute delay caused by a paraglider's crash landing, with Holyfield winning after the interruption. — Sugar Ray Leonard vs. Tommy Hearns II (1989) was declared a controversial draw, although many believed Hearns deserved the win. — Sugar Ray Robinson vs. Jake LaMotta II (1943) was a brutal fight in their famous rivalry. — Arturo Gatti vs. Micky Ward trilogy (2002-2003) produced three crowd-pleasing, action-packed fights, with each man winning at least once and all bouts noted for their intensity. Froch-Groves II could fall into either category—another letdown or a classic rematch.

article_content: The winners of the 2009 Pulitzer Prizes were announced on Monday, with The New York Times earning five awards. Jon Meacham won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography for 'American Lion: Andrew Jackson in the White House.' The New York Times secured victories in breaking news reporting, investigative reporting, international reporting, criticism, and feature photography. Its work covering conflicts in Afghanistan and Pakistan earned the international reporting prize. In the arts categories, 'Olive Kitteridge' by Elizabeth Strout won for fiction, 'Slavery by Another Name: The Re-Enslavement of Black Americans from the Civil War to World War II' by Douglas A. Blackmon won for general nonfiction, and Meacham's 'American Lion' was honored for biography. Other journalism winners included the Las Vegas Sun for public service, Steve Breen of the San Diego Union-Tribune for editorial cartooning, and Eugene Robinson of The Washington Post for commentary. For the first time, all 14 Pulitzer journalism categories allowed entries from news organizations publishing exclusively online. Previously, fully online entries were accepted only for breaking news coverage and photography. While newspaper websites were eligible for all categories since 2006, fully online news outlets had not been allowed to submit entries until this year. Despite this new inclusion, no online-only news organizations won in 2009. Sig Gissler, Pulitzer Prizes administrator, noted that magazine and broadcast outlet websites are ineligible. Amy Mitchell of the Pew Research Center's Project for Excellence in Journalism stated that permitting online-only publications to compete reflects the increasing significance of online media. She cited a survey revealing some journalists worry that prioritizing speed might undermine accuracy in online reporting, but also emphasized the new opportunities presented by digital storytelling across various formats, enabling deeper connections between journalists and audiences. Robert M. Steele of DePauw University highlighted the continuing need to uphold accuracy and fairness, while acknowledging that expanding the prizes to online publications confirms the vital role of digital journalism today. David Plotz, editor of Slate, explained his publication did not apply due to its focus, but praised the overdue recognition for online journalism. Additional Pulitzer journalism awards went to Bettina Boxall and Julie Cart of the Los Angeles Times for explanatory reporting; staff members of the Detroit Free Press and the East Valley Tribune for local reporting; and the St. Petersburg Times staff for national reporting. Individual honors went to Lane DeGregory (feature writing), Mark Mahoney (editorial writing), and Patrick Farrell (breaking news photography). In artistic categories, 'Ruined' by Lynn Nottage won for drama; 'The Hemingses of Monticello: An American Family' by Annette Gordon-Reed for history; 'The Shadow of Sirius' by W.S. Merwin for poetry; and 'Double Sextet' by Steve Reich for music.

article_content: New Delhi: To strengthen the fight against gender-based violence, the Indian government has placed Self Help Groups (SHGs) at the forefront of community outreach, particularly in rural regions. SHGs are being empowered to encourage women facing violence to speak up and seek necessary support to secure their rights. The campaign aims to engage and equip the approximately 98 million women SHG members to amplify awareness around gender-based violence. Gender-based violence is not only a concern in India; it is a worldwide issue, with data suggesting that 1 in 3 women globally experiences GBV during their lifetime. In India, according to the National Family Health Survey-5, over 77% of women still do not report or discuss their experiences of violence. Marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, the Ministry of Rural Development, in collaboration with other ministries and departments, has launched a month-long campaign, ‘Nayi Chetna – Pahal Badlav Ki’, now in its second year and running until December 23. Women SHG members from various states, including Andhra Pradesh and Nagaland, have shared stories of overcoming adversity and advocating for their own rights and those of other women and girls facing domestic violence and child marriages. Officials indicate that the campaign will focus on deepening awareness about different types of violence across life stages and social contexts, encouraging GBV reporting, and coordinating support systems for safer redressal. Over the next month, gender forum meetings will be held at block and district levels, while sensitization workshops will be organized for police personnel, health workers, and other key stakeholders, according to a statement from the Ministry of Rural Development. Over 3,000 Gender Resource Centres established under DAY-NRLM at the block level are vital for helping identified women survivors receive appropriate support through structured referral plans in cases of gender-based violence.

article_content: During the Music Midtown festival in Atlanta, I was unexpectedly subjected to a racist outburst. After I spoke Spanish with guests visiting from Mexico City, a young white woman nearby yelled at me to 'go home to Mexico,' and repeated it in Spanish: 'Vete!'. Although I am a third-generation Mexican-American from Los Angeles—often considered 'too American' by some in the Latino community—this experience showed that, to others, I could never fully belong simply because of how I look. This moment echoed what many Latinos have been experiencing across the country: a rise in open antagonism toward our community, fueled by hostile rhetoric and policies. Feeling the brunt of such hatred in Atlanta was both jarring and revealing. I recalled a similar feeling from my school days, when a visiting jazz instructor dismissed my trumpet playing as 'mariachi music,' a comment for which he later apologized after my family's intervention. My father, proud of his Salvadoran and Mexican ancestry, always encouraged me to embrace our roots and the motto 'Si se puede'—'Yes you can.' Despite the hostility at the festival, the visitors from Mexico City and several bystanders offered me support. One even lifted my hand and said, 'Estamos aqui'—'We are here.' It was a powerful reminder that, no matter what others say, I am just as American and human as anyone in this country. In that moment, my presence was all the answer that was needed.

article_content: A 79-year-old Laramie man was fatally struck by a car on Saturday night while apparently attempting to help an injured rabbit on a Wyoming highway, according to the Wyoming Highway Patrol. The accident took place around 9 p.m. on Wyoming Highway 230, about six miles west of Laramie. The man, identified as William Kieren, had stopped his vehicle and was seen on or near the center line of the road when he was struck by an oncoming car. Kieren was transported to the Medical Center of the Rockies in Loveland, Colorado, where he died the following day. Authorities state that the driver of the vehicle, Samantha Brown, 25, also from Laramie, reported she saw a parked car and switched lanes to pass, but did not see Kieren in the roadway until after the collision. The injured rabbit remained alive on the roadway and was subsequently euthanized by a responding trooper. Funeral arrangements for William Kieren are pending with Montgomery-Stryker Funeral Home.

article_content:
The fund management industry continues to struggle with gender diversity. Data from September 2023 show that only 12.1% of portfolio managers globally are women—a marginal increase of just 0.1% over the previous year, according to the Citywire database. In the U.S., investment managers who are women and/or people of color manage only 1.4% of all assets under management. Progress in two critical metrics—the percentage of female fund managers and the percentage of assets managed by women—has stalled for over a decade.

This lack of advancement persists despite research demonstrating that female fund managers perform as well as, or in some cases outperform, their male counterparts. At the Global Impact Investing Network's Impact Forum in Copenhagen in October 2023, The Woman Fund team presented their insights on what it will take to achieve gender balance in fund management.

100 Women in Finance, a global nonprofit with 29,000 members in 32 locations, is working to increase female representation in fund management by raising visibility, supporting networks, and promoting professional development. However, a significant challenge remains: female fund managers often manage smaller pools of assets, which can prevent them from qualifying for allocations from large institutional investors, leaving them stuck at emerging manager status.

Alexandra McGuigan, Founder and CEO of Singapore-based Inclusive AM, notes, “As female fund managers have smaller assets under management to begin with, they get screened out of the allocation process of the largest institutional allocators and never graduate from an 'Emerging Manager size.'”

To address this, Inclusive AM teamed up with fintech firm Noviscient and institutional investor Singlife. Their goal: to channel institutional capital to diverse fund managers. Kim Rosenkilde, Chief Investment Officer at Singlife, explained that while much of Singlife’s impact investing focus is on climate and renewables, the company found compelling evidence that gender diversity in asset management correlates with strong performance. Despite the underrepresentation of women in the industry, Rosenkilde says, Singlife is committed to addressing this imbalance.

Another example of female fund managers leading in public equities is Emerge, which launched its first set of active sustainable ETFs in October 2022, all overseen by women. Prominent managers include Josephine Jimenez (Channing Global Advisors), Lisa Langley (Emerge Canada Inc.), Cate Faddis (Fernwood Investment Management), Catherine Avery (Catherine Avery Investment Management), and Jane Li (Zevin Asset Management). Together, they investigated scalable methods to identify and support high-performing female fund managers, ultimately leveraging Noviscient’s technology and regulatory infrastructure.

Instead of a traditional fund of funds, they structured a “fund of segregated managed accounts”—allowing institutional investors access to smaller managers via meaningful allocations that can be subdivided, providing portfolio oversight and transparency. Their approach focused on public equities and involved selecting female fund managers who met rigorous institutional criteria: a minimum of $50 million in assets under management, above 0% annualized returns, and a three-year track record, with bonus points for majority female ownership. After interviewing 12 candidates, six managers joined the fund.

“It is clear that for women, outstanding performance alone is not enough to draw the attention of allocators,” said Sharon Bentley-Hamlyn of Aubrey Capital Management, one of the participating managers. She adds, “Pooling our talent in The Woman Fund will help high-performing women managers gain the recognition and allocations they deserve, and encourage more women to enter the field.”

The Woman Fund’s model portfolio, created using the real track records of its six female fund managers, outperformed its benchmarks: delivering a 13.8% annualized return from 2009 to 2019, versus 11.4% for the MSCI World ESG Leaders. The portfolio also boasted a lower carbon footprint than the MSCI ACWI index and invested more frequently in companies aligned with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.

Alexandra McGuigan concluded that if institutional investors make meaningful allocations to female fund managers, it could promote gender equality and enhance the overall sustainability impact of investment portfolios.

article_content: Tal Golesworthy, a 57-year-old engineer diagnosed with Marfan syndrome, used his technical expertise to develop a life-saving device to treat his own heart condition. Marfan syndrome, a genetic disorder, weakens connective tissue and puts the main artery—the aorta—at risk of dangerous enlargement and rupture. Facing difficult surgery and a lifetime of blood-thinning medication, Golesworthy designed a custom-made knitted polyester sleeve to reinforce his aorta. After persuading doctors to allow him to be the first patient, his pioneering operation in 2004 at London’s Royal Brompton Hospital was a complete success. Inspired by the positive outcome, Golesworthy worked with surgeons to make the technology available to others. To date, more than 40 patients, including individuals as young as 16, have received tailored sleeves at hospitals in London, Oxford, and Belgium. Golesworthy now advocates for large-scale trials across Europe to compare his device with traditional treatments. Marfan syndrome affects about 1 in 5,000 people in the UK—around 12,000 individuals—causing bone overgrowth and dangerously thin aortas. Conventional surgery involves repairing or replacing the aorta and often requires lifelong anticoagulant medication to prevent blood clots. The EARS (external aortic root support) device is custom designed for each patient, using detailed scans and computer-assisted drawing. Golesworthy wanted an alternative after fearing the side effects of traditional surgery. Nine years after his pioneering operation, he reports enjoying a 'normal' life without prescription medication and relief from the stress caused by his former heart condition. Patients like Andrew Ellis, a 27-year-old athlete, have also benefitted from the invention and now live healthy lives free from the specter of major surgery. Medical advisors, including Professor John Pepper and Professor Tom Treasure, worked with Golesworthy. He promotes the device through his company, Exstent. Golesworthy lives in Gloucestershire with his wife, Teresa, but has no children, as Marfan syndrome is inherited. While the device shows considerable promise, experts such as Professor Graham Cooper caution that further evidence and trials are needed before the procedure becomes widely adopted. Traditional aortic surgery remains effective and safe, and more comprehensive data will be required to compare outcomes. Marfan syndrome is an inherited disorder marked by tall stature, long fingers, heart and eye problems, and a shortage of the protein fibrillin in connective tissue. Some children inherit it from a parent, while others develop it spontaneously. Severity can vary widely, with no cure available, so treatments focus on symptom management.

Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) has just finished celebrating its first French title in 19 years, but the club is now facing the challenge of keeping manager Carlo Ancelotti. At the French Ligue 1 end-of-season awards on Sunday—where Ancelotti was named Coach of the Year—he confirmed that he has asked to leave the club. Rumors suggest Ancelotti is a key figure in this summer’s managerial changes, with the possibility of a move to Real Madrid to replace Jose Mourinho, who may soon return to Chelsea.

“I’ve asked the club to let me go and now I’m waiting for an answer because I am under contract,” Ancelotti said, after leading PSG to both the league title and the Champions League quarterfinals. If he departs, Ancelotti would be the second major exit from PSG after David Beckham announced his retirement last week.

While Ancelotti may wish to leave, PSG President Nasser al-Khelaifi presents a significant obstacle. “I believe he may have signed a pre-contract with Real Madrid, but I can’t imagine Real Madrid would formalize this because of legal issues,” al-Khelaifi told Al-Jazeera. “There won’t be any confrontation; we just respect our principles, our contracts, and our commitments.” He emphasized the importance of honoring contracts, noting they had even offered Ancelotti another year on top of his current deal.

Mourinho's tenure at Real Madrid has come under scrutiny after a trophyless season, including public criticism of several players. Real’s recent 2-1 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Copa del Rey—its first loss to the local rival in 14 years—has fueled further speculation about Mourinho’s future, with Spanish newspaper El Mundo suggesting he could be dismissed within the week. Real Madrid is set to finish second in La Liga, trailing Barcelona by 13 points, with only matches against Real Sociedad and Osasuna remaining. Mourinho is considered the leading candidate to fill the open managerial position at Chelsea, where he previously won two Premier League titles and an FA Cup from 2004-2007.

Since November, Rafael Benitez has acted as interim Chelsea manager, guiding the club to a third-place league finish and victory in the Europa League. Nevertheless, Chelsea supporters continue to express strong support for the return of Mourinho, the coach they call 'The Special One.'

article_content: Jennie Bryant, an 89-year-old great-grandmother with dementia, died on July 5 following an alleged assault at Brockwell Court nursing home. The incident reportedly occurred during an argument with another resident on June 28, resulting in a blow to her head. After sustaining the injury, Mrs. Bryant was taken to University Hospital North Durham for treatment but passed away a week later. A 71-year-old male resident at the care home was subsequently detained under the Mental Health Act. Dr Leslie Hamilton, assistant coroner for Durham and Darlington, stated that Mrs. Bryant's death was due to blunt force trauma to the head. Investigations by the police and the Care Quality Commission are ongoing. A post-mortem was conducted by Dr Jenny Bolton on July 6, with a second post-mortem carried out at the police's request. Police arrested a 71-year-old male resident on suspicion of assault; he is now detained in a hospital under the Mental Health Act and is no longer residing at Brockwell Court. Durham police confirmed their investigation is continuing, but they have not yet been able to interview the detained individual. The inquest found that Mrs. Bryant died from bronchopneumonia linked to the blunt trauma of her head injury. A review hearing is set for December 9 at Crook Coroner’s Court.

article_content: India's central bank and the National Payments Corporation are working to enhance the country's digital currency (CBDC) by making it available for offline and feature phone users. Their goal is to make digital payments as simple and accessible as using cash. They are also focusing on enabling digital money for very specific purposes, such as targeted government benefits or allowances. Despite initial expectations, the adoption of India's CBDC has been slower than planned. Daily transactions remain well below the target, partly because the widely used UPI already offers simple digital payments and fulfills most consumer needs. One unique aspect of CBDC is its programmability—meaning digital money can be restricted for specific uses, letting authorities or businesses ensure funds are spent exactly as intended. This could be transformative for welfare distribution, corporate payments, or giving restricted pocket money. Currently, many banks lack the required systems to support CBDC features, but fintechs like Xaults are helping to develop necessary tools. Neeraj Singh from Xaults believes that once banks upgrade, the programmable aspect of CBDC will drive more widespread use. The CBDC pilot launched in December 2022 and is still expanding. Banks taking part, including Yes Bank, are taking steps to educate consumers and encourage merchants to accept the currency. The Reserve Bank is also encouraging solutions that work without the need for smartphones or strong internet connections. Industry leaders suggest that creative, high-value use cases—such as those found in other countries for trading or property deals—could spark broader adoption in India. Sharat Chandra from the India Blockchain Forum points to international examples as inspiration. CBDC is still at the early stages of rollout, so it may take time before it becomes a mainstream way to pay. But with more tailored uses and better infrastructure, it could join UPI and debit cards as a common payment tool. To accelerate adoption, the Reserve Bank of India continues to encourage banks and startups to experiment with new applications in regulatory sandboxes, aiming to find compelling uses for digital currency.

article_content: More than 1,200 First Bus drivers in Glasgow have voted to start a seven-day strike over pay, beginning 24 November. Unite union reported that 99% of voting members backed the action, with a 77% turnout. Drivers previously rejected the company's pay offer, arguing it was lower than pay rates at other FirstGroup locations across the UK. FirstGroup, headquartered in Aberdeen and running transport services throughout the UK and Ireland, saw profits rise sharply to £82.1 million last financial year. The planned strike will run from 4:00 AM on Friday, 24 November, until 3:59 AM on Friday, 1 December. It affects drivers working out of Blantyre, Caledonia, Dumbarton, Overtown, and Scotstoun depots. Separately, around 150 engineering staff represented by Unite are also due to strike on 16 and 17 November. Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said FirstGroup has the financial means to meet drivers’ pay demands, promising the union's full support for members’ efforts to achieve better pay and conditions. A First Bus spokesperson said the company had been informed of the industrial action despite putting forward an offer that would raise pay by more than 11%, exceeding inflation rates. They emphasized recent investments in electrifying the bus fleet and enhanced pay, saying these have outstripped company profits and have made the business more sustainable. The company asserts it provides fair wages and working conditions, and is seeking further dialogue with the union to resolve the dispute.

article_content: President Barack Obama departed for Camp David on Marine One Friday, but in an unexpected move, arrived at the presidential retreat by car. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney explained that the decision not to land at Camp David was made beforehand due to weather concerns. Marine One landed at an alternate site near Frederick, Maryland, and the president and his daughter, Sasha, completed the journey in a motorcade. Traditionally, members of the traveling press pool accompany the president when a motorcade is used. Consequently, reporters questioned why the press was not included in the trip or informed about the plan to use a motorcade in advance. CNN’s weather team reported that there was no severe weather in the area when Marine One departed the White House. The White House confirmed that there were no mechanical issues with the helicopter. Kristy Rossignuolo, a customer service representative at Frederick Municipal Airport, commented, 'It was a bit of a surprise because he (Obama) usually does not land here. They usually go all the way to Camp David.' Separately on Friday, a fighter under the direction of North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) intercepted a civilian aircraft near Camp David. The civilian plane left the restricted area and landed at Martinsburg Airport in West Virginia, according to NORAD. No further details were immediately available regarding the incident, which was separate from the Marine One diversion. CNN’s Jessica Yellin and John Branch contributed to this report.

article_content: Soil microbes commonly found in deserts, rainforests, prairies, and forests around the world can also be found beneath New York City's Central Park, researchers have discovered. Scientists were surprised to find thousands of different microbes in the samples they analyzed, most of which were previously unknown to science. Only 8.5% to 16.2% of the organisms found in the park soils, depending on their type, had been previously catalogued in existing microbial databases. The researchers analyzed 596 soil samples collected from across Central Park’s 843 acres. While the types of plants and animals in a particular biome are largely determined by climate, microbes are more affected by soil conditions, such as acidity and available carbon, rather than how hot or dry the environment is. This enables diverse microbial communities to thrive wherever soil conditions are varied, such as in Central Park. Noah Fierer of CU-Boulder, who led the study, commented, 'We found thousands of different organisms, and it was surprising how few had ever been described. Not only do they not have a name, but we don't know anything about them. We don't know what sort of conditions they like to live under or what role they may play in soil habitat and soil fertility.' The study revealed that the breadth of biodiversity beneath Central Park is comparable to what is found across the world, from Arctic tundra to hot deserts and nearly everything in between. According to the results published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B, only 8.5% to 16.2% of the discovered organisms had previously been entered into databases describing microbial life. Fierer, who is also a fellow at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, said, 'If you want to find unique diversity and a wide range of different below-ground organisms, you don't have to travel around the world. You can walk across Central Park.' The only area where soil microbial communities did not overlap with those in Central Park was Antarctica, where Professor Diana Wall has conducted extensive research. Fierer observed, 'No one would ever expect to find an overlap in the types of trees seen in Central Park and those in a tropical forest, but that doesn't seem to be true for the microbes living in the soil. We found all these community types just within Central Park. Below-ground biodiversity doesn't follow the same rules as the plants and animals living above ground.' Professor Diana Wall added, 'The soil microbes in Central Park benefit us, benefit soil health, and are closely linked to the beauty of the trees and other plants we see. The nation's food, cities, clean air and water, and economy all depend on healthy, fertile soils, and that motivates us to understand this fascinating hidden life beneath our feet.' The team also compared Central Park's below-ground biodiversity to 52 soil samples from around the world, including locations from Alaska to Antarctica. Again, the only place without overlapping microbial communities was Antarctica.

Sony, the film’s distributor, unexpectedly released 'The Interview' for streaming on Google Play and YouTube, making it easily accessible and reducing demand for theater tickets. Following this development, Best tried to obtain a refund, citing claims that the theater’s website stated tickets were refundable. Esquire Theatre officials denied the refund, explaining that tickets for special events are non-refundable and that reselling tickets above face value is illegal. Allyson Duncan, the head manager at Esquire Theatre, stated that Best would not be refunded because he was attempting to scalp the tickets. Theater officials instead offered to donate the $650 to charity. Best responded that, although he could not contribute the full amount, he would donate $100 in the theater’s name. The matter remains unresolved.

article_content: Craig Mahon capped a remarkable week—welcoming newborn twins on Friday—by firing the winning goal as Conference side Chester upset League Two’s Southend 2-1 in the FA Cup first round. His low shot from 25 yards out in the 51st minute sent Chester through to the next round. Dover’s Stefan Payne secured a 1-0 win over Morecambe with his fifth goal of the season, as manager Chris Kinnear attributed the victory to team confidence and competitiveness closer than many believe between leagues. Southport held League Two’s Dagenham to a 0-0 draw, keeping their hopes alive for a replay. Dartford reached the second round for the first time in three decades after Tom Bradbrook’s late strike sealed a dramatic 4-3 win at Bromley. Eastleigh progressed past Lincoln 2-1, thanks to Ben Strevens, marking their first entry to the competition's second round. Hemel Hempstead took an early lead at Bury through James Potton but Bury rallied to a 3-1 win, with manager David Flitcroft commending Hemel’s efforts. Two sendings-off doomed Barnet’s hopes of upsetting Wycombe, who came from behind to win 3-1 after Sam Togwell and Andy Yiadom both saw red for Barnet. article_content: Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, has appointed Justice Olayinka Afolabi as acting Chief Judge, effective immediately, following the approval of a House of Assembly resolution. The announcement was made by the Governor’s spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, in Osogbo on Thursday. Justice Afolabi, who is next in seniority to Justice Oyebola Adepele Ojo, was appointed after Governor Adeleke approved the Assembly’s recommendation for Justice Ojo’s suspension. The House's decision was made during plenary, and the deputy governor is set to conduct the swearing-in of the acting Chief Judge at the Executive Lounge, Governor’s Office, Osogbo. Press Secretary to the Speaker, Tiamiyu Olamide, stated that the Assembly tasked its Judiciary, Public Petitions, and Legal Matters Committee to investigate petitions against Justice Ojo, inviting her to respond. The committee has seven days to report its findings. The Assembly clarified that Justice Ojo is to step aside temporarily, not as a disciplinary action, but to allow for proper investigation, in accordance with the powers vested by the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria. The executive was urged to swear in the next most senior judge as acting Chief Judge and notify the National Judicial Council and the State Judicial Service Commission. Justice Ojo has filed a lawsuit at the National Industrial Court in Ibadan against Governor Adeleke, the Attorney General, and the Osun State Judicial Service Commission. Her lawyer, Mr. Oladipo Olasope (SAN), obtained an interim injunction from Justice J.D. Peters restraining the defendants from removing or altering her appointment, salary, or benefits pending further hearing. A similar injunction was granted for Michael Obidiya, the Secretary to the Osun State Judicial Service Commission, who is also contesting his removal. Both matters are adjourned to December 12 for hearing on the motions.

article_content: The Kremlin has acknowledged that it is 'developing military relations' with Iran, but declined to comment on US claims that Iran could supply Russia with ballistic missiles. This comes as Ukrainian forces report shooting down a 'rare' Iranian-built drone during a wave of overnight attacks. On Wednesday, Ukraine’s Air Force announced it had intercepted over a dozen attack drones, as well as a cruise missile, as Russian assaults continued. Authorities in Ukraine’s Odesa region stated that a rare Iranian-designed reconnaissance and strike drone, the Mohajer-6, was destroyed. According to the air force, the barrage originated from southeast Russia, and air defense units across several central regions successfully shot down all 14 Shahed-131/136 drones used in the attack. The X-22 cruise missile, the statement added, failed to reach its target and landed in an open area of the Zaporizhia region. The resulting blast damaged private homes, but there were no reported casualties. Ukraine is bracing for an anticipated increase in Russian strikes against key infrastructure — particularly energy facilities — as harsh winter weather sets in. Last winter, Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure left many residents without heat or power for extended periods. Since then, Kyiv has received additional air defense systems from international allies. Officials in Odesa noted that the intercepted Mohajer-6 drone was designed for both reconnaissance and attack operations, capable of carrying four guided missiles and operating up to 200 km (124 miles) for 12 hours. They believe Russia acquired 30 of these drones last year, with the first successful interception occurring in September. Iran’s military support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has long been a source of concern for the United States. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov refused to comment on White House spokesperson John Kirby’s suggestion that Iran may be considering providing ballistic missiles to Russia. Peskov reiterated that while Russia is developing military-technical cooperation with Iran, he would not address this specific allegation. John Kirby stated that the US will continue to closely monitor developments between Iran and Russia and will respond as appropriate.

article_content: A car bomb exploded in eastern Cairo on Thursday, apparently targeting the motorcade of Egyptian Interior Minister Mohammed Ibrahim, state media reported. The blast, which occurred near the minister’s home in Nasr City around 10:30 a.m., left four people injured, but no fatalities have been reported. According to the state-run Al-Ahram newspaper, Minister Ibrahim was unharmed in the incident. The state news agency EgyNews confirmed that four security personnel were injured, including one policeman who required a leg amputation. An Interior Ministry statement noted that the explosion injured security guards and several bystanders. The incident took place as Ibrahim's convoy was traveling along Mostafa El Nahas Street. Security agencies have launched an investigation, but authorities have not yet identified those responsible. Official news agency MENA cited a security source who said the device was detonated remotely. The attack comes amid ongoing unrest in Cairo, following the military’s removal of former President Mohamed Morsy in July. A government crackdown on Morsy’s supporters last month resulted in hundreds of deaths. Reporting for CNN: Hosam Ahmed in Cairo, Samira Said in Atlanta, and Saad Abedine.

article_content: Scientists warn that rapid agricultural expansion in Tanzania may create ideal conditions for human plague transmission by increasing populations of disease-carrying rats. A new study published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene by University of California researchers shows cropland area has expanded by 70 percent in recent years, resulting in plague-carrying rodents doubling in number. Rats in human settlements are especially effective hosts for plague and are more likely to encounter people, raising the risk of humans being bitten by fleas carrying the bacterium. The study links an increase in maize fields, created to support Tanzania’s growing population, to a twentyfold increase in African rat populations in northern areas. These rats transmit dangerous diseases to humans, including Lassa fever and plague. Lead author Professor Hillary Young said, 'Introducing maize production into natural areas creates prime conditions for plague transmission. Local farmers often store harvested maize near or inside homes, attracting field rats and increasing the risk of human infection. These conditions often lead to outbreaks.' Researchers warned that as more wilderness is converted to farmland, rat populations and disease risks are likely to rise. The study notes plague is less deadly than other epidemics like Ebola, but remains fatal in over 30 percent of untreated cases. Bubonic plague historically caused massive deaths in Europe during the 14th century. As Africa’s population grows and food demand rises, scientists, farmers, and policymakers must balance the need for more farmland with the risk of disease spread. Since 2000, most plague cases have been recorded in Africa. A recent Madagascar outbreak led to 263 infections and 71 deaths. In Tanzania, over 8,000 cases and 675 deaths have occurred over 30 years, according to the International Business Times. Researchers studied three northern Tanzanian regions with a history of plague outbreaks and recent maize expansion. They concluded, 'Lessons from this case are broadly relevant for understanding other zoonotic diseases during rapid landscape change.' Bubonic plague, caused by Yersinia pestis (transmitted mostly by fleas from rats to humans), killed an estimated 100 million people during the 'Black Death' in the 14th century. It can cause gangrene and painful ‘buboes’. Untreated, it can kill up to two-thirds of patients within four days, though antibiotics given quickly greatly improve survival. After the Black Death reached Europe in 1347, plague became common until the 18th century. Today, plague is rare in wealthier countries, with 90 percent of cases now found in Africa. Still, sporadic cases have occurred elsewhere: in the US, 5–15 deaths occur annually (mainly in western states); a fatal case in Kyrgyzstan occurred in 2013; and China has reported isolated rural outbreaks. The study highlights the challenge of balancing growing agricultural needs with disease prevention as populations and food requirements increase.

article_content: The first official headcount of Amur falcons was conducted in Manipur's Tamenglong district at Chuilon village on Friday. Locals from Tamenglong district headquarters, about 155 km from Imphal, reported that fewer migratory birds arrived this year compared to previous years. The Wildlife Explorer Manipur (WEM), with support from Rainforest Club Tamenglong (RCT) volunteers and forest staff, carried out the census at three roosting sites in the forests near the Barak river, working from early morning until afternoon. Drones, GPS devices, and telephoto cameras were used to assist in counting the birds. According to WEM, the final census numbers will be released after all data from the electronic devices across the sites is compiled. Due to poor internet service in the district, immediate data tabulation was delayed, stated WEM secretary Elangbam Premjit Singh. Divisional Forest Officer Amandeep, the initiator of the census, said that the data would help in analyzing the migratory patterns and strengthening conservation efforts for the Amur falcons. Before the census, WEM experts provided short-term training in bird census methods for RCT and village volunteers. Besides the census, awareness campaigns are ongoing in Tamenglong to encourage villagers to protect the falcons during their annual migration. Amur falcons, known locally as Akhoipuina or Kahoipuina in the Rongmei dialect, arrive in Manipur and neighboring Nagaland in mid-October from their breeding grounds in South Eastern Siberia and Northern China. After about a month, they continue their journey to southern and eastern Africa. A team of 11 members from WEM conducted the census at three roosting sites in Chuilon village, supported by RCT volunteers. Each group used drones, GPS devices, and telephoto cameras to record the falcons. The census team was led by Kh Brajeshkumar, who is also a member of the Indian Bird Conservation Network (IBCN), and included members trained by the Wildlife Institute of India (WII).

article_content: India will offer equal incentives for electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing to both domestic and foreign investors, according to senior government officials. This announcement comes amid concerns from Indian automakers about potential import duty concessions for American carmaker Tesla. Sources told the Economic Times that Tesla has requested provisional tariff concessions as a prerequisite for setting up a manufacturing facility in India, but the government is not inclined to grant company-specific exemptions. "The government's policy is designed to benefit the entire industry, not any single company, as there are already strong domestic players in the sector," an official stated. The government is currently developing a policy to encourage local EV manufacturing, just as US-based Tesla and Vietnamese company VinFast prepare to enter the Indian market. Though policy guidelines are still being finalized, local manufacturers argue that concessional tariffs for Tesla could put their prior and upcoming investments at a disadvantage. A senior industry executive said that while formal objections have yet to be submitted, many automakers are concerned that a reduction in import duty would give Tesla an unfair edge, despite its limited investment in India thus far. Along with Tata Motors and Mahindra & Mahindra, which already produce EVs locally, companies like Maruti Suzuki and Hyundai-Kia have announced significant investments for battery assembly plants and plan to launch over a dozen electric models by 2030. Hyundai has committed ₹20,000 crore to facilities in Tamil Nadu, while Suzuki Motor Corp (Maruti’s parent company) has pledged ₹7,300 crore for a battery plant in Gujarat. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, part of the Ministry of Commerce & Industry, is conducting high-level talks to establish a scheme subsidizing EV production linked to investment levels. Local manufacturing is expected to boost employment and reduce vehicle prices. Tesla is reportedly seeking lower customs duties on imported vehicles until its local manufacturing facility becomes operational. Emails from the Economic Times to both Tesla and the Ministry regarding comments on this matter remained unanswered as of Sunday. Consultations are ongoing to determine the investment threshold required for carmakers to qualify for the new local manufacturing incentives. Last week, Commerce & Industry Minister Piyush Goyal visited Tesla’s Fremont, California factory during a trip to the US for the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework. Goyal highlighted Indian talent working at senior levels at Tesla and growing Indian participation in Tesla's parts supply chain, with components imports from India poised to double. He also expressed well wishes to Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who was absent during the visit. Goyal emphasized that no decision has yet been made on Tesla’s entry into India. Elon Musk, after meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi in June, indicated Tesla could establish a manufacturing presence in India in the near future. Australian sport is poised for a resurgence at the upcoming Commonwealth Games, according to Olympic 100m hurdles champion Sally Pearson, after a disappointing performance at the 2012 London Olympics. Australia finished 10th in the medals table in London—seven places behind Great Britain—bringing home just seven gold medals, one won by Pearson herself.

Despite this, Australia has consistently led the medals tally at every Commonwealth Games since 1986, the last occasion Scotland hosted the event. At the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi, Australia earned 74 gold, 55 silver, and 48 bronze medals (177 total), while England placed third. In both 2006 and 2002, Australia outperformed England by significant margins.

Pearson, who now captains Australia’s athletics team, believes the nation is ready to display a new generation of talent in Glasgow. She points out the team’s 103 athletes in track and field, many of them young and upcoming. Pearson attributes previous struggles to a natural rebuilding phase following major retirements after the Sydney Olympics, noting a 14-year investment in developing junior talent. She also highlights the strength of Australian swimmers.

Despite a year disrupted by a hamstring injury and personal challenges—her aunt is currently in intensive care—Pearson remains focused on competing in Glasgow. Expressing her close family bonds, she emphasizes her determination to succeed at the Games. In Glasgow, Pearson will face England’s Tiffany Porter in the 100m hurdles and may again attempt to double up in both the 100m sprint and hurdles, as she did in Delhi in 2010, when she was disqualified from the sprint for a false start.

Australia’s chef de mission Steve Moneghetti has acknowledged that it will be a challenge for Australia to top the medal tally in Glasgow, but Pearson remains confident in the team’s prospects. The Sainsbury’s Anniversary Games at Horse Guards Parade serve as an important competition for Pearson ahead of the Commonwealth Games.

Tickets for the Sainsbury’s Anniversary Games are available at www.britishathletics.org.uk.

article_content: Arsenal vice-captain Mikel Arteta has responded to Jose Mourinho’s ‘specialist in failure’ remark about Arsene Wenger. Ahead of the FA Cup final against Hull, Arteta strongly defended Wenger, calling Mourinho’s comments unfounded. ‘If you look at everything he has done for this club, I have a very different opinion,’ said Arteta. The midfielder added, ‘I don’t like it when someone criticizes my teammates, the staff, the manager, or the club. If someone is right, maybe you accept mistakes. But when it comes in a certain way, I don’t like it. We don’t need to answer to anyone.’ Arteta also voiced concerns over Arsenal’s policy of offering only 12-month contracts to players over 30. The 32-year-old, who will discuss his future with Wenger after the final, has one year left on his contract and was not included in the renewal push that saw Per Mertesacker, Santi Cazorla, Aaron Ramsey, and Laurent Koscielny sign new deals. Arteta said, ‘I don’t assess players by age, whether it’s Tomas Rosicky or Jack Wilshere. There are many factors more important than age. For the club, age may matter, but for me, a bigger asset is someone who has played 125 games in three years, rather than someone who’s played just 25 and is 20.’ Arsene Wenger has faced pressure over Arsenal’s nine-year trophy drought. Arteta emphasized judging players by contribution, not age. ‘I understand the club’s point of view – I’m not a £25 million player because I’m not 22 anymore. But I know what I offer,’ he said. Meanwhile, Samuel Eto’o has announced he is leaving Chelsea after referring to Mourinho as a ‘fool’ following a comment about his age. Earlier, Mourinho was filmed saying: ‘Eto’o is 32 years old, maybe 35, who knows?’ Eto’o replied, ‘I am 33 years old. It’s not because a fool called me an old man that you have to believe it. And you may have noticed that the old man outperformed the youngsters.’

article_content: BRUSSELS: The Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States (OACPS) and the European Union (EU) signed a significant new cooperation agreement on Wednesday. The Samoa Agreement will serve as the legal framework guiding relations between the EU’s 27 member states and 79 African, Caribbean, and Pacific countries for the next 20 years. EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell commented, 'The Samoa Agreement brings together more than half of the United Nations members, from four continents, around shared priorities and interests.' He also highlighted that, 'At a moment when multilateralism is in danger, so many countries coming together to address global challenges is a reason for optimism.' The accord builds upon principles first established with the Cotonou Agreement in 2000, setting out common principles in areas such as human rights, climate change, and migration. Talks for the new deal began in 2018, but progress was delayed. Hungary’s right-wing government initially blocked the agreement over migration concerns, later dropping objections after assurances from Brussels. Soon after, Poland’s conservative officials raised their own objections, resulting in additional delays. The slow progress raised concerns within Brussels about the EU’s reputation, particularly amid efforts to rally support from developing countries concerning Russia’s war in Ukraine. The agreement is provisionally expected to come into effect at the start of 2024.

article_content: Andy Murray's hopes of qualifying for next month's ATP World Tour Finals in London suffered a setback after he was defeated by David Ferrer in the last 16 of the Shanghai Masters on Thursday. Murray lost 2-6, 6-1, 6-2 to Ferrer, allowing the Spaniard to move above him into ninth place in the race for a spot at the season-ending event. Only the top eight players at the end of October will earn spots at the O2 Arena. Murray, coming off a tournament win in Shenzhen and a semi-final appearance at the China Open in Beijing, started strong against the fifth-ranked Ferrer by breaking his serve early and winning the first set convincingly. However, Ferrer responded immediately in the second set, broke Murray for the first time, and quickly leveled the match. In the deciding set, Ferrer pressed his advantage with two more breaks of serve as Murray was unable to create any break point chances. With this victory, Ferrer moves closer to qualification for London, while Murray now finds himself just behind Milos Raonic, who withdrew from Shanghai due to illness, and ahead of players like Grigor Dimitrov, who also exited early. Despite this setback, Murray still has three weeks of tournaments, including the upcoming Paris Masters, to secure a top-eight finish. Other contenders for the Finals, including Stan Wawrinka, Kei Nishikori, and Marin Cilic, also suffered defeats in Shanghai. Djokovic, Nadal, and Federer have already qualified. While Murray looked frustrated after his loss, he remains in contention for a spot in London with important matches remaining this month.

article_content: A recent study suggests that growing up in the countryside may more than double an individual’s risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers found that the highest risk is among people born and raised in rural areas, rather than those who relocate to the countryside later in life. The exact reasons for this increased risk remain unclear, with experts considering factors such as limited access to healthcare, exposure to unknown substances, or socio-economic influences. Dr Tom Russ from the Alzheimer Scotland Dementia Research Centre at the University of Edinburgh, who led the research, said that further studies are underway to better understand this association. Previous investigations into whether living in urban or rural settings influences dementia risk have produced mixed results, partly due to varying definitions of what constitutes rural and urban environments. To gain a clearer understanding, researchers from the University of Edinburgh, the Medical Research Council, and University College London pooled data from dozens of studies conducted around the world over several decades. This meta-analysis aimed to provide a more comprehensive insight into how lifestyle factors may influence Alzheimer’s risk. Their findings, published in the International Journal of Epidemiology, revealed that individuals born and raised in the countryside had more than double the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease later in life. The risk associated with other forms of dementia was much lower. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia, affecting about 820,000 people in Britain. With an aging population, the number of cases is projected to more than double over the next 40 years. The disease is characterized by short-term memory loss, confusion, lack of concentration, and decline in physical abilities. The researchers emphasized the need to investigate why rural upbringing is linked to higher Alzheimer’s risk, with the goal of finding effective preventive strategies. They noted that any preventative efforts may need to begin early in life.

article_content: Air India has successfully introduced 'Maharaja,' its generative AI virtual assistant supported by Microsoft Azure OpenAI service. The system combines advanced generative AI, such as ChatGPT, and traditional machine learning to better understand and resolve customer questions, including more complex ones. Safeguards are in place to minimize biased or inappropriate responses. About 15% of queries are passed on to human agents for further help when needed. Satya Ramaswamy, Air India’s Chief Digital and Technology Officer, highlighted the company’s focus on delivering top-quality service and adapting to how travelers now prefer digital chat experiences for quick, direct support. He noted that Maharaja uses multiple patent-pending innovations, and further features will be introduced soon. Marco Casalaina of Microsoft welcomed Air India's use of Azure OpenAI, seeing it as a major shift in customer service. Forthcoming updates will offer even more personalization and a novel mix of text and visual interactions. Air India also aims to include more Indian languages and new travel-related capabilities, such as inspiration tools and easier booking, making Maharaja an even more reliable travel assistant.

House Republicans ended their Friday lunch meeting with leftover pizza but less clarity about their leadership than when the week started. After another heated debate and a third failed vote for Speaker, Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio lost the support of his colleagues, with 112 Republicans voting against him in a secret ballot. As lawmakers exited, many declined to comment to reporters, and few could predict who would ultimately become Speaker or when the seat would be filled.

It has been 17 days since former Speaker Kevin McCarthy was removed by a small group of dissatisfied Republicans. Since then, House Republicans have considered and rejected both Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jordan for the top role. In the narrowly divided House, a Speaker elected by Republicans can afford only four Republican 'no' votes. Although a majority supported Jordan in an earlier private meeting, he could not secure near-unanimous backing in the public floor vote.

The prolonged effort to replace McCarthy has stirred fears among lawmakers that no candidate can attract enough support from an already deeply divided caucus. Meanwhile, important issues remain unaddressed, such as President Joe Biden’s newly requested $105 billion aid package for Ukraine and Israel.

According to Speaker Pro Tempore Patrick McHenry, Republicans will meet for a candidate forum at 6:30 p.m. Monday, with an internal election planned for 9 a.m. Tuesday. McHenry said a floor vote on Tuesday is the goal, while committees continue working with the White House on national security. He explained the schedule gives candidates time to meet with members. Several contenders have emerged: Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia announced another run, and Reps. Kevin Hern (Oklahoma), Jack Bergman (Michigan), and Pete Sessions (Texas) quickly entered the race. Majority Whip Tom Emmer, Rep. Byron Donalds (Florida), and Rep. Mike Johnson (Louisiana) are seeking support, while Reps. Mark Green (Tennessee), Jodey Arrington (Texas), and Roger Williams (Texas) are also reportedly considering bids.

Punchbowl News reported that McCarthy supports Emmer, a former NRCC chair. Earlier this month, Emmer tried to become majority leader, but faced resistance from Trump allies who questioned his loyalty. Patrick McHenry reiterated he is not interested in the Speakership and aims to return to chairing the Financial Services Committee.

Former Speaker McCarthy declined to say if he would run again, blaming his removal on eight Republicans and expressing frustration about the party’s current division. Many Republicans left the latest meeting visibly annoyed. Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado blamed those who ousted McCarthy for the chamber’s inaction. Some, like retiring Rep. Victoria Spartz of Indiana, voiced optimism that strong voices in the party would eventually resolve the crisis, saying, 'iron sharpens iron.'

article_content: Budget retailer Aldi has secured another win in the UK supermarket price wars, being identified as the supermarket with the cheapest typical shopping basket. A recent comparison of 15 common grocery items found a £6.83 price gap between the least and most expensive supermarkets. According to mysupermarket.co.uk, Aldi offered the best value at £14.75, beating Asda by £1.87. This update comes after Asda and Sainsbury's announced a combined £450 million in price cuts recently to retain customers in the face of rising competition from Aldi and Lidl. Only Aldi had all 15 items available in its basket; all other supermarkets had at least one or two items unavailable. Tesco’s basket was priced at £17.87, Waitrose at £18.82, Morrisons at £20.10, Sainsbury’s at £20.21, and Ocado at £21.58. Items compared included milk, eggs, bread, bananas, and fish fingers, with Aldi serving as the baseline. Many supermarkets, such as Asda, Tesco, Sainsbury’s, and Ocado, offer price comparison schemes with vouchers for shoppers if their basket would have been cheaper elsewhere. However, Aldi has focused on expanding its product range and appealing to a wider market instead. The UK grocery sector has changed significantly in the past two years, with leading supermarkets losing market share for the first time. Discounters Aldi and Lidl, and upmarket competitors like Waitrose and Marks & Spencer, have gained customers. According to Kantar Worldpanel, over the 12 weeks to December 7, Aldi’s market share rose by 22.3% and Lidl’s by 18.3%, while Tesco, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, and Asda declined. Gilad Simhony, CEO of mysupermarket.co.uk, stated that mid-market supermarkets struggle to balance price and quality. He said, 'The supermarket sector has become more competitive, with retailers focusing more closely on their brand identities.' While Waitrose now emphasizes quality, Aldi and Asda have continued to focus on low prices and value. As competition intensifies, supermarkets are expected to further clarify their brand positioning to retain customers. Aldi and Lidl continue to attract more shoppers, though growth has been slower recently, suggesting that industry-wide price cuts may be influencing shopping patterns. Giles Hurley, joint managing director of corporate buying at Aldi, said the company remains committed to consistently low prices rather than short-term reductions. Essential items used in this comparison included: 4 pints of semi-skimmed milk, 6 large free-range eggs, Kingsmill 50/50 medium sliced bread, large vine-ripened tomatoes, 350g medium cheddar cheese, 250g salted butter, organic Fairtrade bananas, 4 x 125g Optifit fat-free yoghurt, 900g frozen peas, 10-pack of fish fingers, a whole fresh broccoli, 500g penne pasta, 500ml washing-up liquid, 500ml antibacterial handwash, and 9 toilet rolls.

article_content: A renewed debate is underway as Justice Secretary Chris Grayling prepares to bring a Bill before Parliament, giving MPs the option to deny prisoners the right to vote. This move seeks to resolve a protracted seven-year dispute prompted by a European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruling. The ECHR ruled that the UK's complete ban on prisoner voting is unlawful and has set a Friday deadline for government compliance. Grayling's Bill will offer several options, such as granting the vote to prisoners serving less than six months or to those sentenced to under four years. However, the draft legislation is also expected to include an option to maintain the current ban, a stance strongly supported by Prime Minister David Cameron, who has said the idea of prisoners voting makes him feel sick. Only a handful of Liberal Democrat MPs are likely to oppose the government on this issue. Ministers believe presenting multiple options to Parliament will meet the ECHR's requirement for 'concrete measures.' Critics caution that inadequate compliance could result in up to £100 million in compensation if the court deems the government's proposal insufficient. Last year, MPs rejected proposed changes to prisoners' voting rights in a non-binding vote. The ECHR's compliance deadline remains Friday. A government source stated: 'The deadline is approaching, and we intend to present a draft Bill.' Prime Minister Cameron has reiterated that prisoners should not have the vote, telling the Commons last month: 'I do not want prisoners to have the vote, and they should not get the vote—I am very clear about that. If it helps to hold another vote in Parliament to clarify the legal position, I am willing to do so. No one should be in any doubt: prisoners are not getting the vote under this government.' In February, the Commons voted overwhelmingly—234 to 22—to keep the blanket ban. This week's Commons vote could create additional tension with the ECHR, which may fine the government for non-compliance. Attorney General Dominic Grieve has warned against defying the Strasbourg court, stating its ruling creates an international legal obligation for the UK. Justice Secretary Grayling argues that Parliament can lawfully reject the ECHR's decision, but acknowledges there would be 'consequences' for Britain's position in Europe if MPs decide to defy the ruling. In 2005, the ECHR said countries may decide which prisoners can be denied the right to vote, but a complete ban is illegal.

article_content: Two children have died and two others were injured in a boat accident in the Katcha Local Government Area of Niger State. According to Garba, the boat was carrying 145 passengers from the Danbo community in Kogi State, who were returning from Katcha Market. Rescue teams have recovered one child’s body, and the search for the second is ongoing. The two injured passengers are receiving medical attention.

Gisele Mesnage, a legally blind woman from Sydney, has initiated legal proceedings against supermarket giant Coles, alleging discrimination due to persistent inaccessibility of its online shopping website. Mesnage relies on a screen-reader to navigate the internet, but she reports that Coles’ website is difficult to use—sometimes taking her days to complete a single shopping order because of repeated web accessibility issues.

Despite raising concerns with Coles since 2008, Mesnage says the problems continue, especially after each website upgrade, resulting in recurring or new issues. She states that legal action was a last resort after numerous requests for resolution went unanswered. “I’m tired of being shut out or spending literally days completing just one order,” Mesnage commented. She added that, when using her screen-reader on the site, she often receives generic error messages or no information about products, making shopping frustrating and time-consuming.

Mesnage is represented by the Public Interest Advocacy Centre and senior solicitor Michelle Cohen. Cohen argues that online grocery shopping should be fully accessible, and compares digital accessibility to physical accessibility in stores: “It's not acceptable for people using wheelchairs to be prevented from shopping in person, so why should people with vision impairment be excluded online?”

Coles has stated that it has made 'significant investments' to enhance its website’s accessibility for all customers, including those who are vision impaired, and works with industry experts to improve the online shopping experience. The supermarket says it continues to review and upgrade accessibility features, and will formally respond to the court action after reviewing documents.

Mesnage has filed two complaints regarding this issue with the Human Rights Commission since 2008.

article_content: Scientists at London’s Natural History Museum may be one step closer to discovering when and where Neanderthals and modern humans first crossed paths and interbred, thanks to a collection of ancient human fossils recently rediscovered after being misplaced for decades. These bones, excavated mainly in the 1920s and 1930s from key archaeological sites in present-day Israel, are around 50,000 years old and were initially studied by pioneering archaeologist Dorothy Garrod. After being in the possession of the Scottish anthropologist Sir Arthur Keith, the fossils ended up in storage and only reached the museum in 2001—where their significance has now come to light. The newly recognized importance of these remains lies in their rarity; very few fossils from the late Middle Palaeolithic period, when early modern humans and Neanderthals may have coexisted in the Middle East, have been found. The collection includes material from renowned sites like Shukbah Cave, known for its association with the Natufian culture, and El Wad, among others. Previous analyses of these remains by Keith and Theodore McCown were published back in 1939 but, until recently, the physical bones were largely forgotten. Researchers such as Dr. Isabelle De Groote and Professor Chris Stringer highlight that DNA analysis of these specimens could reveal crucial details about the migration of modern humans out of Africa and clarify the timing and geography of their interactions with Neanderthals. The current study also demonstrates how careful research on archived collections can lead to major scientific breakthroughs even without new digs. Additionally, recent genetic studies—conducted at institutions like the University of Edinburgh and Wageningen University—show that modern Europeans and Asians carry up to 2% Neanderthal DNA, further evidence that these two groups met and mixed after leaving Africa. This supports the theory that there was direct interbreeding in Eurasia, rather than both groups merely sharing an ancient African ancestor.

article_content: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Shaktikanta Das has warned both banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) to avoid excessive risk-taking in their lending activities. His remarks follow the RBI's recent tightening of rules for personal loans, prompted by fast-growing lending volumes and rising risks. At a Mumbai event on Wednesday, Das cautioned that growth in individual loans should be kept sustainable and urged lenders to steer clear of any form of exuberance. The central bank recently increased the capital banks must set aside when issuing personal loans and loans channeled through NBFCs, in response to soaring demand for small consumer credits. This is expected to raise borrowing costs and slow consumer loan expansion. Das emphasized that these measures are both preemptive and specifically targeted. He also advised financial institutions against overly depending on algorithm-based models, underscoring the need for careful assessment in lending decisions. The new regulations do not apply to home, vehicle, or gold loans, as no significant stress has been observed in these areas, according to the governor. However, he pointed out potential risks resulting from the close ties between banks and NBFCs, recommending that NBFCs broaden their funding sources. Das further addressed microfinance institutions, urging them to ensure that their loans remain affordable for lower-income borrowers, as some MFIs have reportedly maintained high interest margins. He stressed that while MFIs have some discretion in setting rates, this flexibility should be exercised responsibly.

Nouhad Halawi, a Christian saleswoman at Heathrow Airport’s World Duty Free shop, has launched a legal challenge against her former employers, alleging religious harassment by some Muslim colleagues. Halawi was dismissed in July after 13 years with the company, following her reports of bullying by a small group she described as promoting fundamentalist Islam.

Halawi alleges the harassment included pressure to read Islamic literature, derogatory remarks about Christianity, and intimidation of Christian staff. After she defended a fellow Christian colleague, five Muslim coworkers accused her of being anti-Islamic following a workplace dispute. Halawi was suspended and later informed her Heathrow security pass was revoked for 'extremely inappropriate' remarks, making her ineligible for work.

A petition signed by 28 colleagues, some of whom are Muslim, claimed Halawi was dismissed based on false accusations. Halawi’s case for unfair dismissal is backed by the Christian Legal Centre and represented by barrister Paul Diamond. Caroline South Associates and World Duty Free, her employers, declined comment due to ongoing legal proceedings.

Separately, Jewish businessman Arieh Zucker has alleged repeated profiling by security staff at the airport, suggesting he is being discriminated against, and is considering legal action.

article_content: Border guarding forces from India and Nepal will hold a three-day bilateral meeting in Delhi starting Monday to discuss ways to curb trans-border crimes and ensure timely sharing of intelligence, an official said. The seventh annual coordination meeting will be led by India's Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) Director General Rashmi Shukla and Nepal's Armed Police Force (APF) Inspector General Raju Aryal. The talks will take place in Delhi from November 6 to 8. According to an official statement, these meetings between the heads of both forces provide a crucial platform to address border-related issues. The SSB and APF delegations aim to enhance coordination for more effective management of the 1,751 km open and unfenced India-Nepal border. The discussions will focus on developing mechanisms to combat trans-border crime and ensure quick exchange of critical information. The SSB is a central armed police force under the Union Home Ministry, responsible for guarding the India-Nepal border. These annual talks have been held alternately in India and Nepal since 2012.

City had achieved nine straight wins with their Boxing Day victory over West Brom, equaling a previous record from the 2011-12 season and 1912.  Despite Burnley’s 1-0 loss to Liverpool just 48 hours earlier, the team did not appear fatigued. Manager Sean Dyche named an unchanged side and did not make any substitutions. As City's momentum slowed, Burnley seemed to grow stronger.
