The ongoing Chicago teachers strike is not a typical labor dispute over pay. While city officials have offered educators a 16% salary increase over four years—with the current average salary at $74,236—both sides acknowledge that compensation is not the main issue. Instead, the strike centers on disagreements between teachers unions and city leadership, especially over accountability measures and education reform policies introduced by Democrats, including President Obama and Education Secretary Arne Duncan. The unions have long resented Duncan, who served as Chicago’s schools chief and implemented policies echoed in national reforms like 'No Child Left Behind' and 'Race to the Top,' which tie teacher evaluations and school funding to student performance on standardized tests.

This discord highlights divisions within the Democratic Party, pitting education reformers against union advocates. Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a close ally of the Obama administration, faces union opposition after taking a tough stance on these reforms. The strike affects over 350,000 students in Chicago’s public schools, attracting national attention and putting pressure on Democratic leaders during an election season. Organized labor’s support for President Obama has cooled, partly because some unions believe their concerns are not being addressed.

Republican candidate Mitt Romney has criticized the strike, reflecting general Republican opposition to public sector unions. The author notes that decisive action may be needed from Mayor Emanuel, referencing the 2009 mass firing (and subsequent rehiring) of teachers in Central Falls, Rhode Island. The commentary argues that prolonged strikes harm students and disrupt education, calling for Emanuel to confront the union and restore stability. (Opinions are those of Ruben Navarrette.)

U.S. diplomacy in the Middle East and Israel's ongoing conflict in Gaza are closely linked, with Washington providing political and military backing to Israel. Since Israel began its latest offensive in Gaza a month ago, the U.S. has sent two aircraft carriers to the region to reassure allies and deter opponents. Secretary of State Antony Blinken has visited the region multiple times, meeting with Arab leaders to discuss the conflict. During these visits, he consistently reaffirmed U.S. support for Israel and shifted focus from calls for a ceasefire toward prospects for a longer-term peace.

Arab officials have expressed strong condemnation of Israeli military actions, citing a rapidly rising death toll in Gaza, now reportedly over 10,000. Many are frustrated by the U.S.'s reluctance to call for an immediate ceasefire. While Blinken's calls for future peace fell flat with most Arab leaders unwilling to discuss post-war scenarios, he received a warmer reception from the Palestinian Authority (PA) in Ramallah. PA President Mahmoud Abbas indicated openness to participating in a post-war Gaza administration as part of a broader peace agreement.

However, the article questions the PA’s stance, noting it has both condemned Israeli actions at the United Nations and restricted internal dissent within Palestinian territories. The PA has also remained largely silent amid increased Israeli military activity and settler violence in the West Bank. The author expresses skepticism about the PA's ability to govern Gaza effectively and about claims that Israel intends to allow a fully independent Palestinian state.

The piece draws parallels with past U.S.-led peace initiatives—such as President George W. Bush’s two-state vision—which failed to resolve the underlying conflict, leading instead to continued occupation and violence. The article concludes that, given ongoing U.S. support for Israel and the lack of major Israeli political parties willing to compromise on settlements or occupation, meaningful progress toward a two-state solution remains unlikely. Instead, it argues that only widespread resistance combined with concerted international involvement might bring about substantive change.

article_content: Demand for 'phablets'—large devices combining phone and tablet capabilities—is on the rise in Australia. While mobile phones have been shrinking since the large portable models of 1987, recent research suggests Australian users now prefer larger screens, as more time is spent browsing and using apps than making calls. The 'phablet' segment, which refers to devices with screens between 5.5 and 6.9 inches, is projected to grow. Technology research firm Telsyte predicts that by 2016, about 20% of Australian smartphone users will use phablets, a significant increase from less than 5% currently. This expected growth largely depends on Telsyte's forecast that Apple will launch a 5.5-inch iPhone 6 later this year. Foad Fadaghi, managing director at Telsyte, told Daily Mail Australia, 'We think the arrival of an Apple phablet could spur the market to grow faster than it otherwise would. Apple has a strong following and repeat purchase intention among its users.' Fadaghi noted the survey showed consumers want larger screens than what the current iPhone offers; about 40% of those interested in the iPhone 6 said they prefer or would only buy it if it has a larger display. The research also found that one in five Android users not planning to buy an iPhone would reconsider if a larger screen iPhone 6 became available. Fadaghi explained that people’s smartphone usage has changed since 2007: 'When the iPhone first launched, smartphones were primarily used as phone handsets, since there weren’t as many apps or websites. Now we use them more like mini computers in various facets of our lives.' 'The share of phone calls has declined compared to browsing, app use, and video consumption.' Despite improved usability, larger devices can be inconvenient to carry. Fadaghi mentioned that the practicality of larger screens might be an issue for activities like running or fitting into tight clothes. He also pointed out that phones are becoming thinner and lighter thanks to the miniaturization of internal components.

article_content: A rare bottle of Lowenbrau lager recovered from the Hindenburg disaster and the original passenger list from the ill-fated airship are among 15 tons of airship memorabilia set for auction. British airship enthusiast David Kirch, 75, is selling close to 600 items at the end of the month across four auctions, with the collection expected to reach £1 million. The unopened Lowenbrau lager bottle, salvaged from the Hindenburg, is one of only six known survivors and could sell for up to £6,000. The auction features the rare passenger list distributed to the Hindenburg’s 56 passengers, including boxer Max Schmeling, who was returning to Germany after defeating Joe Louis. Memorabilia also includes letters from Lady Grace Drummond-Hay, the first woman to fly around the world by airship. The beer bottle, with a scorched label and missing foil, remains sealed. Fireman Leroy Smith found six bottles at the crash site, buried them, and later retrieved them—keeping one and giving away five. Ninety-seven people were onboard the Hindenburg; 35 died in the 1937 disaster, including one ground crew member at the Lakehurst, New Jersey, site. The disaster ended the airship era. Kirch's collection is being sold by Wallis and Wallis in Lewes. Notable items include a clockwork airship toy with a yellow wind-up propeller (£1,500 estimate) and a first edition of Lady Drummond-Hay's book, 'The First Trans-Oceanic Voyage of an Airliner.' Previous auctions realized £220,000 (March) and £80,000 (July), while the next sale on November 28 is expected to bring in £160,000. Auctioneer Glenn Butler stated: 'There are 596 lots this time, with several star items that could draw big bids. The story behind the Hindenburg beer bottle and Lady Drummond-Hay memorabilia should attract collectors.' Lady Drummond-Hay’s auction lots include her book co-written with Karl H. Von Wiegaud, her 1930 pan-America flight ticket, and personal letters. Each lot is valued between £100 and £200. article_content: On the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People, India reaffirmed its longstanding support for the Palestinian people and advocated for a negotiated two-state solution. Addressing the United Nations General Assembly, India’s permanent representative to the UN, Ruchira Kamboj, highlighted India’s deep historical ties and consistent support for Palestine’s pursuit of statehood, peace, and prosperity. Kamboj emphasized India’s zero-tolerance policy toward terrorism and stated that adhering to international humanitarian law is a universal obligation. She strongly condemned civilian deaths in the conflict, describing such losses as unacceptable, and called on all parties to act responsibly amid the ongoing humanitarian crisis. She urged for collective international efforts to de-escalate tensions and ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid to the people of Palestine, noting that humanitarian pauses are crucial for timely and continuous relief. India has sent 70 tonnes of humanitarian supplies, including 16.5 tonnes of medicines and medical equipment, to Palestine. Kamboj acknowledged that the immediate trigger for the current crisis was the terror attacks in Israel on October 7, unequivocally condemning the violence and stating there is no justification for terrorism or hostage-taking. Expressing concern for hostages held in Gaza, Kamboj called for their immediate and unconditional release. She also noted that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar have maintained close contact with leaders in the region and globally, stressing the importance of preventing escalation, ensuring continued aid, and working toward restoring peace and stability. Kamboj reiterated India’s commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict through dialogue and diplomacy, urging all parties to avoid violence, lower tensions, and foster conditions for peace and renewed direct negotiations. She reaffirmed India’s support for a negotiated two-state solution, leading to a sovereign, independent, and viable Palestine existing in peace alongside Israel within secure and recognized borders. Concluding, Kamboj emphasized India’s ongoing development partnership with Palestine, supporting sectors such as health, education, women’s empowerment, entrepreneurship, and information technology. She confirmed India’s continuing humanitarian assistance and reaffirmed India’s commitment to a just, peaceful, and lasting solution to the Israel-Palestine issue, asserting that a two-state solution, reached through direct and meaningful negotiations, can bring lasting peace.

article_content: A new study projects that, if fossil fuel use continues at the current pace, the world will likely surpass the internationally agreed 1.5°C global warming threshold in just over five years—sometime in early 2029. This new estimate moves the timeline three years closer than previously thought to reaching this critical climate milestone. Crossing the 1.5°C threshold, relative to the 1800s, significantly raises the risk of environmental catastrophes—including the loss of most coral reefs, the potential for irreversible melting of key ice sheets, and dramatic increases in water shortages, heat waves, and deaths from extreme weather, as reported by the United Nations. The new, earlier estimate is influenced by progress in reducing air pollution from aerosols. Though aerosols, such as tiny smoky particles, are hazardous, they also slightly cool the planet and mask some effects of burning fossil fuels. While cleaning up aerosol pollution helps improve air quality, it also means the planet warms more rapidly without this temporary cooling effect. The study, published Monday in Nature Climate Change, recalculates the global 'carbon budget'—the amount of greenhouse gases that can be emitted and still have a 50% chance of keeping warming under 1.5°C since pre-industrial times, as set by the 2015 Paris Agreement. Over the last decade, the world has already warmed on average by 1.14°C (2.05°F) since the 19th century, and last year warmed by 1.26°C (2.27°F). This year is expected to surpass that, according to scientists. According to the study, the carbon budget now stands at 250 billion metric tons, with global annual emissions exceeding 40 billion metric tons and continuing to rise. This leaves roughly six years—but that countdown started in January 2023, so only about five years remain. Study lead author Robin Lamboll, a climate scientist from Imperial College London, noted that exceeding the 1.5°C threshold won't mean immediate defeat in fighting climate change, but it will make achieving the limit much harder. A 2021 United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report set the carbon budget at 500 billion metric tons, pointing toward mid-2032 for exceeding 1.5°C. A newer update aligns with Lamboll's findings, though Lamboll's analysis uses more recent data and improved methods, according to IPCC scientist Valerie Masson-Delmotte. The major difference in recent studies is the larger reduction in aerosols—generated by wildfires, sea spray, volcanoes, and fossil fuel burning—which briefly cool the planet but also obscure the full impacts of greenhouse gas emissions. Both the reduction of carbon emissions and aerosols are accounted for in updated climate models. Lamboll emphasized that depleting the carbon budget doesn't mean the 1.5°C threshold will be reached exactly at that point—it could happen sooner or decades later, but risk increases as the budget runs out. The authors stress that passing the 1.5°C carbon budget does not mean there is no time left to act. The study estimates that the carbon budget to limit warming to 2°C (3.6°F)—with a 50% chance—is 1,220 billion metric tons, or about 30 years at current emissions rates. Co-author Christopher Smith, a University of Leeds climate scientist, said limiting warming even to just above 1.5°C is preferable to allowing temperatures to reach 2°C, and that the effort for every tenth of a degree matters. Bill Hare of Climate Action Tracker observed that surpassing 1.5°C doesn't trigger instant catastrophe but does mark a significant increase in risk. With climate talks approaching in Dubai, leaders maintain that holding the line at 1.5°C is still possible, though Lamboll noted it is technically feasible but politically unlikely. Glen Peters of Norway's CICERO said the carbon budget for 1.5°C is now so small it has become almost symbolic, urging quick action. Piers Forster, another University of Leeds climate scientist, advised people not to panic but to take immediate action, noting rapid efforts can halve the rate of warming this decade.

article_content: The CEO of APX Operating Co., doing business as Boomer Parks, oversees operations in the family entertainment center (FEC), water park, and amusement park sectors. Weather significantly affects the operations and profitability of FECs. With hotter summers and more extreme weather, thorough planning is crucial to success. Excessive heat, heavy rainfall, snowstorms, and wildfires causing poor air quality can all disrupt business, highlighting the ongoing need for preparation. Drawing from experience as an Eagle Scout, and as an FEC operator, the motto 'Be prepared' is integral to daily operations. Proactive planning directly influences safety, staffing, and sales. Here are key considerations for FEC operators: Stay flexible when weather conditions change. While some operators may decide to close during bad weather, it's important to consider opportunities instead. For example, Florida FECs operate through brief rain showers, while in drier areas like California, rain can cause greater disruptions. It is essential to monitor local weather and respond accordingly. Many operators do not adjust staffing levels quickly enough when adverse weather is forecasted. If cancellations occur, reduce staff and operating hours immediately, but consider if the weather can be used to the center's advantage. Chilly evenings can be great for promoting warm beverages by a fire pit, while hot days invite guests to cool off indoors. Rainy days are an opportunity for families to enjoy indoor games. Positioning your FEC as a refuge from the weather can boost revenue. Develop marketing and social media templates in advance to more quickly respond to shifting conditions. Prioritize guest and staff safety and comfort, especially for outdoor activities like miniature golf, kiddie rides, batting cages, or go-karts. Address extreme heat with shade structures, awnings, umbrellas, or misting systems, and provide hydration stations. Selling personal fans, sunglasses, hats, and sunscreen can yield additional income. Ensure staff stay hydrated and comfortable with suitable uniforms, frequent breaks, and appropriate gear for all weather conditions, some of which can be branded and sold to guests. During wildfires or when air quality is poor, protect staff and focus on indoor attractions such as arcades or laser tag, which can provide climate-controlled fun. Use pre-planned advertising to promote these options in real time. In summary, having a detailed plan for any type of weather ensures smoother operations and increased profitability. Prepare strategies for minor and major weather events, monitor conditions closely, and be ready to act quickly. Preparedness can drive both safety and profits. article_content: Sam Burgess has expressed his disappointment at missing the 2014 Four Nations Series but still hopes to contribute to the England team as they prepare to face Samoa. Burgess is recovering from a fractured eye socket and cheekbone, injuries he sustained early in his man-of-the-match performance for South Sydney during this month’s NRL Grand Final. However, he was already ruled out of England’s Four Nations campaign after signing a three-year contract with Bath Rugby Union. Burgess, who will be introduced by the Aviva Premiership club next week, was described as emotional when he addressed the England squad on Thursday, just after becoming the first English winner of the RLIF award. ‘He presented me with my shirt, which was a huge honor,’ said Hull forward Westerman, speaking from Brisbane. ‘Growing up, I played against him. He’s always been a fantastic player, but what he did in the Grand Final and throughout his career is amazing. It was a proud moment for me.’ Burgess played the entire 80 minutes of the NRL Grand Final with his injuries. ‘He gave a lot of advice to the group and everyone appreciated it. It was emotional for him; he wishes he was out there playing with us.’ Westerman, 24, is a year younger than former Bradford forward Burgess and will make his England debut in place of injured captain Sean O’Loughlin, his roommate during England’s camp at Sanctuary Cove Golf and Country Club on Queensland’s Gold Coast. Chosen by head coach Steve McNamara as a direct replacement for O’Loughlin—who is expected to be fit for England’s next match against Australia in Melbourne—Westerman is determined to fight for his place on the team. Burgess previously scored a try for England against New Zealand in the 2013 Rugby League World Cup semi-final. ‘It’s been great rooming with Lockers,’ said the former Castleford forward. ‘He’s very professional and a great player, someone I’ve always looked up to. I try to play like him. I’ve got my opportunity this week and I’ll do my best. Hopefully I’ll play well enough to keep my place next week. Lockers is one of the best loose forwards in the world, but if I perform well, it’s up to Steve to decide the line-up.’ Westerman, who has had an outstanding year with Hull FC in 2014, is the club’s only representative in the England squad but will reunite on Saturday with former teammates Michael Shenton, Daryl Clark, and Brett Ferres. ‘I played with Shenny and Daryl at Cas and Brett as well,’ he added. ‘It’ll be good to share the field with them again. I was thrilled to be selected for the initial squad, and being picked to start is a dream come true. I want to make the most of this opportunity. Playing in the stadium will be emotional, but it’ll be a great day, especially for my family. It’ll be a very proud day.’

article_content: Funding for the Education Department could soon be reduced, putting key student-loan programs at risk. The House Appropriations Committee has already passed seven out of twelve funding bills for federal agencies for the next fiscal year. Details recently released for one of the remaining bills—the Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies bill—show significant proposed cuts. Federal Student Aid (FSA), which manages student-loan repayment and servicing, is a main target. The committee proposes funding FSA at $1.8 billion, which is $264 million below its current level and nearly $884 million less than what President Biden requested. These cuts could disrupt several Education Department initiatives intended to support borrowers, such as streamlining the borrower defense to repayment process. This program allows students who believe they were defrauded by their school to apply for loan forgiveness. Republican lawmakers have inserted language into the bill prohibiting funds from being used to improve the borrower defense program. The committee also plans not to provide additional funding for the new SAVE income-driven repayment plan, which aims to make monthly loan payments more affordable. These proposed cuts are coming just over a month after federal student-loan borrowers began repaying loans again, following a pause of more than three years. Since payments resumed in October, millions of borrowers have experienced issues like late billing statements and inaccurate account information. Both loan servicers and the Education Department have said that increasing FSA funding is crucial to managing the complex transition back to repayment. However, GOP appropriators argue that the Department diverted taxpayer money to costly, partisan student-loan policies instead of preparing for an efficient resumption of payments. They also criticized the Department for repeatedly delaying return-to-payment deadlines, claiming this created uncertainty. Virginia Foxx, the top Republican on the House education committee, told Insider she believes FSA does not need additional funding. She stated that the Department should operate within its means and that most federal agencies are already overfunded. Despite these debates, funding for federal student aid remains a top concern. Deputy Under Secretary of Education Ben Miller said the Department has sought increases for FSA, but currently lacks the resources to hire additional staff or expand key programs.

article_content: The Anti-Crude Oil Theft Patrol Team from the Nigerian Navy’s Forward Operating Base in Igbokoda, Ondo State, has arrested and destroyed 15,775 litres of illegally refined diesel (automotive gas oil). The operation took place in Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area, on Sunday. According to Commander Humphrey Nnaji, the Executive Officer of the Base speaking on behalf of Commanding Officer Captain Wasuku Alushi, the destroyed products were valued at millions of naira. The action was in line with the Joint Task Force’s Operation Delta Safe (OPDS) mandate. Commander Nnaji explained that the team, acting on credible intelligence, intercepted a wooden boat (often called a Cotonou boat) loaded with crude oil, about 12 nautical miles off the coast of Ojumole and Obe communities in Ilaje. The crew abandoned the vessel on sighting the Navy. He reiterated the base’s commitment to eradicating crude oil theft and related crimes in the region. The Navy plans to strengthen intelligence gathering, surveillance, and increase deployment at key chokepoints within their area of operation. Within six weeks of the current Commanding Officer’s assumption of duty, the base has achieved significant successes in arresting and destroying illicit products as directed by OPDS. Court hearings began Friday in Madrid for 11 people, including two Spanish professional football players and a Serb-French football agent, after their recent arrests on cocaine smuggling charges, according to a police source quoted by CNN. Spanish police allege the group exploited their football contacts and trips to Latin America to organize the trafficking of cocaine from Argentina to Spain.

Authorities carried out arrests mainly in Madrid on Thursday, seizing 600 kilograms (1,320 pounds) of cocaine, which they say was shipped from Argentina earlier this month. The suspected head of the operation is Zoran Matijevic, a Serb-born football agent and French citizen, police say. Other alleged participants include Pedrag Stankovic, a former player for second-division Hercules in Alicante; Carlos de la Vega Diaz, a current player for Rayo Vallecano in Madrid; and Pablo Acosta, a football agent.

The investigation had started in mid-2008 when police began tracking drug smuggling routes from South America to Spain. The cocaine—divided into 45 packages—was hidden within wind farm equipment and shipped from an Argentine port in February. It transited through Tangiers, Morocco, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar, and arrived at the port of Algeciras in southern Spain.

The shipment was transported by truck to Madrid, but before the suspects could claim and distribute the cocaine, police intervened, arresting seven people in Madrid, three in Valencia, and one in Alicante. The suspects reportedly include a Peruvian national. Authorities emphasize that Spain's vast Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines make it a major entry point for drugs intended for Spain or the wider European Union.

article_content: Researchers at the University of British Columbia have found that babies as young as nine months can differentiate between individuals who are similar to them and those who are not. The study revealed that infants tend to favor those who are kind to similar individuals and even seem to prefer when dissimilar individuals are treated less favorably. Led by psychologist Professor Kiley Hamlin, the team observed babies first choosing between crackers and green beans. Afterwards, the infants viewed a puppet show in which one puppet shared their food choice while another had a different preference. Additional puppets either helped, harmed, or stayed neutral toward the similar or dissimilar characters. When asked to select a favorite, the babies showed a strong preference for puppets that supported those like themselves and were antagonistic toward the differing puppet. In some cases, infants showed signs of affection toward the familiar puppet. According to Professor Hamlin, these behaviors are early signs of social bias, a tendency that is observed in adults as preferences for those with shared characteristics. However, Hamlin warns that such biases, if unaddressed, can lead to negative social outcomes. She stresses that while these biases appear early, they do not make divisive behavior inevitable. The study emphasizes the importance of social education and intervention to help counteract these natural preferences. Full findings are published in the Association for Psychological Science journal.

Player of the match van der Dussen noted how the middle-order built on the platform set by him and de Kock to reach an imposing total. New Zealand captain Tom Latham admitted that his team struggled to recover from South Africa's massive partnership and were unable to establish strong batting partnerships themselves. The result marks a significant step for South Africa as they aim for a semifinal spot in the tournament.

article_content: Recent Israeli military actions in Gaza have triggered widespread criticism from the Arab public, but Arab governments have mostly responded with limited measures. Unlike previous conflicts, this escalation has raised concerns about broader regional impacts. Clear actions from Arab leaders were mainly prompted by popular outrage, but their official responses remained largely rhetorical. At an Arab League meeting on October 11, foreign ministers condemned attacks on civilians on both sides, placing both Palestinian resistance groups and Israeli forces on similar ground, without detailed condemnation. These statements coincided with renewed Israeli offensives, prompting analogies to the 1948 Palestinian exodus. The bombing of al-Ahli hospital in Gaza on October 17, said to have killed about 470 Palestinians, intensified international and regional anger, leading Arab states to push for a United Nations resolution urging an immediate humanitarian truce. Although the resolution drew significant support, it did not impact Israel’s military plans, which continued despite international pressure. Since Egypt signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, Arab government support for the Palestinian cause has generally diminished. Key setbacks include the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon and the resulting shifts in regional alliances. A series of subsequent wars and uprisings further disrupted Arab unity on this issue. While Arab leaders often express support for Palestinian rights, their actions frequently do not match their statements. Utilizing the Palestinian cause for domestic legitimacy is common, but meaningful support is rare. This trend allowed Iran and Turkey to exert more regional influence as Arab states sometimes sought new alliances — such as with Israel — in hopes of gaining external security assurances, which have not always delivered real stability. Some Arab governments blame Iran and Hamas for escalating conflict, viewing their actions as attempts to undermine new relationships with Israel and incite further unrest. Still, widespread protests across Arab countries demonstrate strong popular backing for Palestinians and displeasure with government inaction. Observers warn that continuing limited official action may lead to greater instability if public discontent grows. The analysis calls on Arab leaders and the Palestinian Authority to reevaluate ties with Israel and adopt stronger measures to protect Palestinian civilians, emphasizing regional unity as the best means to curb further violence and foreign intervention.

Hundreds of thousands of people in England and Wales are set to receive free access to “life-changing” diabetes technology over the next five years via the NHS. Experts announced on Tuesday that hybrid closed-loop insulin pumps, often called “artificial pancreas” devices, are a cost-effective solution and should be rolled out for many people with Type 1 diabetes. These systems continuously monitor blood sugar and automatically deliver insulin, offering better glucose control than manual injections according to research. This could help people stay healthier for longer by preventing serious and costly complications from high blood sugar. 

Type 1 diabetes occurs when the body doesn’t make enough insulin, a hormone responsible for moving sugar from the bloodstream into cells. This differs from Type 2 diabetes, which involves reduced sensitivity to insulin—about 90% of diabetics have Type 2. For people with Type 1 diabetes, regular insulin use is essential, but dosing is complex due to many factors, including food intake, exercise, stress, and even temperature. Too little insulin leads to high blood sugar, tiredness, and, if untreated, potentially fatal diabetic ketoacidosis or long-term complications such as heart disease, blindness, kidney failure, and nerve damage. Too much insulin can cause dangerously low blood sugar, triggering confusion, sweating, shaking, and communication difficulties.

Hybrid closed-loop systems combine a continuous glucose monitor, an insulin pump, and a smart algorithm to automatically calculate and deliver the right insulin dose. While patients still need to input food and exercise details, experts say these devices greatly reduce the burden of daily calculations. Professor Jonathan Benger, Chief Medical Officer at NICE, described these systems as "game changing," saying they will improve health outcomes, reduce complications like disabling hypoglycemia, strokes, and heart attacks, and ultimately save NHS resources.

According to new guidance, anyone in England or Wales with Type 1 diabetes who is under 18 or pregnant should be offered the technology. Adults with Type 1 who struggle to control their average blood sugar with current methods also qualify. The charity Diabetes UK welcomed the updated recommendations, which are broader than those outlined in earlier drafts, noting that expanded access reduces inequalities.

Rollout will take place in phases over five years, starting with children, pregnant people, and those already using traditional insulin pumps. Consistent funding is considered crucial, with allocation decisions resting with local NHS bodies. Diabetes UK has urged national and local authorities to set clear funding agreements to ensure equal access across all areas. Colette Marshall, Diabetes UK’s chief executive, called hybrid closed-loop technology transformative, emphasizing that funding is key to reaching all people in need.

article_content: Asteroid 2012 DA14 is about to pass extremely close to Earth on February 15, reaching speeds of 17,450 mph. Although Earth's gravity will tweak its path, NASA confirms there is zero danger of an impact. Dr. Don Yeomans, who leads NASA's research on near-Earth objects, assures us the orbit is well charted, so there's no risk. This flyby will be the closest on record for an asteroid its size—closer than many satellites. Despite its velocity, the asteroid won't enter our atmosphere because of its specific trajectory. People in Eastern Europe, Asia, and Australia may get the best view of the asteroid using binoculars or telescopes, but it's too small—about half a football field long—to see with the naked eye. Scientists are eager to observe 2012 DA14 up close. NASA plans to bounce radar signals off the asteroid as it passes just 17,200 miles from Earth to learn more about its makeup. Researchers estimate hundreds of thousands of roughly similar-sized asteroids may be in Earth's neighborhood, yet most remain undetected. This one was spotted less than a year ago in Spain. Now, experts monitor these bodies and map their paths for decades ahead to both better understand any risks and to evaluate their potential benefits. Asteroids could be valuable resources. NASA and companies like Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries hope to mine them for materials like metals or water ice—useful for space missions and stations far from Earth. Direct impacts by such asteroids are highly unusual, happening once every 1,200 years. If 2012 DA14 were to hit (which NASA insists it won’t), it would cause regional destruction but not a global catastrophe. For example, a similar metal asteroid created Meteor Crater in Arizona about 50,000 years ago, and a stone asteroid exploded over Tunguska, Russia, in 1908, flattening a massive forested area. All in all, asteroid 2012 DA14’s approach is historic and exciting for science and exploration, but there’s no reason to panic.

article_content: The SAG-AFTRA strike isn’t the only industrial action happening this fall. Striking hotel workers staged a loud protest—complete with drums and vuvuzelas—outside the AFM’s Méridien Delfina headquarters in Santa Monica today, as part of ongoing efforts for more equitable contracts and conditions. Hundreds of workers joined a rally and march, moving from the Delfina to the Viceroy (another hotel involved in the strike), and onwards to Santa Monica City Hall. Hotel employees in Santa Monica have been striking for months, seeking fairer contracts. This year's American Film Market (AFM), which concludes tomorrow, found itself in the midst of the labor action after moving its venue to the Delfina from its longtime base at Loews. The hotel was the subject of a recent LA Times report alleging it employed staffing agencies to hire homeless migrants as replacement workers. State Senator Maria Elena Durazo addressed these claims in a press conference last month. The Writers Guild of America also sent an open letter to Jean Prewitt, President & CEO of IFTA/AFM, urging support for the hotel strike, and asking AFM participants to refrain from patronizing the affected hotels until fair contracts are reached. Prewitt responded by noting: “We are not party to union negotiations with Los Angeles hotels or their hiring practices.” Pete Hillan, spokesperson for the California Hotel & Lodging Association, added: “Our hotels hire employees directly and through third-party contractors, always following California employment laws.” The noisy protests were organized by hospitality workers’ union Unite Here Local 11, which also led today’s march. For AFM attendees, logistical issues at the new venue, such as slow elevators and confusing corridors, have been a recurring complaint. Concerns have also been raised about the suitability of the venue for future editions. Some industry professionals have suggested moving AFM to a different city, naming Miami as a possible alternative, but IFTA has a multi-year contract to keep the event at the Méridien Delfina. Despite rumors to the contrary, the organization clarified there is no immediate option to exit the contract. Jean Prewitt acknowledged the challenges at the new venue, stating: “After each market, we gather feedback from participants, which is especially important this year. There were definitely growing pains, but business was conducted effectively, and that will continue in the future.” She emphasized that canceling or relocating the event would be harmful to the independent industry and its stakeholders. Exhibitor numbers at AFM remain stable, and deals are still being made despite the ongoing SAG-AFTRA strike and a difficult economic climate. Organizers and attendees agree that in-person interaction at the LA-based event continues to be an important advantage. While AFM faces calls for change and ongoing controversy with hotel staff strikes, both organizers and participants view it as a work in progress supporting the independent film industry.

article_content: A local court has granted interim bail to three of four Amity University students arrested by Noida Police on Monday for allegedly supplying drugs to colleges and hostels across Gautam Buddh Nagar district. The court said on Tuesday that bail was granted so the students could take their university exams, noting that only a small quantity of drugs was recovered from them. Police have stated they intend to challenge the bail order. Law student Aditya Kumar (21) and MBA students Apoorv Saxena (28) and Sagar Bajaj (21) received bail until December 1. After this, they must appear before the court and provide sureties. The three were arrested along with Amity student Darshan Jain (21) and five others at Mayur roundabout under Sector 126 police station jurisdiction. According to police, Darshan Jain and Aditya Kumar were found smoking marijuana in public during a patrol. Upon frisking, police recovered marijuana from them. Police then allegedly found a larger quantity of marijuana from Shillong and MDMA in their room. During interrogation, the accused identified additional individuals: Akshay Kumar (32) from Ghaziabad; Rajan Singh (20) from Delhi; Satendra Srivastava (21) and Anit Som (22), both from Gautam Buddh Nagar; and Narendra Kumar (28) from Rajasthan, who were also taken into custody. Police stated they seized 15.1 kg of marijuana, 30 grams of cocaine, 20 grams of MDMA, 150 grams of hash, 65 grams of original Californian marijuana, an SUV, and mobile phones. The estimated value of the drugs is over Rs 30 lakh. Police allege that Akshay Kumar was the ringleader, sourcing Californian marijuana from Taiwan, where his wife is employed, while Narendra Kumar supplied marijuana from Rajasthan. According to police, Aditya Kumar and Satendra Srivastava managed orders, while Sagar Bajaj, Anit Som, and Apoorv Saxena acted as bike taxi drivers to deliver drugs in small packets.

article_content: John Covington, superintendent of Kansas City, Missouri schools, has stood by a contentious plan to close nearly half of the district's schools. On Thursday, he admitted that closing schools is a tough process for both families and the wider community, but stressed it is necessary to strengthen the academic performance of the remaining schools. Covington noted that the district's schools are under-enrolled, with only about 60% of seats filled in elementary schools, 40% in middle schools, and even less in high schools. After prolonged debate and years of declining enrollment, the Board of Education narrowly approved the 'right-size' plan, which will close 29 facilities, including 26 schools. The plan triggered strong reactions. Some parents voiced worries about their children's safety and future, while students expressed sadness over losing their school communities. Parent Deneicia Williams said she was uncomfortable with her young children being educated alongside older students, and senior Prince Jones described his sadness at graduating in Westport High School's final class. Covington argued the closures are necessary to safeguard the district's future, pointing out the elimination of 700 jobs and $50 million in projected savings to tackle a growing deficit. School districts across America face similar dilemmas due to budget cuts, with some adopting four-day school weeks in at least 17 states. Enrollment has plummeted in Kansas City schools—from more than 35,000 students in 1999-2000 to around 17,000 in 2009-2010. Covington sees the closures as the first phase of adjusting the district to its size and needs, claiming that having too many under-enrolled schools drains resources needed for all students. Despite passing, four of the nine board members voted against the closures, citing limited data on student achievement. Community activists and local leaders also opposed the plan, fearing it could harm neighborhoods and drive families away. Covington plans to further address the closures in a news conference.

article_content: In southern Gaza, hundreds of thousands of refugees are enduring dire humanitarian conditions that continue to worsen each hour, testing the limits of all available support systems. The influx of people fleeing ongoing Israeli airstrikes in northern Gaza has led to mass movement along the Salah al-Din road, with many traveling on foot while carrying only their children and what little they manage to bring. Deir al-Balah, a central city identified as a 'safe zone,' is now struggling to accommodate a huge number of displaced people. Repurposed school buildings – operated as UN shelters – are severely overcrowded with up to 70 people sharing a single classroom. Residents face unsanitary conditions and outbreaks of diseases such as chickenpox, scabies, and lice. Hassan Abu Rashed, a 29-year-old blacksmith who recently arrived from Jabalia with his family, describes the overcrowding: “We sleep on our sides because there is not even enough room to lie on our backs... we hope we will find a few slices of bread per day to eat. The sewage system is broken.” Others, like Khaled Filfel, a 42-year-old father, highlight specific challenges. “My 21-year-old daughter is disabled and I cannot get any nappies for her,” he says, adding that water and food have been scarce. Before the escalation, the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) planned for 1,500 people per school, but each facility in the south now houses about 6,000, according to UNRWA's Gaza director Thomas White. “Sanitation is overwhelmed; we’re averaging about 125 people per toilet and 700 per shower unit.” To escape the crowded schools, some families spend their days at the beach. Mahmoud al-Motawag, a farm worker from Jabalia, explained his family’s reliance on the sea for washing, cleaning, and occasionally as a water source when clean supplies cannot be found. He, his wife Duaa, and their two young children have lived in a tent with 50 others for three weeks. Duaa, eight months pregnant, voices fears about giving birth in such challenging conditions, with limited access to medical care and a lack of supplies. The Al-Aqsa hospital, like others in Gaza, is overwhelmed and running out of medicines and equipment. Dr. Khalil al-Duqran, an emergency doctor, reports a continual influx of wounded from ongoing strikes and the hospital’s critical shortages. Aid agencies warn that food is running out across Gaza. The World Food Programme reports that all participating shops are out of basic supplies, and bakeries have no gas for bread. Residents queue for hours but often leave empty-handed. With shelters full, many displaced people construct makeshift shelters outdoors, seeking proximity to UN flags for a sense of protection. Aid staff warn that worsening weather will increase their vulnerability. Daily life is defined by hardship, uncertainty, and the search for basic needs.

She said the school threatened to place the girls in isolation as punishment. Selby explained, 'We tried to flatten it down and make it more discreet, but the school was still not happy. People who have seen it don’t understand the issue and point out that boys at the school have similar hairstyles. There appears to be a trend, but Abby seems to have been singled out.' 'We have always supported the school's disciplinary decisions regarding Abby, but we don't agree with them in this situation.' Samworth Academy declined to comment on specific cases but referred to their school policy. A spokesperson stated, 'We regularly communicate our expectations and make every effort to resolve any issues that arise. If a situation is not remedied after meetings with the student and their family, we may, as a last resort, impose a more serious sanction such as a fixed-term exclusion.' Selby reiterated her view that the girls’ hairstyle is part of a current trend and said the school appears unhappy about it.

article_content: Sam Standerwick, a 41-year-old project manager from Tredegar in south Wales, experienced significant weight gain over the years, reaching over 21 stone. Her love for watersports since childhood was challenged when, on her 40th birthday, she realized she could no longer fit into a wetsuit to go kayaking. This realization spurred her to adopt healthier habits. While Sam's food choices were generally healthy, she often ate much larger portions than needed—sometimes finishing an entire chicken or packs of crisps in a single sitting. Even though her meals were balanced, the quantities impacted her well-being. Motivated to return to her favorite activities, Sam embraced an active lifestyle, incorporating running, cross training, and weight lifting. Over a period of 14 months, she lost almost 9 stone and reduced her clothing size from 28 to 14, now weighing 13 stone 1 lb. Sam avoided drastic diet measures, choosing to eat around 2,000 calories a day to fuel her fitness efforts. She believes sustainability is key, saying, "It's not about starving yourself or doing crash diets. If you're always hungry, it's impossible to keep going. Small, steady changes are more effective than extreme restrictions." Sam also took on running challenges, completing two half-marathons, three 10k races, and 26 5k park runs. She credits her healthy and lasting transformation to consistency and not cutting out the foods she enjoys. Her current meals are balanced with proteins and vegetables, and she allows herself treats in moderation. She typically starts the day with a granola bar or protein shake, enjoys a large salad with low-fat cottage cheese and prawns for lunch, and has fish or chicken with lots of vegetables for dinner. Sam's story underscores how small, sustainable changes can lead to remarkable improvements.

Sam’s story proves that sustainable changes can lead to huge victories.

Whether you’re hiring a professional or taking the DIY route, several key elements are critical for a successful logo design. Font Selection: Font choice is crucial and can be time-consuming. Remember to review each font’s licensing agreements—some are free, while others require a purchase for commercial use. Graphics: Deciding whether to include a graphic or acronym in your logo depends on your industry and brand message. Files: Once your logo is complete, request the original design files, such as PDF, PSD, AI, JPG, and PNG. Having these allows for future edits or adjustments, whether by you or a different designer. article_content: Maria Alyokhina, a 24-year-old member of Pussy Riot, ended an 11-day hunger strike protesting her treatment by prison authorities. Her protest began after she was barred from attending her own parole hearing in a penal colony in Berezniki, Ural Mountains. Alyokhina and her lawyer, Irina Khrunova, report that officials imposed stricter security and encouraged other inmates to turn against her. Rules now require prisoners to wait—sometimes up to an hour—for guards to escort them to work, delaying medical care. During her hunger strike, Alyokhina was moved to the colony’s hospital, according to Pyotr Verzilov, husband of member Nadezhda Tolokonnikova. Alyokhina, Tolokonnikova, and Yekaterina Samutsevich were convicted last August for 'hooliganism motivated by religious hatred' after a protest performance criticizing President Vladimir Putin inside a Moscow cathedral. All received two-year sentences; Samutsevich was later freed on appeal. Recently, Tolokonnikova was denied parole. Samutsevich claims the new crackdowns are retaliation for Alyokhina’s advocacy for prisoner rights. Previously, Alyokhina spent five months in solitary and says she was purposely housed with violent offenders who threatened her. Khrunova alleges authorities filed false psychiatric reports and questionable disciplinary actions. Judges have overturned some reprimands, but concern about Alyokhina’s treatment continues. Sir Paul McCartney has written several times to Russian officials supporting Alyokhina’s right to attend hearings and requesting her release. Alyokhina’s mother, Natalia, doubts the courts will grant parole, citing her lack of trust in the justice system. Officials argue alleged misconduct—disrespect toward staff and rulebreaking—makes her ineligible for parole. Many of the group’s supporters see the prosecution of Pussy Riot as a sign of broader efforts to silence dissent during Putin’s presidency.

article_content: Veterinary laboratories in several states are investigating an unusual respiratory illness in dogs and urging people to take basic precautions to keep their pets healthy as veterinarians work to determine the cause of the sickness. States including Oregon, Colorado, and New Hampshire have reported cases of this illness, which results in persistent respiratory disease and pneumonia and does not respond to antibiotics. Symptoms include coughing, sneezing, nasal or eye discharge, and lethargy. Some pneumonia cases can progress rapidly, making dogs very sick within 24 to 36 hours. The Oregon Department of Agriculture has recorded more than 200 cases since mid-August and urges pet owners to contact their veterinarians if their dogs show symptoms. The agency is coordinating with state researchers and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory to identify the cause of the illness. According to Kurt Williams, director of the Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Oregon State University, some dogs have died, but without a clear definition or test for the disease, it's difficult to know how many. Williams advised dog owners not to panic and to ensure their pets are current on vaccines, especially those protecting against respiratory illnesses. Laboratories across the country are sharing information to help identify the cause. David Needle, senior veterinary pathologist at the University of New Hampshire, has investigated the condition for almost a year. His team has studied samples from dogs in Rhode Island, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts, with more to come from Oregon, Colorado, and potentially other states. He reported no large increase in deaths but still recommended owners limit their dogs’ contact with other dogs. Researchers from the Barrow Neurological Institute have revealed that living in areas with moderate air pollution can increase the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease by 56% compared to living in the least polluted regions. This study, set to be published in 'Neurology,' used sophisticated mapping techniques to highlight, for the first time, a strong nationwide connection between exposure to fine air particles and the incidence of Parkinson’s disease in the U.S.

Findings show the risk is especially high in areas like the Mississippi-Ohio River Valley, central North Dakota, parts of Texas, Kansas, eastern Michigan, and southern Florida, while the western states have lower rates. These regional differences may be linked to the specific mix of pollutants—particularly in places with heavy industry and dense road networks.

The research team reviewed data from nearly 22 million Medicare recipients, identifying close to 90,000 Parkinson’s cases. By analyzing where each patient lived alongside pollution levels, and accounting for age, sex, race, smoking behavior, and healthcare usage, they established a significant link between long-term exposure to fine particulate pollution and developing Parkinson’s disease later in life.

Lead researcher Dr. Brittany Krzyzanowski noted that although prior studies mostly examined pesticide exposure, this new research emphasizes air pollution as a vital environmental factor. The team hopes their findings will support the development of stricter pollution controls to help reduce the risk of Parkinson’s and related illnesses.

article_content: What qualifies a death scene in a horror movie as 'cool'? Is it the blood, gore, or sheer outrageousness? Absolutely! However, it’s also about how memorable or iconic that death is—and sometimes just how frightening it can be. There’s no simple formula; as the old saying goes, 'I know it when I see it.' Why do we gravitate towards scenes like Jigsaw’s brutal traps in 'Saw' or Leatherface’s mayhem in 'The Texas Chainsaw Massacre'? The truth is, their shock and creativity fascinate us. With that in mind, here are seven undeniably cool horror movie deaths—perhaps not the scariest or most famous, but certainly unforgettable. James Gunn, now renowned for blockbuster hits like 'Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3,' surprised audiences in 2006 with his body horror homage 'Slither.' The film, a slimy throwback to the 1980s genre, earned praise from both BBC and the Los Angeles Times. In 'Slither,' an alien parasite crashes to Earth, aiming to breed using humans as hosts. The most memorable death? Brenda’s grotesque fate: chained in a barn, forced to eat as thousands of alien slugs grow inside her, until she swells to enormous proportions and explodes when the slugs are ready to hatch. It’s gruesome, creative, and impossible to forget. In 'Final Destination,' a group of students board a 747 to Paris only to experience a catastrophic crash in the opening scene: violent turbulence triggers an electrical fire and explosion that rips the plane apart, sucking passengers out. The sequence is riveting, playing on deep-seated fears of aviation accidents. This scene stands out for its ability to tap into anxieties about flying—making it a harrowing and memorable cinematic moment. Though rated PG-13, 'Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark' delivers a surprisingly disturbing sequence with the 'Pale Lady.' In a hospital nightmare, Chuck is confronted and ultimately enveloped by the monstrous figure, absorbed into her body in a slow, chilling embrace. While not the most terrifying in horror history, this scene is both disturbing and impressive, demonstrating that PG-13 films can push boundaries and achieve box office success, grossing over $104 million worldwide. 'Urban Legend' remains a divisive horror entry, but its inventive take on slasher tropes stands out. The film’s most notorious scene adapts the classic 'Aren’t You Glad You Didn’t Turn on the Light' legend: Natalie assumes her roommate’s sounds are harmless, only to later discover a gruesome murder occurred just feet away. The execution is bold, unsettling, and plays perfectly on familiar folklore. While Johnny Depp’s death in 'A Nightmare on Elm Street' is famous, Tina’s is arguably the most shocking. Audiences initially follow Tina, believing she is the final girl, only for Freddy Krueger to upend expectations. Her death—levitating, blood-soaked, and violently thrown across walls and ceiling—made a statement through its use of practical effects, setting a new bar for the genre and breaking from slasher conventions of the era. The death of Dallas in 'Alien' is pivotal, marking the audience’s first close encounter with the xenomorph. As Dallas crawls through the Nostromo’s air ducts, tension mounts via radio exchanges with the crew. The scene’s masterful use of claustrophobia and suspense leaves viewers haunted—even as the director’s cut reveals an alternative, more gruesome fate in the alien’s cocoon. Regardless, the original vent sequence remains an iconic horror moment. Few horror scenes are as iconic as Drew Barrymore’s opening fate in 'Scream.' The suspenseful phone exchange with Ghostface and sudden, brutal attack created an unforgettable sequence that redefined modern horror. Interestingly, despite initial executive doubts and necessary edits to avoid an NC-17 rating, the sequence remains a masterclass in suspense and impact.

article_content: San Francisco is slated to break records with the construction of its tallest-ever apartment tower. Thanks to Assembly Bill 2011, a new California law designed to fast-track affordable and mixed-income housing, the city’s southern financial district will soon see a 71-story residential high-rise replacing an old parking lot and a four-story office building. The project is pushing forward without the usual environmental or city-level approval hurdles—requirements bypassed under AB2011—making it only the second San Francisco development to utilize the law. This streamlined approach comes at a critical time. San Francisco has long struggled with soaring housing costs and complicated permitting processes that slow new construction and make meeting homebuilding targets nearly impossible. Of the 672 planned apartments, 67 will be offered at below-market rates, catering to those most impacted by the affordability crunch. Residents will also have direct access to Salesforce Park, a five-and-a-half-acre rooftop green space, via a connecting bridge. The new building, set for 530 Howard Street, will not only be San Francisco's tallest residential development but also the city’s third-tallest structure overall, according to the San Francisco Chronicle. Developer Paul Paradis, already known for his work on the Salesforce Tower and the JPMorgan Chase building, believes the 840-foot-high complex will offer exceptional views and raise the bar for rental housing in the city. AB2011 is part of a recent legislative push in California meant to increase housing supply, loosen strict regulations, and accelerate the construction of affordable and dense urban housing. Last month, Governor Gavin Newsom signed over 50 housing-related bills, further easing rules that have historically slowed development. Mayor London Breed has also advocated for cutting red tape and praised these reforms as key to building a more resilient and vibrant city. She highlighted the transformation of a parking lot into mixed-income housing as an example of progress, calling it a win for San Francisco’s future and its economic health.

article_content: Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, may soon face espionage charges in the United States after a court highlighted his alleged role in the acquisition of classified military documents. During the pre-trial hearing for U.S. Army Private Bradley Manning—who stands accused of leaking around 700,000 confidential files—prosecutors shared chat logs they say demonstrate Assange advising Manning on how to bypass military computer passwords. These alleged online messages, recovered from Manning's laptop, suggest Assange was actively helping Manning as the secret files were transmitted. According to prosecutors, Manning, using the alias 'Nobody,' communicated with someone named 'Nathanial Frank,' whom authorities believe was Assange. In these exchanges, Manning asked for assistance with hacking techniques, like cracking password hashes to allow anonymous login. The alleged Assange account responded with information about using 'rainbow tables,' a tool for password cracking. Although Assange has denied direct contact with Manning, his legal representatives believe the evidence could underpin a U.S. espionage conspiracy case against him. David Coombs, Manning's defense lawyer, argued that the leaks did not compromise national security and accused the government of using severe charges to coerce a plea bargain. Presiding officer Lt. Col. Paul Almanza is set to recommend by January 16 whether Manning will go to trial for aiding the enemy, among 21 other charges. The proceeding at Fort Meade attracted notable attendees, including Jennifer Robinson, Assange's lawyer, and Daniel Ellsberg, famous for leaking the Pentagon Papers. Assange is presently on bail while appealing his extradition to Sweden, where he faces separate allegations.

article_content: Hundreds of traders at Rumuwoji (Mile 1 Market) in Port Harcourt remain hopeful that the ultra-modern market, completed and commissioned during the Nyesom Wike administration, will soon reopen. Despite being finished over two years ago, the facility is still locked, leaving traders without proper premises. A fire about five years ago forced traders out, and since then, they have operated in a nearby space meant for car parking. Many say their businesses have suffered and the Rivers State government's promise to relocate and resettle them in the new market has not been fulfilled. Ike Wigodo, the immediate past Chairman of the Rumuwoji Community Council, explained that reconstruction began after a major fire in 2003 or 2004. Different sections of the market were completed sequentially by governors Peter Odili, Celestine Omehia, Rotimi Amaechi, and finally Nyesom Wike, who commissioned the last phase. However, trading has not resumed in the market. A building was purchased to provide additional parking for the market, but this project is still unfinished. Several traders say the open car park space leaves them vulnerable to weather extremes and poor storage, damaging their goods. Mrs. Blessing, who sells snail, plantain, and ogbono, praised the new facility but pleaded with Governor Siminalayi Fubara to open the market. She described hardships from working in the open, including loss of goods due to rain, sun, and occasional theft, even with available security. Gift Okpara, another trader, confirmed these challenges, emphasizing that the finished market offers sufficient space and customer parking. She urged the government to act so traders can better support their families. Kenneth Eze, Chairman of the Open Extension Market, also appreciated the standard of the new facility but said traders have endured tough conditions for nearly five years. He called on Governor Fubara to resolve the matter and ensure legitimate traders receive shop allocations. Anthony Ohams, who sells watches and glasses, mentioned that a legal challenge over the allocation of shops by some traders further delayed the move-in. He asked the new government to revisit and resolve this dispute. Attempts to reach the Commissioner for Works, Daks George-Kelly, for comment were unsuccessful as of the time of reporting.

Many homeowners—especially short-term rental hosts—feel that typical security systems are either too expensive or too intrusive for their needs. Cameras and motion detectors can make guests uneasy and compromise privacy.

To offer a better solution, Form Devices, founded by former Apple designer Nils Mattisson and partners, introduced Point—a device that quietly monitors your home for out-of-the-ordinary events using microphones and environmental sensors, without streaming or recording audio. When Point senses unexpected noises, temperature fluctuations, or potential signs of smoke, it notifies owners through a smartphone app. These alerts let people know if, for instance, a window broke or someone’s having a loud gathering, all without invading anyone’s privacy.

Point handles all data processing on the device itself, eliminating concerns about eavesdropping or cloud hacks. The companion app gives owners an easy-to-read timeline of detected events.

The product is tailored for users wanting straightforward, low-maintenance monitoring for their homes or offices—without the complexity or invasiveness of traditional security setups. While products like Dropcam store footage in the cloud and can be susceptible to breaches, Point keeps all audio data local and secure.

Form Devices has successfully raised $150,000 via Kickstarter and is beginning production, with the first batch going to an office rental management firm. They plan to offer Point for about $100 to consumers next year, and are looking to expand its use to hotels and a wider market.

Mattisson and his team—including Marcus Ljungblad, Fredrik Ahlberg, and Martin Lööf—envision a new era for smart home security, focusing on simple, privacy-first devices rather than simply adding connectivity to existing appliances. Their vision taps into a growing demand for smarter, more considerate technology.

article_content: Lasse Andresen, CEO of IndyKite, highlights that while sourcing software for business needs is simpler than ever, this ease has led to increased complexity in managing IT systems. Organizations, often dealing with outdated infrastructure, tend to adopt popular or high-performing solutions, creating a mosaic of disconnected tools. These choices commonly result in companies being tied to older, standalone systems not built for integration, ultimately increasing costs and reducing efficiency. Andresen suggests that since legacy products still dominate much of the software market, market disruption is unsurprising. Rather than pursuing risky and challenging overhauls of the entire stack, he recommends starting with a focus on connecting and leveraging existing business data. Making current data accessible and usable throughout an organization can deliver better value and efficiency. He emphasizes that new software acquisitions should factor in not just immediate functionality, but also how solutions integrate and share data with other tools. Adopting this mindset pushes companies to think strategically, using each software purchase to improve overall technical capability. Methods like data cataloging and mapping can help identify information silos, duplication, and other areas for improvement. According to Andresen, vendors should develop products that both complement current systems and extend the value of existing technology investments. This is especially important in identity and access management (IAM), a sector that’s used the same core technologies for years. With fresh, data-driven IAM tools emerging—and Gartner predicting that organizations using advanced data management in IAM will speed up value delivery by 40%—the industry is poised for change. However, as established IAM providers consolidate, customers may face increased challenges. Andresen concludes that legacy solutions are on the path to extinction, and encourages businesses to align with innovative vendors to ensure continued progress.

article_content: Michael Schumacher is reportedly responding to instructions as doctors begin the process of waking him from his medically induced coma. The seven-time Formula 1 world champion has also been observed blinking during neurological tests, according to France’s L’Equipe newspaper, which cites reliable sources. Schumacher has undergone several neurological exams since Monday and has shown positive responses. He has been in a medically induced coma at Grenoble University Hospital since his skiing accident in the French resort of Meribel on December 29, 2013. Initially described as critical, his condition stabilized following surgery. Doctors led by Dr. Emmanuel Gay have gradually reduced Schumacher’s sedation and are closely monitoring his neurological reflexes. In the early stages of the process, Schumacher reportedly blinked, an encouraging sign according to the sports daily. To support healing, Schumacher has been kept at a reduced body temperature while sedated to minimize brain swelling and energy consumption. His wife Corinna and their children have remained at his bedside, with the family expressing gratitude for worldwide support. Sabine Kehm, Schumacher’s manager, stated: 'Michael's sedation is being reduced in order to begin the waking-up process, which may take some time.' Kehm clarified that no further details on his condition would be provided to the media at this time. Brain experts note that the process of reducing sedation and bringing a patient out of an induced coma is gradual and can carry risks if rushed. If signs such as increased intracranial pressure or seizure activity reappear during weaning, the patient may be returned to an induced coma. Medical specialists, like Dr. Clemens Pahl and Dr. Anthony Strong, emphasize the importance of monitoring whether Schumacher can respond to commands, breathe unassisted, or react to pain stimuli. These signs help determine his neurological function and awareness. Experts caution that recovery can be slow and it may be months before Schumacher’s long-term prognosis is clear. Dr. Tipu Aziz of Oxford University warns that lasting brain damage remains a possibility due to the extent of Schumacher’s injuries. Schumacher, renowned for his impressive and sometimes controversial racing talent, retired from Formula One in 2012 with a record 91 race wins and seven world championships. He was injured during a family vacation while skiing with his son.

A recent article in OMICS: A Journal of Integrative Biology highlights the feasibility and importance of providing research-based learning opportunities in life sciences to high school students worldwide. Led by Gayane Ghukasyan from Yerevan State University, Armenia, and co-authors Vardges Tserunyan, Mher Kurghinyan, and Lusine Hovhannisyan—independent scholars from Yerevan—the study describes their work with the International Group Project (IGP). This initiative built upon the 2022 International Biology Olympiad held in Yerevan, an annual global competition for high school students.

Through the IGP, 72 students from 32 countries collaborated digitally via videoconferencing. Each team, made up of four students from different countries, formulated a research question and presented their findings to the public with posters. This structure promoted intercultural exchange and encouraged new collaborations between students with diverse backgrounds and skills.

According to the authors, such experiences not only introduce students to the authentic practices of scientific research but also help identify future researchers. The article underlines the value of introducing research-based life science education at the high school level, with broad relevance for youth education in omics systems science, integrative biology, and life sciences more generally. Editor-in-Chief Vural Özdemir notes that the initiative fosters innovative thinking and collaborative problem-solving—essential efforts given current global challenges such as the climate emergency. The findings underscore the urgent need for collective solutions and highlight the benefits of engaging youth in scientific research.

article_content: Whoopi Goldberg defended Bill Cosby amid increasing allegations of sexual assault by more than a dozen women. On 'The View,' Goldberg voiced skepticism regarding Barbara Bowman’s claim that the comedian drugged and assaulted her in 1985. Bowman said she sought help from a lawyer at the time, but her allegations were dismissed. Goldberg questioned why Bowman did not report the incident to police or seek medical evidence, suggesting authorities might have believed her. Co-host Rosie O’Donnell referenced the 2006 civil lawsuit by Andrea Constand, which ended in a settlement with Cosby. Bowman explained she delayed reporting because she feared Cosby’s fame would prevent her from being believed and did not share the incidents even with her mother. Last month, Bowman recounted to MailOnline how Cosby allegedly drugged her at his home when she was 17, resulting in her passing out and awakening partially clothed, convinced she had been assaulted. She also claimed Cosby attempted to assault her again in 1987 and said she has never accepted money from him. Cosby, whose net worth is reportedly $400 million, has remained silent on the allegations, declining to address them when questioned on NPR. Bowman detailed her experience to MailOnline, describing how she was allegedly drugged and assaulted as a teenager. Goldberg expressed doubts, stating, 'Having been on both sides of similar situations, I have questions for the accuser. Maybe she’ll come on the show.' In November 2006, Cosby settled a civil lawsuit with Constand, who alleged he drugged and assaulted her in his Philadelphia-area home in 2004. Thirteen other women were identified by lawyers as having similar experiences, though the settlement came before they could testify. Joan Tarshis is another woman who has come forward, stating that Cosby assaulted her in 1969 while she worked as a writer for him. Tarshis acknowledged that false accusations against celebrities are difficult. Goldberg expressed her hope for justice but said she would reserve judgment pending further facts. Co-host Nicolle Wallace commented that it's 'a tragedy' whether the accusers were assaulted or Cosby is being falsely accused. Thirteen women joined the 2005 lawsuit filed by Constand. Bowman said she provided testimony in the case but did not receive a settlement. Cosby’s lawyer has denied the latest allegations, stating Cosby would not 'dignify' them with a response. article_content: At 18, Fred Swaniker began his journey in education when his mother, facing the family's financial challenges after the loss of his father, asked him to help run a new school for young children in Botswana. Taking on the roles of headmaster and teacher, Swaniker found his passion for nurturing talent. Inspired by this start, and after completing his MBA at Stanford in 2004, the Ghanaian entrepreneur dedicated himself to empowering Africa’s youth through transformative educational ventures. Understanding Africa's complex hurdles—from healthcare to governance—Swaniker determined he could make the biggest impact by cultivating a generation of innovators and leaders. This idea led him to co-found the African Leadership Academy (ALA) in Johannesburg, which selects around 250 outstanding students annually from across the continent for a unique two-year leadership and entrepreneurship program. Building on the success of ALA, Swaniker established the African Leadership University (ALU) in 2015, with campuses in Mauritius and Rwanda, offering bachelor’s degrees in fields like entrepreneurial leadership and software engineering to approximately 2,000 students each year. Responding to the rapid growth of Africa's tech sector and the reach of online education, Swaniker then set up ALX—a digital platform providing intensive, short-duration courses in areas like software engineering, cloud computing, and data analytics. To date, over 97,000 learners have completed ALX programs. Alumni from Swaniker’s schools have launched careers across multiple sectors: Joseph Rutakangwa, an ALU graduate, founded Rwazi, which helps companies access consumer data in emerging markets and recently secured $4 million in seed funding; Spencer Horne, an ALA alumnus, started Cloudline, which uses solar-powered drones to deliver essentials to underserved rural areas and just unveiled its first airship at the Paris Air Show. Altogether, more than 200,000 students participate in Swaniker’s programs every year. Yet his ambitions reach further: he aims to train 3 million African leaders by 2035, embracing the demographic reality that Africa could represent 40% of the world’s population by 2050. Swaniker sees this enormous youth pool as key to strengthening the future global workforce. Swaniker’s visionary work has been acknowledged by the TIME100 Impact Awards. The next recognition ceremony is set for November 17 in Kigali, Rwanda.

By October 2023, Toyota Kirloskar Motor had already sold 192,000 vehicles, exceeding its previous annual record of 172,000 units set in 2012. Gulati anticipates that SUV trends will keep accelerating, with buyers prepared to pay extra for upgraded features and more safety options. He reiterated that the small car segment is facing headwinds and its progress will be observed closely. As for electric vehicles, Gulati stated that Toyota is consistently studying the market, considering both the nation’s push for decarbonization and the realities of India’s energy mix and EV infrastructure. The company remains prepared to roll out new technology solutions as and when consumer adoption and infrastructure readiness align. The article also mentioned recent moves by India’s market regulator on fractional real estate investment, the impact of multinational firms’ capability centers on engineering job prospects, and renewed growth expected in India’s smartphone market in 2024.
