article_content: Exoplanet research has rapidly advanced, with scientists now focusing not only on finding new worlds but also on studying their atmospheres and searching for potential signs of life. Over 5,500 exoplanets have been confirmed so far, spread across thousands of planetary systems. This progress has shifted the field’s emphasis from detection to detailed characterization. A wave of powerful telescopes—like NASA’s James Webb and the Roman Space Telescope, ESA’s upcoming PLATO mission, and massive ground-based observatories including the ELT, GMT, and TMT—promise breakthroughs in exoplanet exploration. However, refinements and upgrades to existing facilities are also proving instrumental. One such advancement is the HiRISE instrument, newly implemented on the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (VLT). Led by Dr. Arthur Vigan of CNRS, HiRISE combines SPHERE’s high-contrast imaging and the CRIRES spectrograph’s detailed spectral analysis via optical fibers. This setup allows for direct imaging of exoplanets and detailed atmospheric studies at a much higher resolution. Direct imaging provides scientists with reflected light from exoplanets, giving valuable information about their atmospheric makeup in a way that indirect methods, like the transit or radial velocity techniques, cannot. Dr. Vigan points out that, although challenging due to the faintness of the planets compared to their bright stars, HiRISE’s precision opens new scientific possibilities. Specialized for observing giant exoplanets in infrared light, HiRISE can identify atmospheric features such as water vapor, helping scientists understand these distant worlds’ compositions and dynamics. Early results show improved measurement accuracy, stability, and the ability to analyze a planet’s movements. Rather than constructing costly new observatories, upgrading instruments like HiRISE provides a faster and more economical boost to existing telescopes’ capabilities. The HiRISE project took approximately five years and cost around €1 million, notably expanding the research potential at a fraction of the price and time it takes to build facilities like the ELT. Dr. Vigan and his team hope that HiRISE will serve as a model for similar upgrades elsewhere and inspire future exoplanet-focused instruments, ultimately pushing the boundaries toward finding and characterizing Earth-like planets.

article_content: Judith Weir is considered a frontrunner to become the next Master of the Queen’s Music, a role traditionally held by celebrated male composers such as Sir Edward Elgar and, more recently, Sir Peter Maxwell Davies. If selected, Weir would be the first woman in the position’s nearly 400-year history. An official announcement is expected next month, according to a Palace source, and it is widely believed the chosen candidate will be a woman. Weir, who received the Queen’s Medal for Music in 2007, is a 60-year-old Cambridge graduate who studied with the late Sir John Tavener. She is well known for her operas, including 'The Vanishing Bridegroom.' The Queen has previously broken tradition in artistic appointments. In 2009, Carol Ann Duffy became the first female Poet Laureate. Other possible candidates for Master of the Queen’s Music include Sally Beamish, who composes for film, TV, and the BBC Proms; Michael Berkeley, a composer and crossbench peer in the House of Lords; and John Rutter, known for composing the anthem for Prince William and Kate Middleton’s wedding. Previously, the Master of the Queen’s Music was appointed for life. Sir Peter Maxwell Davies, after treatment for leukemia, fulfilled a ten-year term, which he completed in March, but agreed to continue until a successor is named. The post includes an honorary stipend, and appointees compose for royal occasions. The Palace will announce the new appointment in due course. He suggested the suspects might have been previous recipients of the foodbank’s support and reflected on a rise in local break-ins. According to police, the burglary was reported on Sunday morning. Both suspects have been released on bail until March 10.

article_content: Frank Lampard says there is no point in dwelling on Manchester City's recent form and believes Manuel Pellegrini's side can still overtake Chelsea in the race for the Barclays Premier League title. The former England midfielder admitted City have had a difficult few weeks, following an FA Cup exit to Middlesbrough and falling seven points behind his former club in the league. However, ahead of Wednesday night's trip to the Britannia Stadium to face Stoke City, Lampard remains optimistic. Lampard is confident Manchester City can regain form and close the gap on Chelsea. He stressed the importance of focusing on improving results rather than lamenting recent struggles. 'It's been a frustrating month for us,' the 36-year-old explained. 'We had a strong run through December, playing every three or four days, but January has disrupted our rhythm. With fewer games and changing results, if you don't perform and win, the points gap can widen. There's no point in feeling sorry for ourselves—all we can do is respond and start winning again.' A defeat on Wednesday and a Chelsea victory over Everton could extend the gap to ten points, but Lampard insists that nothing is decided yet. article_content: Portugal will end its special tax regime for new non-habitual residents in 2024, Prime Minister António Costa announced. The scheme, which grants tax benefits for 10 years to people relocating to Portugal, taxes domestic income at 20%. Generally, income from abroad is exempt, except pensions, which are taxed at 10%. In contrast, Portuguese citizens outside this regime may face taxes up to 48%. On Monday, the government confirmed it will discontinue the program, with Costa telling CNN Portugal that the scheme contributes to 'fiscal injustice.' He said, 'It is no longer justified and is a biased way of inflating the housing market, which has reached unsustainable prices.' According to Eurostat, house prices in Portugal showed the fourth highest increase (8.7%) in the EU in the second quarter of 2023. Last Saturday, tens of thousands across 24 cities protested the property market crisis, calling for housing rights. Earlier this year, the government stopped issuing residence permits for investment, known as 'golden visas.' More than 90% of these visas issued from 2012 to 2023 were linked to property purchases, according to the Portuguese Immigration and Borders Service.

article_content: OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman is set to return as CEO just days after his abrupt ouster, ending a brief but intense leadership dispute that shook the tech world. The San Francisco-based AI company announced late Tuesday that it reached an agreement in principle for Altman’s return, with a newly formed board of directors. Intense negotiations took place over the weekend following Altman’s dismissal, focusing on his future role, the board’s composition, and company governance, according to an informed source. An independent investigation into his removal will continue, while previous board statements cited an erosion of trust without detailing any serious misconduct. The lack of transparency over Altman’s firing sparked internal conflict and significant pressure from key investors, particularly Microsoft, which promptly hired Altman and co-founder Greg Brockman, and offered opportunities to over 700 OpenAI employees. The crisis underscored differing visions for AI development—Altman’s push for rapid commercialization versus board concerns over AI safety. Notably, chief scientist Ilya Sutskever reversed his stance and advocated for Altman’s reinstatement and the board’s resignation. Ultimately, most of the board stepped down, with a new lineup headed by Bret Taylor (former Salesforce co-CEO), joined by Larry Summers (former U.S. Treasury Secretary) and Adam D’Angelo (Quora CEO and the only returning board member). Experts, such as Johann Laux of the Oxford Internet Institute, say these events highlight the current fragility of AI governance. Investor Vinod Khosla criticized the previous board’s reliance on effective altruism ideology, arguing it hindered AI’s benefits. Microsoft, a major investor, played a central role in resolving the dispute, with CEO Satya Nadella publicly welcoming the changes. Altman, too, expressed optimism about renewed collaboration. The only two female board members, Tasha McCauley and Helen Toner, departed amid the shakeup. With governments racing to regulate AI—such as the EU developing new rules—big tech firms are shaping the path of advanced AI. Founded as a nonprofit committed to safe, beneficial AI, OpenAI later adopted a for-profit structure overseen by a nonprofit board. Previous leadership strife includes Elon Musk’s 2018 departure and officials founding competitor Anthropic. The board’s future structure remains uncertain, but OpenAI’s mission entails directing profits beyond a cap to public benefit and deciding when AI surpasses human abilities in economic tasks, affecting Microsoft’s licensing rights. Interim CEO Emmett Shear, who briefly led the company during the turmoil, expressed satisfaction with the outcome. OpenAI and the Associated Press hold a technology and licensing agreement that allows the AI firm partial access to AP’s text archives. Additional reporting by Kelvin Chan in London and Thalia Beaty in New York.

article_content: A major state-funded study has found that married couples report being happier than those who live together without marrying. According to the 'Enduring Love?' study conducted by the Open University, mothers were identified as the happiest group overall. The study also observed that couples without children tend to be more satisfied with their relationships than parents. Nevertheless, married couples, regardless of whether they had children, rated their overall happiness higher than unmarried couples. Based on surveys of nearly 5,000 couples, the research indicated that marriage is linked to greater happiness, even though married couples were more open about challenges in their relationships. Simple, daily gestures such as bringing a partner a cup of tea were found to have a significant positive impact on relationship satisfaction. Researcher Dr. Jacqui Gabb noted that small, loving actions are often as meaningful as saying 'I love you,' and that everyday support can outweigh grand romantic gestures. Married couples were more likely than others to express concerns about household chores or finances, rather than shared values, and more likely to report feeling distant than to be captivated by each other's humor. Despite these admissions, they still reported being happier than cohabiting couples. The report also revealed that both married and unmarried couples without children are generally more satisfied with their partners than those with children. However, married parents were just as happy with life overall as childless couples, and both groups scored higher on life satisfaction than unmarried couples, whether parents or not. These results align with government efforts to measure national well-being, such as surveys by the Office for National Statistics, which have also found married people to be more satisfied with their lives. The findings come amid ongoing debate over government policies supporting marriage, including a proposed tax break for lower-income married couples, which has faced criticism from some political groups. The research further highlighted that mothers tend to rate their happiness higher than any other group, sometimes regardless of their relationship satisfaction with their partners. The report suggested that children may be a primary source of happiness for mothers. Over years of study, evidence has shown that married individuals generally experience better health and their children often perform better at school than those from unmarried families. The Open University study, funded by the Economic and Social Research Council, found that both married parents and childless married couples rated their overall happiness at approximately 4.1 out of 5, compared to just over 3.9 for unmarried couples regardless of parental status.

article_content: RANGPO, India: The death toll from flash floods triggered by a glacial lake bursting its banks in India's Himalayas rose to 74 on Monday (Oct 9), with 101 people still missing, according to local officials. After several days of heavy rainfall in the northeastern state of Sikkim, torrents of water swept down river valleys from Lohnak Lake, damaging a dam and causing widespread destruction in villages and the town of Rangpo, about 50 km south of the state capital, Gangtok. Sikkim's chief secretary, Vijay Bhushan Pathak, told Reuters that 25 bodies were located in the state, while the bodies of eight army personnel washed away were found in neighboring West Bengal. He added that 101 people remain missing in one of the region’s worst disasters in over 50 years, driven by extreme Himalayan weather. Fourteen army personnel are among the missing, according to a defense ministry statement. Rescue operations are hampered by damaged roads, poor communications, and adverse weather conditions. Residents continue to clear sludge and debris. Parveen Shama, top district official in Jalpaiguri, West Bengal, said 41 bodies have been found in the district.

article_content: On Tuesday, human rights organizations urged Indonesia to investigate allegations that state-owned arms companies may have supplied weapons to Myanmar after the country's 2021 military coup. Feri Amsari, a legal adviser to the group, said a complaint was filed with Indonesia’s National Human Rights Commission on Monday. The complaint names three Indonesian defense firms—PT Pindad, PT PAL, and PT Dirgantara Indonesia—and claims they provided military equipment to Myanmar via True North, a firm reportedly owned by the son of a Myanmar military minister. The complaint was submitted as Myanmar remains engulfed in violence following the military ouster of elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi more than two years ago. The groups involved include Myanmar-based organizations along with former Indonesian attorney general Marzuki Darusman. The activists allege that Indonesia's companies supplied Myanmar with pistols, assault rifles, and armored vehicles. PT Pindad and PT PAL did not immediately respond to media requests, though PT Pindad had previously stated it hasn't sold anything to Myanmar since 2016. PT Dirgantara Indonesia said it never had contracts with Myanmar or related third parties. True North also did not respond, but Reuters reviewed an undated company profile describing the Indonesian firms as 'strategic partners.' As ASEAN chair, Indonesia has tried to mediate between Myanmar's military and opposition but with little success, and it supported a UN resolution calling on countries to halt arms transfers to Myanmar. An Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson said the complaint is being reviewed; the defense ministry gave no comment. Darusman argued the state should investigate, since these firms are state-owned. The UN special rapporteur recently said Myanmar’s military imported over $1 billion in arms after the coup, mainly from Russia, China, Singapore, Thailand, and India.

article_content: Many of America's most complex problems, including health concerns, environmental threats, and economic burdens, are closely linked to the way animals are treated in industrial agriculture. Every year, roughly 9 billion cows, pigs, chickens, turkeys, and lambs are killed in the United States, almost all of them raised in crowded factory farms. Animal welfare groups, such as Mercy for Animals, PETA, and the Humane Society of the United States, have uncovered widespread mistreatment and abuse through numerous investigations. For example, a recent Humane Society undercover operation at a New Jersey veal slaughterhouse exposed such severe abuse that the USDA halted its operations temporarily. Common industry practices—like tail docking and castrating piglets without anesthesia, keeping pigs in small crates, and cutting off the beaks of egg-laying hens—are recognized as inhumane by animal advocates including Paul Shapiro of the Humane Society. These standard procedures often conflict with mainstream American values about animal welfare. The consequences extend beyond animals. In the United States, two out of three adults are overweight or obese—a problem especially severe in low-income populations. This trend has grown alongside the rise of meat- and dairy-centered fast food. Studies highlight a strong connection between high consumption of animal products and chronic health issues, including heart disease and diabetes. Research suggests that adopting plant-based diets can help prevent obesity, particularly in children. Financially, obesity-related healthcare expenses reach as high as $190 billion annually, with added costs for those suffering from these conditions. Federal agricultural policies continue to fund large-scale operations that prioritize crops for processed foods over healthier options such as fruits and vegetables. Environmental impact is significant: animal agriculture is a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions through rainforest destruction, methane, and intensive resource use. The United Nations estimates livestock production is responsible for up to 22% of global greenhouse gases. Events like Hurricane Sandy, influenced by climate shifts, have caused tens of billions of dollars in damage. World hunger is worsened by the inefficient use of resources; a considerable portion of crops are fed to livestock instead of people. Bill Gates, a supporter of meat alternatives, notes that producing beef is a poor use of grain and calories in a world facing population growth. Notable individuals, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, are calling for dietary changes and new food technologies because of sustainability and health concerns. Experts argue that the current level of meat production cannot sustainably support the expected global population of over 9 billion by 2050. Ultimately, the article advocates for consumers to consider ethical and sustainable food choices, as these decisions could play a critical role in addressing both human and environmental challenges.

The Indian Premier League (IPL) 2024 auction will be held in Dubai on December 19, marking the first time the auction takes place outside India. The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) has confirmed this, according to the Times of India. The auction will coincide with the second One Day International of India's tour of South Africa, scheduled for the same day in Gqeberha.

All ten IPL franchises must submit their lists of retained and released players by November 15, after which the auction pool will be finalized in early December. Each team’s budget has been increased to INR 100 crore (approximately USD 12.02 million), up from last year’s INR 95 crore. The available funds for each franchise during the auction depend on their unspent purse from 2023 and the value of any released players.

As per current figures, Punjab Kings lead with INR 12.20 crore (USD 1.47 million) remaining, while Mumbai Indians have the least—INR 0.05 crore (USD 0.006 million). Other teams' available purse amounts are: Sunrisers Hyderabad – INR 6.55 crore (USD 0.79 million); Gujarat Titans and Delhi Capitals – INR 4.45 crore each (USD 0.54 million); Lucknow Super Giants – INR 3.55 crore (USD 0.43 million); Rajasthan Royals – INR 3.35 crore (USD 0.40 million); Kolkata Knight Riders – INR 1.65 crore (USD 0.20 million); and Chennai Super Kings – INR 1.5 crore (USD 0.20 million).

While the 2024 event is a single-day auction—unlike the two-day mega auctions previously held every four years—recent mini-auctions have resulted in some of the highest bids, especially for foreign players. Last year, Sam Curran became the most expensive player in IPL history when Punjab Kings bought him for INR 18.5 crore before the 2023 season.

This year, several top international cricketers are expected at the auction, including Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc, who has confirmed his return after eight years, and Pat Cummins, who missed last season but is likely to participate. Other notable names include Travis Head, Chris Woakes, Alex Hales, Sam Billings, and Gerald Coetzee.

article_content: A rare echidna species, believed extinct for over six decades, has been rediscovered in a remote part of Indonesia. The expedition also revealed the existence of a previously unknown species of tree-dwelling shrimp. The Attenborough long-beaked echidna (Zaglossus attenboroughi), named for British naturalist David Attenborough, was last seen in 1961. Echidnas are nocturnal and shy, making them hard to find, and this species has only ever been recorded in the remote Cyclops Mountains of Papua, Indonesia. James Kempton, a biologist from the University of Oxford who led the expedition, explained that these echidnas are among the last remnants of an ancient animal lineage. 'The reason it appears so different from other mammals is because it is a monotreme—an egg-laying group that branched off from the rest of the mammals about 200 million years ago,' he noted. The British-Indonesian team spent four weeks using 80 camera traps before finally capturing footage of the elusive echidna on the last day of their expedition. 'This discovery is the result of years of thorough planning and relentless effort,' Kempton said. He emphasized the essential support of the local community, who guided the team through challenging terrain and sacred areas. Besides rediscovering the echidna, the team identified a honeyeater bird last recorded in 2008 and several new underground species—including blind spiders, blind harvestmen, and a whip scorpion—in a cave system uncovered when a team member fell through a mossy entrance. The novel tree-dwelling shrimp was a surprise. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, the lead entomologist, suggested that high rainfall in the region creates enough humidity for the shrimp to thrive away from water. Despite dangerous conditions—Davranoglou broke his arm and another researcher endured a leech in his eye for over a day—the team described the experience as magical. They hope their findings will spotlight the urgent need for conservation in the region and Indonesia's remaining forests. As Davranoglou underscored, 'Tropical rainforests are among the most important and most threatened terrestrial ecosystems.'

article_content: Patrick is an executive coach and mindfulness teacher at Creative Balance Coaching, with experience as a tech executive in the finance industry. Technical experts often find it challenging to communicate effectively with senior leaders. What seems logical to them may not resonate with executives. This article discusses the communication gap and provides practical strategies to convey messages successfully. Technical specialists tend to delve into extensive background and challenges before arriving at their main point, which can overwhelm or confuse executive audiences. Executives typically prefer to hear key information first: the main point, required actions, urgency, and top recommendations. To communicate effectively, start with your primary point or request, clarify the urgency, outline your recommendation, and offer to share further details if needed. For example: 'Susan, I'd like your approval to hire a tech writer for the SuperBig project. We’ve identified a strong candidate who may accept another offer soon. May I review the costs and deliverables with you? It should only take about 10 minutes. Does that work?' By contrast, providing too much background before the actual request can cause confusion or loss of focus. Use this executive communication pattern throughout the discussion, avoiding unnecessary backstory and sticking to main points. Some specialists worry that being concise might oversimplify their message or reduce its nuance. Recognizing this concern is an important step toward improving communication. Technical specialists may believe others need all details to make informed decisions and truly appreciate their expertise. The article encourages specialists to experiment with executive-oriented communication, seek feedback, and view effective communication as a skill to build over time. Communicating clearly with decision makers outside your area of expertise is vital throughout your career. The Forbes Coaches Council is an invitation-only group for leading business and career coaches.

A Fury vs. Joshua fight has been discussed for years and is regarded as one of the most significant matchups in boxing. Fury had been expected to comfortably beat Ngannou, setting up an undisputed fight against Oleksandr Usyk on December 23. The Hall of Fame promoter claims that Joshua previously passed up offers and is now out of the title picture. Warren told Mail Sport: 'No, he (Joshua) didn’t want to fight him last December. We made the offer. So you know where he is now. He’s at the back of that long queue.' Warren added, 'They were not interested in fighting for a world title after losing twice to Usyk. He didn’t want to fight for a world title, otherwise he would have taken the opportunity when it was offered to him.' Joshua has secured two victories in 2023 as he attempts to rebuild after consecutive losses to Usyk. The former two-time world champion appears to be positioning himself for a future showdown with Fury, but Warren noted that potential rematches with Usyk and Ngannou mean Joshua is unlikely to be considered as Fury’s opponent any time soon.

article_content: On Thursday, Oregon’s attorney general Ellen Rosenblum declared that the state will not defend its ban on same-sex marriage in court, asserting the law cannot withstand a federal constitutional challenge. Despite this, Rosenblum noted in court documents that Oregon must continue to enforce the ban while related federal litigation is ongoing. The legal stance arrives in response to a federal lawsuit aiming to overturn the state’s prohibition of same-sex marriage, a law enacted through the voter-approved Measure 36 in 2004. That amendment defined marriage in the state constitution exclusively as a union between one man and one woman. Previously, in 2013, Oregon officials instructed state agencies to recognize same-sex marriages performed out of state. The latest filings stress that the marriage ban lacks constitutional support at the federal level, but that enforcement will persist until the courts deliver a decision.

article_content: India's 14th National Electricity Plan (NEP) sets out to more than triple the country's renewable energy capacity by 2030, according to a report released on Wednesday by the global energy think tank Ember. However, achieving this goal will require an estimated USD 293 billion in investment. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has called for a global tripling of renewable energy capacity and a doubling of energy efficiency by 2030 to help phase out fossil fuels and limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Over 60 countries, led by the US, the European Union (EU), and the UAE, have pledged to pursue these targets. The G20 nations, during India's presidency, also endorsed tripling global renewable energy capacity by 2030. The UAE, host of this year's UN climate conference (COP28), is advocating for a formal global agreement on these goals. Ember's analysis shows India will need an additional USD 101 billion to expand its renewable energy capacity further and align with the IEA's net-zero emissions scenario. The IEA's Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario outlines a global path to net zero CO2 emissions, starting with advanced economies reaching net zero before others. In essence, 'net zero' means balancing greenhouse gases emitted with those removed from the atmosphere. According to Ember, India is already planning a significant increase in renewables, making the tripling target achievable. But to align with the IEA's net-zero scenario, India would need even more ambitious targets, generating about 32% of its energy from solar and 12% from wind by 2030. To reach this, India needs to add 115 GW of solar and 9 GW of wind capacity by 2030 — above the targets laid out in NEP14. This would bring India's total renewable capacity to 448 GW of solar and 122 GW of wind by 2030. India currently targets 500 GW of installed capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030. Between 2023 and 2030, the country needs USD 293 billion to meet its solar and wind goals. To align with the IEA scenario and net-zero pathway, an additional USD 101 billion will be required. Ember's report also highlights issues such as payment delays and challenging regulations that discourage much-needed investment. The required financing to reach both NEP14 and the IEA net-zero scenario far exceeds India's current investment capacity. Neshwin Rodrigues, Ember’s India Electricity Policy Analyst, noted: 'Despite investment risks, India needs financing to build capacity in renewables, storage, and transmission to meet the NEP14 targets. Achieving alignment with the global net-zero pathway will require much more financing at competitive rates. Access to such finance is crucial for India, especially to avoid adding new coal capacity to meet rising demand in the coming decade.'

article_content: Chapel Hill police are actively searching for a second individual in connection with the murder of University of North Carolina student body president Eve Carson. Enhanced surveillance images from an ATM showed an unknown male in the back seat of Carson's Toyota Highlander when her card was used, while a different unidentified man, wearing a hooded sweatshirt and an old-school Houston Astros cap, appeared in the driver's seat. Carson, just 22 years old, was discovered fatally shot near the UNC campus. Her vehicle was recovered abandoned close to her home the day after her death. Medical officials confirmed she died from gunshot wounds and found no evidence of sexual assault or other injuries. The incident has brought the community together in mourning. Over a thousand people gathered for her funeral in Athens, Georgia. UNC has announced a memorial service to be held after spring break. During a significant campus basketball match, UNC players wore 'Eve' patches on their uniforms and Duke supporters wore blue ribbons as signs of respect, with both groups observing a moment of silence. article_content: Valentina Drofa, Co-Founder and CEO of Drofa Comms—a leading PR firm in finance and fintech—offers her insights on the growing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in business operations. As of 2023, AI continues to be a major topic of discussion, with the market valued at $207 billion. Some recent studies indicate that integrating AI into the average workplace could potentially disadvantage workers. Drawing from her own leadership experience, Drofa explores how AI can be utilized in company operations and the possible repercussions. AI supports better scheduling and time management for company leaders. Tools powered by AI can automate meeting arrangements by considering participant availability and time zones, as well as recommending efficient meeting times and planning travel routes, accounting for traffic, weather, and transportation costs. This automation enables executives to concentrate on more pressing tasks, thereby boosting productivity. Although some argue that personal assistants can manage such responsibilities, the ability of AI to rapidly process large data sets brings considerable efficiency, making daily routines more streamlined. AI is also useful for automating routine management responsibilities like documenting client meetings, preparing regular progress reports, and issuing reminders. This allows managers to focus on higher-level strategic work that benefits from human input. Nonetheless, ethical considerations arise, especially regarding the use of AI chatbots in client communications. In public relations, many clients appreciate personal contact; thus, it is recommended to discuss with each client the intended use of AI before commencing long-term collaborations. There are ongoing concerns about workforce reductions due to AI, underscored by cultural references and real events. For example, nearly 4,000 tech jobs in the U.S. were cut in May 2023 as companies such as IBM, Google, and Dropbox cited AI-driven changes. This trend is leading to calls for regulatory frameworks to safeguard jobs. Drofa concludes that AI should enhance, not replace, human employees. By leveraging AI’s efficiencies alongside human expertise and emotional intelligence, businesses can drive innovation and improved results.

article_content: Cricket fans from all corners of the country are headed to Ahmedabad, eager to witness what many consider a once-in-a-lifetime sporting event. The Narendra Modi Stadium, which seats over 130,000 spectators, is preparing to host the highly anticipated ICC World Cup final between India and Australia this Sunday. The buzz around the match has sent demand skyrocketing across several sectors. More than 100 charter flights have been booked, ferrying high-profile guests to the city. This intense demand has pushed airfares up by six to eight times their usual rates, with hotel prices increasing by as much as 29 times. Car rental companies are thriving, and liquor permit applications in Gujarat—a dry state—have reached an all-time high. For instance, the lowest one-way flight from Hyderabad to Ahmedabad on Sunday costs Rs 40,000, while fares from Bengaluru and Delhi stand at Rs 29,000 and Rs 22,500 respectively. Charter flight operators are overwhelmed with requests, and the cost of hiring a six-seater Beechcraft now ranges between Rs 8 and 12 lakh per day, with prices rising due to soaring demand. Assembly elections have intensified the logistics situation. In hospitality, five-star room rates, which would typically be Rs 6,500-12,500 (excluding taxes), have now surged to between Rs 25,000 and Rs 2 lakh for the weekend. Even budget hotels are charging more than ten times their usual rates. The unprecedented hike in flight and hotel prices began before India's qualification for the final, and has only accelerated since. Bharatt Malik of Yatra Online described this level of demand as previously unseen. Ahmedabad airport is gearing up to manage the rush, granting extra flight slots and reserving 16 parking bays for charter aircraft. Operators will drop off travelers and then relocate to nearby cities, such as Surat, Bhavnagar, Rajkot, and Vadodara, for parking. Additional processes are in place in case of overflow, ensuring parking on unused areas of the airport. Some lucky fans have managed to secure flights, while others are undertaking long road trips, covering nearly 1,000 km to reach Ahmedabad. The economic excitement is palpable, with airlines, hotels, and car rental companies experiencing robust growth. The airport and hospitality industry are working to ensure smooth operations during this historic event.

article_content: Javier Bardem and his family are closing their Madrid restaurant, La Bardemcilla, after two years of ongoing financial losses. This closure is a result of Spain's ongoing economic crisis, which has had a significant impact on small businesses. A statement from Bardem, his mother Pilar, and his siblings Monica and Carlos confirmed that the restaurant in the Chueca district will permanently close, resulting in eleven staff members losing their jobs. The family’s other restaurant in the Santa Ana area will remain open. Reporting by EFE news agency revealed that the family tried to save the restaurant by injecting funds several times but ultimately found the business model unsustainable. It is not yet certain if the restaurant’s staff will receive severance pay. The Bardem family's statement emphasized that, like many small companies in Spain, La Bardemcilla must close its doors without government assistance. The closure comes just months after Bardem drew criticism from a politician in Spain’s ruling party after he suggested to El Pais that high unemployment figures benefit the government. Bardem, married to actress Penelope Cruz and winner of the 2007 Best Supporting Actor Oscar for No Country for Old Men, was born in Gran Canaria. Spain’s unemployment has reached a record high, with over five million people out of work and more than 56% of young adults between 18 and 25 unemployed, as the recession continues for a fifth year.

Nelba Marquez-Greene, whose six-year-old daughter Ana Grace was among the 26 victims of Adam Lanza’s attack at Sandy Hook Elementary School on December 14, 2012, wrote a heartfelt message to America’s teachers as the new school year began. Her open letter, published on the Education Week website, expressed gratitude and admiration for educators, describing them as heroes and commending their bravery after the tragedy. She highlighted the courage of the Sandy Hook teachers, six of whom lost their lives protecting students, and praised those who returned to work despite enduring unimaginable trauma. Marquez-Greene—a marriage and family therapist and the mental health director at the nonprofit Sandy Hook Promise—shared her hope that teachers, through courage, faith, and love, would support children recovering from trauma.

At a January press event, Marquez-Greene and her husband Jimmy Greene spoke about promising to face the future with resilience after losing their daughter. She urged that no parent or caregiver should have to experience such pain and advocated for tougher gun laws. The couple emerged as prominent voices for anti-violence initiatives, speaking publicly and appearing on national news outlets like ABC News.

Marquez-Greene encouraged teachers to pay special attention to students who seem isolated, noting that even small gestures can provide comfort and security. She suggested that teachers are especially important for students facing difficult odds, possibly preventing future tragedies. Though she received 15,000 letters after the shooting, Marquez-Greene keeps just one by her bedside—from her own high school English teacher—emphasizing the lasting impact educators have. As she wrote, 'Real heroes don’t wear capes—they work in America’s schools.'

article_content: MONROVIA, Liberia — Liberian President George Weah is seeking re-election in Tuesday’s polls, hoping that his record on infrastructure, such as improving roads, healthcare facilities, and extending electricity, will outweigh the nation’s ongoing economic difficulties. Weah faces 19 opponents, including main challenger Joseph Boakai, who was vice president under Ellen Johnson Sirleaf — Africa’s first democratically elected female president. Weah, 57, a celebrated former international football player, voted with his family at a Paynesville elementary school and stated: “Liberians are exercising their democratic rights... It is the people’s election and they will decide who becomes their president.” Boakai’s campaign focuses on what he calls a 'rescue mission,' criticizing Weah’s leadership and pledging to reverse hardships faced by many Liberians. At a rally at Antoinette Tubman Stadium, Boakai said he and his running mate embody hope for change and relief from current struggles. Accusations against Weah include falling short on promises to fight corruption and to provide justice for victims of the country’s long civil wars, which cost about 250,000 lives between 1989 and 2003. In the 2017 election, Weah won with 61.5% of the vote, while Boakai secured 38.5%. Whether Weah can repeat his previous victory remains to be seen. Liberia’s 2.47 million eligible voters will also choose new legislators. According to political analyst Zoe McCathie from Signal Risk Consulting, 'Weah’s political position this election is not stronger than in 2017, given his mixed performance.' She noted that while policies like free public university have been well received, promises to fight corruption and improve the economy have not materialized, leading to decreased support. Election-related violence has already claimed at least two lives in Foya, Lofa county, with both ruling and opposition parties blaming each other for the clashes on September 29. Liberia, initially founded in 1822 as a settlement for freed slaves from the United States, declared independence 25 years later. Its systems and capital, Monrovia, maintain historic ties to the U.S. Weah’s 2017 election marked Liberia’s first peaceful democratic transfer of power since the civil wars. He pledged to raise Liberia from a low-income to a middle-income country, but his government is widely seen as underperforming, especially economically. The economy has shrunk in two of the six years under his rule, with growth declining since 2021. Many Liberians, like voter Seah J. Trustmo, describe business conditions as 'turmoil' and life as 'very, very hard.' Persistent corruption continues to hinder growth, with Afrobarometer’s 2023 research indicating most Liberians feel corruption has increased and the government is not addressing it effectively. Weah has also faced criticism for being abroad for seven weeks late last year, including at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to watch his son play for the U.S. national team. Widespread protests have taken place during his presidency, and analysts caution that disputed electoral results could lead to further unrest, although most believe Liberia’s overall stability is not at risk. Despite political challenges, Weah remains Africa’s only Ballon d’Or winner, having played for clubs such as Paris Saint-Germain, AC Milan, Chelsea, and Manchester City. His son Tim Weah, age 23, plays for Juventus and the U.S. national team. Report by Chinedu Asadu from Lagos, Nigeria, with contribution from Krista Larson in Dakar, Senegal.

article_content: It seems being removed from a flight has become something of a celebrity rite of passage. Over the years, numerous stars have made headlines for disruptive behavior at 35,000 feet—from public outbursts and rule-breaking to outright confrontations with airline staff or fellow passengers. Here are some of the most notable incidents: Cranberries lead singer Dolores O'Riordan was detained after an alleged violent incident on a flight from New York to Ireland in 2014. Reports differ on details, but the event stemmed from a disagreement involving a scone, and passengers complained about the band's disruptive actions, including smoking and swearing at crew members. Gallagher later quipped he would 'rather walk to Australia than fly with Cathay Pacific.' She admitted to kicking and spitting at police officers and was subsequently sentenced to community service and fined after pleading guilty to assault. According to other passengers, Baldwin responded aggressively to requests to turn his device off. Following the incident, the game saw a surge in popularity. Ivana Trump was escorted off a Palm Beach–New York flight in 2009 after reportedly shouting and swearing at children and other passengers. The disturbance prompted the pilot to return the plane to the gate, where local law enforcement assisted in her departure. Green Day frontman Billie Joe Armstrong was removed from a Southwest flight in 2011 after refusing to pull up his sagging trousers, despite a request from airline staff. After the incident, Armstrong tweeted about his ejection; Southwest Airlines later apologized and offered him a new booking. French actor Gerard Depardieu was asked to leave a CityJet flight in 2008 after urinating into a bottle while the plane was still on the tarmac and the toilets were locked. Some urine reportedly spilled on the carpet, resulting in a two-hour delay for cleaning. No charges were filed in the case.

article_content: A massive car pileup involving at least 140 vehicles occurred Thursday on Interstate 10 near Beaumont, Texas, resulting in two deaths and injuring at least 80 people. The collision left vehicles stacked on top of each other and prompted a large emergency response along a two-mile stretch of the highway. Debra Leggio, 60, and her husband, Vincent Leggio, 64, residents of Pearland, Texas, died after their 2007 Chevrolet SUV was struck by an 18-wheeler. Vincent Leggio worked as an electrician, and both were grandparents. The first crash in a series of collisions began around 9 a.m. as hundreds of drivers traveled for Thanksgiving. Dense fog along the highway reduced visibility, causing vehicles to slam into the wreck, which quickly escalated. More than 50 people were taken to hospitals in Beaumont, Port Arthur, and Winnie, with at least eight critically hurt. The most seriously injured were transported to Houston, about 75 miles away. Baptist Beaumont Hospital received at least 21 patients, including three with head injuries who were sent to Houston. According to Deputy Rod Carroll of the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office, the fog was so thick that first responders initially didn't realize there were multiple accidents. The westbound lanes have since reopened, but the eastbound lanes remained closed for much of Thursday. Chief Charles Sonnier of the Labelle-Fannett Volunteer Fire Department reported that seven tractor trailers collided, including two carrying hazardous materials, though no leaks were detected. Firefighters had to use the jaws of life to free people from vehicles. The pileup included cars, minivans, pickups, tractor-trailer trucks, and several FedEx vehicles. Video footage showed mangled vehicles and people receiving medical attention along the roadside. Uninjured drivers aided the wounded and supported emergency workers at the scene. Authorities stressed the importance of community support and highlighted the challenges faced due to holiday traffic and low visibility.

article_content: Pope Francis appointed 19 new cardinals on Saturday in a ceremony held at St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican. This marks the first time he has named new cardinals since becoming pope in March of last year. The newly appointed cardinals hail from around the globe, including Brazil, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, South Korea, and Haiti. Each received the traditional biretta—a red cap—and a ring during a formal ceremony called a public consistory. The biretta's scarlet color represents the cardinals' readiness to sacrifice their lives for their faith. Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI, appearing frail, attended the ceremony alongside current cardinals in St. Peter's Basilica. Benedict, who became the first pope in nearly 600 years to resign last year, had said he would lead a life of seclusion and study. His presence at the ceremony, together with Francis and the cardinal-electors, was highly unusual. According to Vatican Radio, 16 of the new cardinals are under 80 years old and are eligible to vote in a papal conclave. The remaining three, chosen for their exceptional service to the Vatican and the Catholic Church, are over 80. Among them, 98-year-old Archbishop Loris Capovilla—former secretary to Pope John XXIII—was not present but will receive his biretta in the coming days. Two of the new cardinals already occupy significant roles within the Vatican: Archbishop Pietro Parolin serves as Secretary of State, and Archbishop Gerhard Mueller heads the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the Church's chief doctrinal office. No Americans were among the new cardinals, but Canadian Archbishop Gerald Cyprien Lacroix from Quebec was included. In a letter sent last month to the newly selected clergy, Pope Francis advised that becoming a cardinal is not a promotion, honor, or decoration, but a call to serve with broader vision and greater humility. Vatican spokesman Father Federico Lombardi highlighted the geographic diversity of the appointees, noting that the selection of cardinals from countries such as Burkina Faso and Haiti demonstrates the Church's concern for populations affected by poverty.

A Reuters investigation has uncovered more than 600 previously unreported workplace injuries at SpaceX sites across the U.S. since 2014, including severe injuries such as amputations and head trauma, along with one death. These incidents were particularly prevalent at major SpaceX facilities in Texas and California, where injury rates were significantly higher than the industry standard.

In response, three Democratic lawmakers—Zoe Lofgren and Mark Takano from California and Donald Norcross from New Jersey—are pressing for heightened oversight. Lofgren called the findings "deeply concerning," while Takano labeled them "deeply troubling" and emphasized the need for accountability, especially in light of SpaceX's lucrative federal contracts. Norcross echoed these concerns and advocated for a comprehensive investigation into the safety lapses.

SpaceX has not publicly addressed the injuries or the congressional criticism. NASA, which has awarded SpaceX $11.8 billion to date, said its contracts mandate a strong safety culture and that the agency can enforce these requirements, though it has not offered public comment on SpaceX's record. Lori Garver, former deputy administrator at NASA, urged the agency to probe SpaceX's safety practices, highlighting the need for standards at least as rigorous as elsewhere in the industry given their government partnership.

Amid the scrutiny, SpaceX was preparing for another Starship test launch in Texas, following an earlier failed attempt.

article_content: Thirteen U.S. Army soldiers are currently quarantined at an American base in Vicenza, Italy, following a 30-day mission in Liberia supporting efforts against Ebola. None of the soldiers have shown symptoms of the virus, according to Major General Darryl Williams, commander of U.S. Army Forces in Africa, who is also quarantined. Speaking via video conference on Tuesday, General Williams reported that during the first three days of the 21-day quarantine, soldiers have eaten meals together, exercised, and communicated with their families through video calls. Morale remains high and the troops are proud of their contribution in Liberia. The quarantined soldiers are housed in a complex with barracks, a dining hall, and a gym. They are kept separate from other base personnel. Meals are dropped off by a team who leaves before the soldiers enter, and after eating, utensils, including plastic cutlery, are burned. Each soldier undergoes twice-daily temperature checks. General Williams said, 'We have what we need to eat well and stay active. I’m able to video chat with my family, including my granddaughter.' The soldiers were isolated after returning from Liberia, where they spent their deployment building treatment centers and training local health workers. The Army’s three-week quarantine for returning soldiers is currently unique among U.S. military branches, despite no direct contact with Ebola patients during their mission. The measure aims to reassure both military families and Italian authorities about the Army’s vigilance concerning Ebola. More than 3,000 U.S. troops are expected to participate in the operation in West Africa, with an additional 75 soldiers set to enter quarantine later this week. A decision on a unified military quarantine policy is expected soon from Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel.

article_content: Cows are among agriculture’s biggest contributors to climate change because they emit methane, a greenhouse gas much more potent than carbon dioxide. Around 940 million cows globally account for nearly 10% of greenhouse gas emissions, largely through digestion and manure. This has sparked major investment into ways of reducing emissions—ranging from biodigesters that capture methane from waste, to feed additives like seaweed and essential oils designed to limit methane production inside cows. A new project led by Nobel laureate Jennifer Doudna is putting $70 million toward gene-editing cows' gut microbes to lower their methane output further. With worldwide demand for meat and dairy growing, these innovations are crucial in meeting global climate goals. Yet some ask: why not just replace cattle products with plant-based foods? Research shows that cutting back on meat can lower a person’s carbon footprint by up to 75%. But in the US—home to the world’s fourth largest cattle herd and leading producer of beef and dairy—the cattle industry is deeply embedded, worth $275 billion, and cultural preferences run strong. Switching the country to plant-based diets is a major challenge. Beyond deep-rooted food traditions (like the average American eating about a pound of mozzarella each month), the farming economy and the country’s nutrition needs are closely tied to livestock agriculture. That’s why experts like EPA engineer Stephen Sturdivant recommend a broad mix of solutions instead of only focusing on diet changes. Meat and dairy consumption in the US remains on the rise. In 2021, beef consumption reached 20 billion pounds and Americans ate 12% more cheese, butter, and ice cream compared to the year before. But the environmental costs are high: making beef produces roughly 100 times more greenhouse gases than peas, while cheese production emits about eight times more than tofu. Even with America’s efficient livestock systems, 92 million cattle produce 4% of the nation’s total greenhouse gases, accounting for 40% of farm-based emissions. Even removing all cattle wouldn't solve everything. Studies show a completely animal-free agriculture system would only lower US emissions by about 2.6%—equivalent to three times Portugal’s annual emissions, but far from eliminating the problem. The change would also reshape what gets grown: acres formerly for cattle feed could shift toward crops like corn and soybeans, but these changes come with their own climate impacts. Livestock and crop farming depend on each other. Cattle provide manure, a natural fertilizer, and recycle byproducts (like peels and hulls) that would otherwise turn to landfill waste. Removing livestock would boost total calories produced by about 25%, but it would likely leave many short on vital nutrients such as vitamin B12, calcium, iron, and healthy fats. This could especially impact pregnant women, the elderly, and other vulnerable groups. These nutrition trade-offs often get overlooked when advocating for broad dietary shifts. Still, most beef is consumed by a small group, and not everyone’s food choices are swayed by climate concerns. Studies highlight the powerful role of social norms: changes are more likely when people see their friends and communities shifting diets. Encouragement and positive examples help more than guilt or criticism. Tackling the food sector’s climate impact requires a collective, multi-pronged strategy. Reducing food waste, making agriculture more efficient, and encouraging people to eat more sustainably are all key, according to the EPA’s Sturdivant. Many questions remain after an off-duty Alaska Airlines pilot, riding as a passenger in the cockpit, allegedly tried to shut down the plane's engines mid-flight, putting everyone on board at risk. Three passengers have now filed a lawsuit demanding a "forthright public explanation" from the airline about what happened. According to court documents, Joseph Emerson, the pilot, admitted he had not slept for 40 hours, was struggling with depression, and had taken psychedelic mushrooms two days before the incident. The plaintiffs are calling for improved security and mental health screening procedures for airline crew, arguing these measures could help prevent similar incidents in the future.

"The airlines need a wake-up call. We understand that most pilots are heroes every day for safely operating our airliners, but even they can suffer from sleeplessness, substance use, or mental health challenges," said Daniel Laurence, an aviation lawyer at The Stritmatter Firm, which represents the plaintiffs.

The article notes that pilots who disclose mental health concerns are often barred from flying, and suggests that the push for more thorough screenings faces resistance due to the insular and rigid culture within the industry. Emerson has been charged with 83 counts of attempted murder.

article_content: Annette Bhatti, a mother of two from Southampton, passed away at 49 from mesothelioma, a cancer linked to asbestos exposure. As a child, Annette was unknowingly exposed to asbestos because her father, Lawrence Ramplee, worked at shipyards where asbestos dust was common. She would greet him with hugs after work and help her mother wash his contaminated work clothes by hand, activities that released dangerous asbestos fibers into the family’s home—risks they were unaware of at the time. Annette was diagnosed with mesothelioma in June 2010. One month later, she married her long-term partner, Bal Bhatti. She lost her life just 18 months after her diagnosis, in December, leaving her family devastated, particularly her father, who feels deep guilt over her illness. Her asbestos exposure spanned from birth until she moved out at 18. Lawrence Ramplee’s employment at Hills Construction and Harland and Wolff in Hampshire exposed him, and by extension his family, to asbestos regularly. With her mother suffering from lung disease, Annette often took on the responsibility of washing her father's work clothes by hand, increasing her exposure. Coroner Keith Wiseman emphasized that while Annette’s situation is tragically familiar—family members being indirectly exposed to asbestos from a worker's clothing—it is unusual for someone as young as Annette to die from such exposure. After her passing, her brother Stuart shared how Annette continued to live life fully, travelling to places like Hong Kong, New York, Australia, the Seychelles, and Dubai in her final year. Her resilience and kindness inspired many, with hundreds attending her funeral. Annette is remembered by her husband and loved ones as selfless and compassionate, always prioritizing others and leaving an unforgettable legacy. The Bhatti family is pursuing compensation, supported by a recent Supreme Court decision that ruled insurance liability for asbestos diseases applies from the moment of exposure, not from when symptoms appear. This landmark ruling, praised by unions and victims' families, is expected to help thousands quickly secure compensation following lengthy legal disputes with insurers.

article_content: A student has taken the NekNominate craze for risky drinking dares to new heights by drinking a pint in the cockpit of a plane. Thorfinn Stout, 21, uploaded a video of himself seated at the front of a light aircraft, with one hand on the control column and the other holding what appears to be a pint of lager. It remains unclear who filmed Stout, a Stirling University student from Kirkwall, Orkney, as he performed this stunt. Stout was a passenger, not a co-pilot, and there is no evidence to suggest he was intoxicated. According to Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) regulations, it is illegal for a passenger to be drunk on board an aircraft. A representative from a Scottish flying school explained they ban all alcohol from their light aircraft for safety reasons. In the video, Stout says, 'Ready for a pint.' He quickly drinks the entire pint with his hands on the controls in front of him. After posting the video on Facebook, his friend Andy Croy jokingly commented about reports of an aircraft swerving over Kirkwall. CAA guidelines state that pilots should not allow passengers under the influence of alcohol, as they could endanger the flight. Drunkenness in an aircraft is a criminal offence under UK law. Stout, who is studying business studies and sports studies at Stirling University, could not be contacted for comment. The NekNominate trend, which reportedly originated in Perth, Australia, has gone global via social media. The game involves drinking, nominating someone else, and posting the video online, sometimes leading to extreme risks. Recently, there have been reports of fatalities linked to NekNominate, as some individuals consume large amounts of alcohol during these dares. Jack Simpson, an instructor at Edinburgh Flying Club, said allowing passengers to drink alcohol on light aircraft is 'inadvisable.' He stated, 'Alcohol and planes do not mix. Although it is not illegal for passengers to drink, it is strongly discouraged.' At his flying school, they require at least eight hours between drinking alcohol and flying. A spokesman for the CAA said: 'Passengers are not prohibited from drinking alcohol on board, but they must follow the instructions of the pilot at all times. If a passenger’s actions interfere with the pilot’s control of the aircraft, they could be charged with recklessly endangering the aircraft, which is a serious offence.' Stout’s mother, Anne Stout, from Kirkwall, said her son was not acting as co-pilot and declined to comment further. In another NekNominate video, Samuel Dyer, 29, from Haverfordwest, West Wales, risked his life by jumping off a cliff into rough seas while drinking alcohol as part of a dare.

The incident took place on August 17, as reported at an inquest. The couple left behind matching suicide notes before their deaths. Witnesses recalled seeing the car being driven deliberately across the downs and through a fence before plunging over the edge. No signs were observed from inside the vehicle suggesting either tried to escape. In the period preceding the tragedy, both Paul and Jacqueline appeared unhappy. They were last seen alive sharing a meal at the Culver Haven Inn, where staff noted no visible signs of distress. Bar manager Leslie Dyke mentioned an earlier occasion when a couple talked about driving off the cliff, although he could not verify if it was the same pair. Witness Edward Lyon described the vehicle maintaining a consistent speed as it crossed the grass and went over the cliff. Detective Sergeant Clare Crane testified that suicide notes were found with Paul Charles and at Jacqueline’s home. She said Jacqueline had previously discussed a suicide pact with friends, although at one point indicated she did not want to proceed. Police determined there were no suspicions of foul play, and the inquest continues.

Researchers at Nagoya University, led by Akira Yokoi, have developed cellulose nanofiber (CNF) sheets sourced from wood that can capture extracellular vesicles (EVs)—small, cancer-related particles involved in cell communication. Unlike conventional methods that need much larger samples and take longer, these eco-friendly, porous CNF sheets are capable of absorbing and preserving EVs from tiny amounts of bodily fluids and even from organ surfaces during surgery. Their gauze-like texture allows them to be easily applied and removed.

Published in Nature Communications, this breakthrough offers a promising new path for early cancer detection and personalized therapy. Using the CNF sheets, the team successfully isolated and studied EVs and their microRNA contents in mouse models of ovarian cancer and in human organ samples. The analysis revealed that unique microRNA patterns are associated with tumors and can change following surgery, giving doctors a new tool to assess disease status and tailor treatments—addressing the complexity within individual tumors.

Dr. Takahiro Ochiya, a recognized expert in the field, has called this method an exciting advance likely to spur new medical applications. The research group plans to further explore the use of EV analysis with CNF sheets to improve diagnosis and bring personalized medicine closer to reality.

article_content: Following the recent escalation between Israel and Hamas, German institutions have increasingly limited opportunities for Palestinian viewpoints—a move the authors warn could intensify anti-Semitism, violence, and suffering. Earlier this year, as researchers focused on Yugoslav socialism and the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), we were asked by Berlin’s Maxim Gorki Theatre to participate in an event on the modern significance of NAM, titled 'Lost – You Go Slavia.' The Maxim Gorki Theatre, established in 1952 in East Berlin and named after the writer Maxim Gorki, is recognized for being an inclusive and diverse theater venue. We felt privileged to speak on topics we deeply care about at such an esteemed institution. The Non-Aligned Movement originated during the Cold War, promoting alternatives to the era’s bipolar power structure and championing anti-colonialism, self-determination, and peaceful coexistence. As we noted in our announcement: While the world today is not simply divided as it was during the Cold War, risks of global conflict are growing; thus re-examining non-alignment is more important than ever. We looked forward to the October event until the situation was upended on October 7, when Hamas attacked Israeli civilians, causing around 1,400 deaths and kidnapping dozens. Israel responded with a siege and airstrikes in Gaza, leading to over 8,000 reported civilian deaths within several weeks. In the wake of those events, several German venues and organizations quickly restricted Palestinian speech. Litprom’s cancellation of a Frankfurt Book Fair award honoring Palestinian author Adania Shibli brought international outcry, spurring hundreds of writers—including Nobel laureates—to advocate for open space for Palestinian voices. The Maxim Gorki Theatre, too, postponed a performance of 'The Situation' and stated support for Israel after the Hamas attack, arguing that war divides the world into friends and foes and leaves little space for nuanced debate. After long reflection, we decided to withdraw from the event in protest against the theatre’s unilateral position regarding The Situation, drawing on our knowledge of Yugoslav history and rejecting the narrative that war demands binary divisions. We also maintain that condemning attacks on civilians cannot justify harming more civilians. Civilian casualties on all sides are tragic, and no aim can legitimize war crimes or ethnic cleansing, as past experiences have underscored. The ongoing debate about the Non-Aligned Movement’s history and its enduring support for Palestinian rights is essential, especially when such discourse is under threat in Germany. Our withdrawal is not meant as abandoning the conversation—it is a call for German institutions to rethink their current policies and to promote inclusive and critical dialogue on Israel-Palestine. We disagree with the notion that past wars offer no insight for today. The Yugoslav conflicts and the international community’s failures then provide clear lessons as we witness the violence in Gaza now. Yugoslavia under Tito supported establishing Israel and welcomed its Jewish community, while also upholding the right of Palestinians to self-determination and condemning colonialism and racism. NAM resolutions consistently paired support for the Palestinian cause with recognition of Israel’s legitimacy. The first NAM summit in 1961 supported regaining Palestinian rights in accordance with the UN Charter. Yugoslavia cut ties with Israel after the 1967 war, and did not reestablish them before Yugoslavia’s dissolution. At a 1977 NAM ministerial, Israeli settlements were criticized as major peace obstacles. Overall, NAM and Yugoslav stances show it’s possible to challenge colonialism and racism while supporting Israel’s right to exist—an often-overlooked view in Germany now. Germany and several Western countries appear to enforce a 'Denkverbot'—a ban on challenging established narratives—on Israel-Palestine issues. Our decision to leave the Gorki Theatre event protests this restrictive approach. We mourn all victims and vigorously reject anti-Semitism, but warn that suppressing discussion of Palestinian issues can backfire, leading to more divisions and making Middle East peace even harder to achieve.

The global cryptocurrency market continues to feel the effects of last year’s turbulent collapses, including the high-profile downfall of crypto exchange FTX. Prices, trading volumes, and venture capital (VC) funding remain well below their peaks from 2021.

Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, is currently on trial in New York, facing seven charges of fraud and conspiracy related to FTX’s sudden collapse in November 2022. He has pleaded not guilty.

FTX’s collapse was part of a series of events that sent Bitcoin to its lowest value since 2020. Although Bitcoin and other major tokens have partially rebounded, the sector is still far from the excitement and highs of late 2021.

Below are five charts highlighting changes in the crypto landscape:

BITCOIN’S PERFORMANCE
Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency and the main indicator for market sentiment, has recovered about 37% since November 1. After reaching a record $69,000 in November 2021, Bitcoin’s value was hit hard as central banks raised interest rates in early 2022. Riskier assets like cryptocurrencies suffered as investors sought safer, higher-yield returns. Bitcoin subsequently lost over 65% of its value in 2022, following the collapse of the stablecoin terraUSD. This event led to Singapore hedge fund Three Arrows Capital filing for bankruptcy, creating further instability.

Additional collapses followed, with FTX’s failure pushing Bitcoin below $16,000 in late 2022. Bitcoin experienced another setback when Silvergate Bank, a key banking partner for the crypto sector in the U.S., announced its closure in 2023. Despite these issues, Bitcoin has regained about three-quarters of its value this year amid renewed interest from major financial firms like BlackRock and expectations that rate hikes may slow. As of this Monday, Bitcoin traded at around $28,089.

Ben Laidler, global markets strategist at eToro, commented, “The FTX debacle came at the end of an annus horribilis that had already seen a tech sector collapse, sharply higher interest rates, and self-inflicted industry wounds.”

MARKET CAPITALIZATION DROP
The total market capitalization for cryptocurrencies peaked at $3 trillion in November 2021. It plunged to a two-year low of $796 billion as FTX collapsed in late 2022. Since then, the market has partly recovered, hovering above $1 trillion for much of this year.

Usman Ahmad, CEO of Zodia Markets (owned by Standard Chartered), noted, “The issues with FTX have undoubtedly hit confidence in the crypto ecosystem at large.”

CHANGING BITCOIN VOLATILITY
Although known for volatility, Bitcoin has stabilized somewhat in 2023. Still, some observers say this stability could reduce opportunities for quick gains, which attract many investors. Anders Kvamme Jensen, founder of crypto firm AKJ, said, “We expect low to medium volatility over the near term.”

SLOWING VC INVESTMENT
VC funding poured into crypto in 2021 and continued through 2022 but slowed sharply this year as several firms sustained losses from the market’s downturn. U.S. VC investments in crypto totaled $6.12 billion in Q1 2022 but decreased to $870 million in Q1 2023, according to PitchBook. article_content: Christine Levinson went to the United Nations on Monday seeking answers about her husband, Bob Levinson, a former FBI agent who disappeared in Iran in 2007. Christine Levinson sought assistance from Zalmay Khalilzad, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N. She traveled to New York with three of her seven children, hoping to meet Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, who was at the U.N. for a scheduled speech on Tuesday afternoon. However, Ahmadinejad declined to meet with her. "I'm disappointed," she said. Levinson did meet with Ambassador Khalilzad, who told her he would do everything possible to help. She was accompanied by her children: Susan, 31, Sarah, 28, and Douglas, 14. Bob Levinson vanished in March 2007 during a business trip to Kish Island, Iran. He is a retired FBI agent from Coral Springs, Florida. After his career with the FBI, Levinson worked as a security consultant focusing on cigarette smuggling. Over the past year and a half, Christine Levinson has worked tirelessly to bring attention to her husband's disappearance. She has given interviews, met with State Department officials, launched the website www.helpboblevinson.com, and organized a rally. She also offered a $5,000 reward, primarily targeted at Iranians who might have information. So far, these efforts have not produced any leads. "Nothing," she said. Last year, Christine Levinson traveled to Iran to retrace her husband's steps. Iranian officials told her they would investigate and contact her with information, but she has not received any updates. "They told me they would let me know when they have information and would continue searching for Bob," she told CNN. Christine Levinson has denied her husband was on U.S. government business when he disappeared, stating he was a private citizen, and both the State Department and the FBI have also denied he was working for the government. The State Department has demanded that Iran release Levinson if he is being held. Christine Levinson notes her husband suffers from diabetes and high blood pressure, but she remains confident he is alive because "I haven't heard anything bad." At times, she listens to his voicemail just to hear his voice. "I still firmly believe he is alive," she says. "Every day, I tell my children to take things one day at a time. I just want him to know I'm still looking for him. I'll never stop looking for him."

article_content: In a significant policy shift, the United States announced Wednesday that it will join direct talks between the United Nations, European powers, and Iran regarding Tehran's nuclear program, according to the State Department. This move is part of the Obama administration's effort to engage Iran diplomatically. State Department spokesman Robert Wood stated that the Obama administration has requested European Union foreign policy chief Javier Solana to invite Iran to new negotiations with the five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council and Germany. "If Iran accepts, we hope this will be an opportunity to seriously engage Iran on resolving the issues that have persisted in recent years and to cooperatively address international concerns about its nuclear program," said Wood. Iran has thus far refused to comply with Security Council demands to halt its uranium enrichment, asserting that the enriched uranium is for nuclear power generation. The United States has accused Iran of concealing attempts to develop a nuclear weapon, and the U.N.'s nuclear watchdog agency has stated that questions about Iran's nuclear program remain unresolved. Previously, the Bush administration demanded that Iran suspend its nuclear activities before any direct talks could occur. Wednesday’s announcement marks a continued effort by the Obama administration to open diplomatic channels with Iran after nearly thirty years without formal relations. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton briefly commented on the decision, noting, "Pursuing careful engagement on many issues that affect both U.S. and global interests with Iran makes sense." Clinton added, "There is nothing more important than convincing Iran to end efforts aimed at obtaining a nuclear weapon." These remarks came during a meeting with Panama’s foreign minister at the State Department. Since 1980, the U.S. has not had diplomatic ties with Iran, and previously participated in talks only as an observer. Wood declined to speculate about the possibility of direct U.S.-Iran meetings. "It’s too early to discuss that," he said. Iran’s initial response to U.S. overtures has been cautious. On Wednesday evening, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad said on state television, "Washington has no right to dictate how other nations should live." He further stated, "Those who possess nuclear bombs are behind the times, because the era of threats is over." The official IRNA news agency reported Ahmadinejad expressed readiness to cooperate on nuclear disarmament, provided it does not obstruct countries intending to produce nuclear fuel for civilian purposes. No date has been set for the next 'P-5 plus 1' meeting, which includes the U.S., Britain, France, Russia, China, and Germany. The announcement reflects ongoing signals from both the U.S. and Iran suggesting the possibility of significant diplomatic change. In March, President Obama addressed the Iranian people through a televised message offering diplomatic engagement. Clinton also attended a conference in the Netherlands where she met an Iranian official, but they did not hold direct one-on-one talks. During his presidential campaign, Obama advocated for talks with Iran without preconditions—a stance that had been criticized by Clinton and others. Obstacles to improving U.S.-Iran relations remain, such as the recent charging of American journalist Roxana Saberi with espionage in Iran. Clinton stated that the U.S. had asked Switzerland—representing U.S. interests in Iran—for updated information about Saberi, who has been jailed for almost three months. At the March 31 meeting in the Netherlands, the U.S. delivered a note requesting a response about Saberi and other detained or missing Americans in Iran. U.S. officials report they are still waiting for a response. Reported by CNN’s Charley Keyes.

article_content: The entire South Devon hamlet of Bantham will go on the market this Friday, including its beach, boathouses, golf course, and pub. The 728-acre estate, owned by the same family since 1922, is listed for £10 million. Bantham is known for its tranquil atmosphere, featuring one pub and a village shop. Most properties have been rented by residents for generations. The village's 21 homes and other properties are being listed for sale after a dispute involving a food van. Gillian Goddard, one of the estate's directors, permitted a 'gastrobus' to serve visitors, sparking complaints from locals who opposed increasing commercial activity. Following the backlash, Goddard changed her mind about bequeathing the estate to the community and amended her will to require the property be sold. Goddard passed away in November, and the sale is being managed by estate agents Strutt and Parker. If no single buyer emerges, the estate may be divided into six lots. Many residents, who rent their homes, are concerned about what might change. Rod Seymour, landlord of The Sloop Inn, noted that most families have been in Bantham for generations, and only one property has sold in the past five years. Other residents expressed fears that an outsider might evict tenants and convert cottages into a boutique hotel.
