article_content: Paris is grappling with a notable increase in bed bug presence, with sightings across public transport and at the Charles-de-Gaulle Airport. The issue, gaining attention in the lead-up to the city hosting the 2024 Summer Olympics, has officials calling for swift and decisive intervention. Social media users have shared videos of their encounters with bed bugs, adding to public concern. In reaction, French Transport Minister Clement Beaune is organizing discussions with public transit authorities this week. Paris city leaders are urging the federal government to form a special task force to battle the surge. Deputy Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire recently pressed Prime Minister Elisabeth Borne for a national action plan to address bed bugs, emphasizing the urgency due to the upcoming Olympic and Paralympic Games. Gregoire stated on social media that the problem can affect anyone. Bed bugs, known scientifically as Cimex lectularius, have a long history of plaguing humans and nearly disappeared in the mid-20th century thanks to effective pesticides. Their comeback is attributed to evolved resistance to such chemicals and a rise in global travel. An ANSES report indicated that from 2017 to 2022, more than 10% of French households dealt with infestations. The issue crosses social divides, but the cost of proper extermination can especially burden low-income families. Bed bugs do not transmit diseases, but their bites cause significant irritation. Some scientists suspect their presence could make allergies worse, though this link is still under investigation.

The station has encouraged supporters to contact Verizon in protest. Bridges TV was launched in 2004 with the goal of fostering diversity and innovation in media. Recently, a judge approved a settlement awarding shares in the channel to the Hassan children, including Muzzammil Hassan's two older children.

Ohio's new constitutional protections for abortion and reproductive rights take effect on December 7, following a decisive 57% majority vote last month. The amendment guarantees an individual’s right to make and carry out personal reproductive decisions. Although this marks a notable victory, making Ohio the seventh state to support abortion access in statewide votes since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, the timeline and manner of these changes remain uncertain.

Abortion-related lawsuits have resumed now that voters have settled the issue, raising questions about how the amendment will be implemented. The amendment itself did not repeal any of Ohio’s existing abortion laws, so the courts now must determine which remain valid and which are inconsistent with the new constitutional protections. Legal scholars, such as Professor Laura Hermer from Mitchell Hamline School of Law, expect complex and potentially lengthy judicial processes ahead, alongside minimal immediate action from the Republican-led legislature.

Democrats in the Ohio House responded soon after the vote by introducing legislation to repeal major restrictions, such as the state’s ban on most abortions after fetal cardiac activity is detected (about six weeks) and the 24-hour waiting period. Representative Beth Liston and House Minority Leader Allison Russo emphasized the importance of comprehensive solutions and expressed hope that courts would uphold the will of voters.

Chief Justice Sharon Kennedy requested that attorneys for both the state and abortion clinics explain how the amendment influences current litigation regarding Ohio’s six-week abortion ban, which is on hold. Meanwhile, a federal judge made a similar request in a separate lawsuit challenging operational requirements for abortion providers.

Anti-abortion groups like Faith2Action continue to urge lawmakers to counter or limit the effects of the amendment, but Republican leaders—including House Speaker Jason Stephens and Senate President Matt Huffman—have ruled out immediate efforts to overturn or undermine Issue 1 in 2024. Attorney General Dave Yost has stated that the amendment introduces a new legal standard for abortion access, which could put many existing Ohio laws at risk of being invalidated, though he notes that his prior legal analysis is not binding.

As Ohio’s government, judiciary, and advocacy groups navigate this evolving legal environment, the full impact and practical effects of the state’s new constitutional protections remain to be seen.

Many leaders imagine that inspiring speeches and passionate motivation are at the heart of strong leadership. Well-known figures such as Steve Jobs and Winston Churchill often serve as models for this intense, charismatic style. However, research indicates that employees usually prefer leaders who are more collaborative and supportive. According to data from over a million participants in the 'What's Your Leadership Style' test, the most favored leaders are Idealists—people who inspire optimism, encourage participation, and promote individual growth. While Idealists work hard, they prioritize ensuring everyone has a voice and can contribute creatively.

Too much intensity from leaders can overshadow others and suppress input. Studies reveal that dominant leaders can boost the energy of quiet or passive teams, but proactive and outgoing employees may find such intensity overwhelming. In those cases, a more balanced, inclusive leader is more effective.

Leadership IQ research found that only 24% of employees reported their leaders consistently encouraged and recognized their suggestions. Those who do feel heard are about 12 times more likely to recommend their workplace as a great employer.

Today’s workers are eager to share their ideas and feel listened to, not just be lectured at. Employee engagement is strongly linked to leaders who pay attention to feedback and support improvement. While traditional culture has celebrated commanding, outspoken leaders, many successful leaders embrace the importance of stepping back and creating space for others.

Julian Francis, CEO of Beacon Building Products, suggests leaders should 'occupy as little space as possible,' particularly in decision-making. While leaders must sometimes take center stage, empowering teams by stepping aside encourages growth and engagement.

article_content: On July 30, 2012, President Barack Obama visited New York City to attend an exclusive fundraising dinner costing $40,000 per person, which was expected to cause significant rush hour traffic delays. This trip came just six weeks after a star-studded fundraising event at actress Sarah Jessica Parker’s Manhattan home, which raised $4.5 million for the President’s re-election campaign. It is unclear how the expenses for the trip—including Obama’s travel on Air Force One and Marine One—were covered. New York State Republicans criticized the President, dubbing him the ‘Campaigner-in-Chief’ and urging him to prioritize job creation and economic growth instead of focusing on the upcoming November election. Upon arrival at JFK Airport shortly before 5 p.m., Obama greeted young New Yorkers who had assembled to see him. He then traveled to Manhattan on Marine One, followed by a motorcade to the upscale NoMad Hotel in the Flatiron District. Around 8 p.m., he addressed approximately 60 prominent donors at the event, which reportedly raised $2.4 million for his campaign against Republican opponent Mitt Romney. During the dinner, Obama expressed confidence about the election, while emphasizing the importance of keeping pace with Romney’s campaign spending, particularly from super PACs investing heavily in negative ads. He noted that Democrats did not need to match spending dollar-for-dollar but had to ensure their message reached voters effectively. Obama also discussed ongoing efforts to address economic challenges, acknowledging that recovery had not yet reached all Americans. The President returned to Washington, D.C., around 10 p.m. As a security requirement, Obama uses official government aircraft and travels with a significant Secret Service detail. For campaign-related travel, it is standard practice for the Democratic Party to reimburse some of these expenses to the government. Often, fundraising events are combined with official presidential duties, meaning costs are shared between taxpayers and the campaign. Republicans have consistently criticized Obama’s focus on fundraising rather than economic matters. Ed Cox, chairman of the New York State Republican Party, pointed out that Obama’s Jobs Council had not met publicly in six months, while in the same period, Cox claimed, the President attended over 100 fundraisers and played 11 rounds of golf. In June, Obama visited Manhattan for two campaign fundraising events that collectively raised $4.5 million. One event was hosted by Sarah Jessica Parker with Anna Wintour, and another at the Plaza Hotel featured a performance by Mariah Carey.

article_content: Ilham Tohti, a prominent Uyghur academic, received a life sentence from a court in Xinjiang's capital, Urumqi, on charges of separatism after a tightly controlled two-day trial. Previously an economics professor at Minzu University in Beijing, Tohti also had all his assets seized. Detained with several students in January, he spent months in custody before being formally accused of trying to undermine China's unity. Tohti's lawyers argued that he sought not independence but constructive discussion to improve policies affecting Uyghurs. Throughout the proceedings, they emphasized his calls for human rights, legal protections, and meaningful autonomy for Xinjiang—all carried out through peaceful advocacy. China's judicial system, under Communist Party control, posts a conviction rate nearly 100%, with few acquittals. The verdict provoked swift international backlash, with organizations like Amnesty International and U.S. officials labeling the sentence unjust and a violation of human rights. American authorities described Tohti as a bridge-builder between Uyghur and Han communities. Prosecutors accused Tohti of collaborating with foreign entities to stir division, promoting separatist beliefs, and encouraging students to oppose the state. In response, his defense insisted his actions amounted only to critical commentary and nonviolent reform efforts. Accounts from Tohti's legal team highlighted difficult jail conditions, including shackling, lack of warm clothing, and a hunger strike staged by Tohti in protest. While a few family members were allowed to observe the trial, diplomats and journalists were kept away. Ongoing tensions in Xinjiang stem from claims by Uyghurs of systematic discrimination in jobs, education, religious practice, and business opportunities. Human rights groups and exiled activists have traced recent unrest to stricter government controls—a stance Chinese officials reject.

article_content: Wayne Head, a 35-year-old convicted robber, escaped from HMP Leyhill, an open prison in South Gloucestershire, to get away from the widespread drug culture that was affecting his life, according to the court. He reportedly spent his savings on 'legal highs' that were easily accessible inside the jail. Before his transfer to Leyhill, Head was described as a model inmate. He left the Category D facility and traveled to Plymouth, Devon, where he visited family memorials at a local crematorium. After being at large for four days, he surrendered to police following a public appeal. Head pleaded guilty to absconding from custody in August and was sentenced to four months in prison. He is now in a more secure facility. Head had already served over six years for a robbery committed in August 2007, for which he had received an indeterminate sentence. His defense barrister, Ali Rafati, told Plymouth Crown Court that Head had maintained a good record until his transfer to Leyhill in April. There, access to legal highs led him to spend all his savings. Mr Rafati said, 'It became too much for him, so he stepped over the fence.' After arriving in Plymouth, Head visited the crematorium before a family member encouraged him to turn himself in. Head is expected to be transferred to Channings Wood prison in Denbury, Devon, about 35 miles from his home. Judge Recorder Malcolm Galloway told Head that escaping could harm his prospects for parole and release, which was anticipated in December. UK prisons are categorized from A (highest security) to D (open prisons). Category D facilities are for low-risk prisoners preparing for release, often allowing them to work in the community and visit home. The judge told Head, 'They may have difficulty concluding you are no longer a risk because you absconded.' A Prison Service spokesperson said that anyone who absconds is returned to a secure prison and may face further charges. The spokesperson added that there are ongoing efforts to keep drugs out of prisons, including random drug testing and cooperation with the police, and expressed support for a proposed bill that would allow for testing for legal highs. HMP Leyhill is a minimum-security prison that holds some prisoners serving life sentences and has come under scrutiny due to a lack of a perimeter fence and several escapes. Former Energy Secretary Chris Huhne was moved from Wandsworth Prison to Leyhill early in his sentence for perverting the course of justice. Leyhill has drawn attention in recent years for its security challenges. Legal highs, sometimes marketed as plant food or other seemingly harmless products, are easily found online and have dangerous effects. In a related case, Timothy Stern, 31, left Leyhill in September and then requested to return to a different prison in order to be closer to his family. He had been moved to Leyhill for good behavior but turned himself in after 24 hours. Drug experts compare the use of legal highs to 'Russian roulette' because their effects are unpredictable. Official statistics reveal that deaths involving legal highs increased by 80% from 2011 to 2012, rising from 29 to 52 per year. Examples of such drugs include mephedrone ('meow meow'), Black Mamba, and Benzo Fury; these have since been banned. Despite these bans, the number of deaths related to these substances continues to climb. Deaths involving cathinone, for instance, tripled from six in 2011 to 18 in 2012, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Nicolas Maduro was sworn in as Venezuela's acting president on Friday, following Hugo Chavez's death from cancer earlier in the week. Chavez, who had been battling cancer, named Maduro—his vice president—as his chosen successor before his death. 

During the inauguration, Maduro sharply criticized both the United States and Venezuela's political opposition. The ceremony itself was controversial; according to the country's 1999 constitution, the National Assembly speaker should take on the interim presidency after a president-elect's death or inability to serve, with new elections called within 30 days. 

Opposition leader Angel Medina announced a boycott of the event, resulting in most opposition legislators abstaining from attendance. The ceremony was attended by notable international figures, including former U.S. presidential candidate Rev. Jesse Jackson and Ecuadorian President Rafael Correa. Fireworks lit up the Caracas sky as Maduro was sworn in.

Maduro and National Assembly President Diosdado Cabello pledged to uphold Chavez's socialist vision. Maduro repeated previous allegations that Chavez’s cancer had been caused by the U.S., referring to its 'very strange' progression. 

He stressed his loyalty to Chavez and commitment to enforcing the constitution and continuing his predecessor's policies. Maduro affirmed the support of the Venezuelan military, which he called 'the armed forces of Chavez.' Critics expressed concern about the military's public backing of the ruling party, which contradicts constitutional rules against military involvement in politics.

Maduro appointed Science and Technology Minister Jorge Arreaza, Chavez’s son-in-law, as vice president. Opposition figures, notably Henrique Capriles—expected to run against Maduro in the upcoming election—criticized Maduro for allegedly turning Chavez’s funeral into a campaign event. Maduro, previously a bus driver, union leader, and foreign minister, had been a visible presence with Chavez during his treatments and led the funeral events in Caracas after Chavez’s death.

article_content: A mural inside the White Temple (Wat Rong Khun) in Chiang Rai, Thailand, has sparked criticism for depicting the 9/11 terrorist attacks alongside comic book characters and celebrities. The White Temple is the unique, ongoing project of Thai artist Chalermchai Kositpipat. The mural features scenes of planes crashing into the Twin Towers, fictional characters such as Spiderman, Harry Potter, the Terminator, celebrities including Michael Jackson, and images of fighter jets and spaceships. Additional pop culture references from movies like Star Wars, The Matrix, and Kung Fu Panda are blended with traditional Thai and Buddhist symbols, such as dragons and demons. Characters like Po from Kung Fu Panda and Jigsaw from the Saw series also appear. Photography is prohibited inside the temple, though one visitor managed to take a picture using a phone. A 31-year-old insurance broker from Nottingham described the visit as strange, saying, 'Inside, I was shocked to see a painting of planes flying into the Twin Towers. I just think it's totally inappropriate.' Outside, surreal sculptures like Predator sunk into the ground contribute to the unconventional atmosphere. Visitors cross a bridge over a pit of sculpted demonic hands and skulls to enter the temple. Design began in 1997, with a team of about 60 artists working under Kositpipat. Completion is expected by 2070, and the temple is already a major tourist destination. Another visitor, Alexey Statsenko, a 38-year-old business owner, remarked: 'It was so different from anything I had seen before. There were images of Michael Jackson, Terminator, Kung Fu Panda, Harry Potter, and more. I didn't know what to think. It seemed almost like a mockery.' On his blog, Statsenko commented: 'Generally speaking, it's an out-of-the-box (for a Buddhist temple) and creative way of expressing ideas.' Kositpipat says his style is influenced by traditional Thai temple art, which often depicts contemporary daily life alongside Buddhist imagery. Art at the White Temple ranges from the macabre to the ornate, with the outside covered in intricate designs and mirrors that reflect sunlight rather than paint. 'Only death can stop my dream, but cannot stop my project,' said Kositpipat in 2003, expressing his hope that the work will be his legacy. He is also responsible for murals at Wat Buddhapadipa in London, combining Thai motifs with global pop culture figures such as punk rockers, Charlie Chaplin, and Margaret Thatcher. Despite maintaining that his approach is rooted in Thai tradition, Kositpipat continues to receive criticism from officials, religious leaders, and other artists.

article_content: A North Carolina man accused of plotting to participate in violent acts overseas also allegedly planned an attack on the U.S. Marine base at Quantico, Virginia, according to new charges announced Thursday. Daniel Patrick Boyd had previously been charged with conspiracy to support terrorists and conspiracy to commit murder. The new indictment against Boyd includes three counts, with authorities describing him as the leader of a group training in North Carolina for 'violent jihad.' Boyd and Hysen Sherifi are accused of conspiring to murder U.S. military personnel. "Boyd conducted surveillance of the Marine Corps Base in Quantico, Virginia, and obtained maps of the base to plan an attack," the new charges state. During an August bond hearing, an FBI agent testified that authorities found weapons, thousands of rounds of ammunition, and $13,000 in cash at Boyd's home near Raleigh. The original indictment alleged the men practiced military tactics in a North Carolina county bordering Virginia. The latest indictment also charges Boyd, Sherifi, and Boyd's son, Zakariya, with possessing weapons in furtherance of a crime of violence. Boyd faces an additional charge of providing a rifle and ammunition to a convicted felon. Boyd and seven others have already been charged with conspiracy to provide material support to terrorists and conspiracy to murder, kidnap, maim, and injure others. One man is believed to have fled to Pakistan, while the remaining suspects are in custody. In August, a federal judge denied bail for the seven men in custody but expressed reservations about the charges against them. Magistrate Judge William Webb stated the defendants had made several statements about holy war, noting such remarks could be seen as bravado when viewed alone. However, he agreed to keep them detained because some had collected arsenals and taken part in firearms training.

article_content: India is likely to raise less than half of its targeted funds from planned sales of state-owned companies this fiscal year, and is set to miss its divestment targets for the fifth consecutive year due to shifting government priorities ahead of elections. Reuters reports that according to two government sources, the government may fall short of its divestment target by about Rs 30,000 crore in 2023/24. The government had aimed to collect Rs 51,000 crore from divestments in the current fiscal year ending March 2024. About Rs 30,000 crore of the target was expected from sales of stakes in IDBI Bank and the privatization of NMDC Steel. However, the Reserve Bank of India's ongoing review of potential buyers for IDBI Bank has delayed the sale beyond the 2024 federal elections, while the sale of NMDC Steel is also unlikely this year because of impending state and federal elections, along with union opposition in Chhattisgarh, where NMDC’s main plant is located. Though some minor divestments could still happen this fiscal year, the government is projected to fall well short of even half its overall target. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has struggled since 2019 to advance privatization in sectors like steel, fertilizer, and oil and gas, dealing with complications such as land rights and union opposition. The finance ministry has not immediately responded to requests for comment. Subhash Chandra Garg, former federal finance secretary, noted that no major privatizations are expected under the current government, citing a lack of political momentum for privatization until after elections. The government has so far raised 80 billion rupees this year through minority stake sales in state-run companies, according to official data. Some of the gap from divestment proceeds is being filled through increased dividends from profitable state-run enterprises. The government expects to exceed its 430 billion rupee dividend target, having already received 203 billion rupees from state-owned firms due to strong profits and steady demand. Rahul Bajoria, an economist at Barclays Investment Bank, said missing divestment targets is not damaging as long as the government meets its overall fiscal goals. A government official added that the privatization delays will not affect the current fiscal deficit target of 5.9% of GDP. Despite Indian stock markets reaching all-time highs, the government has only managed to sell minority stakes in five companies via stock exchange offers. An index of state-owned companies reached a record high of 13,242 on November 16. Women are increasingly visible in senior leadership and boardroom disputes in Indian companies, reflecting a shift toward greater gender representation. Tesla has expressed willingness to invest up to $2 billion in setting up a local factory, provided it secures a concessional 15% import duty for its first two years of importing vehicles into India. The upcoming Finance Commission may be tasked with giving greater weight to the Human Development Index and Sustainable Development Goals when recommending how resources are distributed among Indian states.

Following the case of nurse Pauline Cafferkey, UK airports have implemented tighter Ebola screening procedures. Cafferkey, who had been working with Ebola patients in Sierra Leone, developed the virus after returning to the UK and was permitted to travel from Heathrow to Glasgow despite reporting a fever. 

Previously, only temperature checks and a questionnaire were used to screen returning volunteers. The updated protocol now requires anyone feeling even slightly ill to receive detailed medical assessments, regardless of their temperature. Advice from tropical disease specialists will be sought, and those affected will be monitored for several hours when necessary.

Currently, Cafferkey, 39 and from Glasgow, is in a critical but stable condition at the Royal Free Hospital in London. Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt, addressing Parliament, outlined these enhanced measures and praised Cafferkey, expressing the country's appreciation for her bravery and stating she exemplifies the best of NHS values.

article_content: Researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed an advanced dual-laser nonlinear optical microscope platform to investigate muscle satellite cells (MuSCs) during muscle regeneration. This innovative technology enabled the discovery of new mechanisms by which MuSCs contribute to muscle repair, presenting potential pathways for targeted therapies addressing muscle-related disorders. Regeneration of skeletal muscle relies on the complex collaboration between MuSCs and various cell types. After muscle injury, myeloid cells such as macrophages migrate to the affected area, while MuSCs activate. Earlier studies identified diverse forms of quiescent MuSCs within the muscle environment, with specialized cellular adhesions and spatial arrangements essential for maintaining their inactivity. However, a lack of suitable live imaging techniques previously limited the study of MuSCs’ interactions with other cells. In collaboration, Prof. QU Jianan’s team from the Department of Electronics and Computer Engineering developed the dual-laser multimodal nonlinear optical microscope for high-resolution imaging in live skeletal muscle, while Prof. WU Zhenguo’s team from the Division of Life Science contributed expertise in muscle biology and regeneration. The research overturned the conventional belief that non-myogenic cells are the primary triggers of MuSC activation. Instead, MuSCs demonstrated an inherent ability to sense and respond to regenerative cues independently. Time-lapse in vivo imaging of injured muscle allowed visualization of interactions between activated MuSCs, macrophages, and other non-myogenic cells during proliferative stages. Findings showed that cell-to-cell contact between MuSCs and non-myogenic cells was transient. While macrophages were not essential for MuSC activation, they played a critical role in MuSC proliferation and differentiation. Their reduction led to impaired cell division and increased fibrosis, underscoring a stage-dependent function in muscle regeneration. The study also revealed that sustained direct contact between MuSCs and non-myogenic cells is not required for MuSC activation or division. Paracrine signaling, where secreted factors mediate communication, was found to regulate MuSC proliferation. Prof. Qu emphasized that the use of advanced imaging techniques enabled the comprehensive study of the cellular dynamics underpinning muscle regeneration and brought to light novel behaviors of MuSCs, which could guide targeted treatment strategies for muscle diseases. Prof. Wu’s team designed and conducted experiments with live reporter mice and analyzed MuSC dynamics using molecular and cellular approaches, while Prof. Qu’s team created the imaging platform and handled computational analysis. Their interdisciplinary collaboration encouraged creative problem-solving and enabled the development of new methodologies, resulting in an enhanced understanding of muscle regeneration. The findings were published in Science Advances.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is constructing a new storage facility near the England-Scotland border, according to government sources. The £86 million depot, located in Longtown, Cumbria, is scheduled to open in October 2024 and will support approximately 450 jobs. An MoD spokesperson described the new site as a "key asset" for supporting all three branches of the armed forces.

This project is part of a broader overhaul of the MoD’s storage sites, many of which date back to World War Two. Initial MoD estimates indicate that about 300 jobs will be supported in northern England and 150 in Scotland.

Spanning 7.5 hectares (18.5 acres), the facility will store equipment such as engines and other large spare parts. Dr Neil Hudson, Member of Parliament for Penrith and the Border, called the initiative a "monumental project." He said, “This investment will contribute greatly to the prosperity and growth of our border communities as well as strengthen our national defence infrastructure. I look forward to witnessing the positive ripple effects of this project, fostering economic development and job opportunities.” Minister for Defence Procurement James Cartlidge also described the new depot as a “hugely important strategic facility.”

article_content: Michael Phelps remains hesitant to call it a 'comeback,' but all indications suggest the legendary swimmer may return to the pool for the 2016 Rio Olympics. In a strong sign that retirement might not be permanent, Phelps has rejoined the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency's drug testing program—a step required for any athlete wishing to compete in Olympic sports. During a phone interview with The Associated Press from Minneapolis, where Phelps attended an Arena Grand Prix meet and did some impromptu training, he said, 'I have no idea what's going to happen. If I start getting excited and want to do it, I can make that choice. If not, at least we've prepared.' Phelps stressed that this move simply gives him the option to compete again and that 'nothing is set in stone.' The anti-doping program requires athletes to be available for random testing and keep officials updated on their whereabouts, which Phelps called 'a challenging thing to do.' With 18 gold medals and 22 total Olympic medals, Phelps is the most decorated Olympian ever. He is famous for breaking Mark Spitz's record by winning eight gold medals in a single Olympics (Beijing 2008). USADA confirmed that Phelps was tested twice in the third quarter ending September 30. According to his coach Bob Bowman, Phelps re-entered the testing pool near the end of the second quarter but wasn't tested then. He could be eligible to compete as early as March. Bowman noted, 'I think he's feeling good about swimming. We're just beginning to work on his fitness, and we'll see how it progresses.' Phelps has been training with Bowman’s team at the North Baltimore Aquatic Club, swimming a couple of times a week, spending time in the weight room, and focusing on core strength. He’s lost about 15 pounds, getting closer to his competition weight. 'If I decide to keep swimming, I’ll compete. If not,' he joked, 'I guess I’ll re-retire. Just don’t compare me to Brett Favre.' Speculation about Phelps’ return has circulated for over a year, with fellow swimmer Ryan Lochte suggesting that Phelps would eventually return. By completing the required drug testing, Phelps gives himself plenty of time to prepare before major competitions like the 2015 World Championships in Kazan, Russia—an important step toward the Rio Olympics. FINA rules require an athlete to be in the testing pool for at least nine months before competing in sanctioned events. Phelps attended the 2013 World Championships in Barcelona as a spectator, expressing enjoyment and excitement about being involved in the sport again. Teammates, like Conor Dwyer, welcome the idea of his return, saying it would benefit U.S. swimming. A possible rematch with Chad Le Clos, who beat Phelps in the 200m butterfly at London 2012, is an intriguing storyline. Le Clos once had photos of Phelps on his wall and has become a top rival. Outside the pool, Phelps is one of the most recognized athletes, rivaling stars from mainstream sports such as LeBron James. He retired after the 2012 London Olympics, saying his goals were achieved and he had no desire to swim into his 30s. Still, many elite swimmers, including Ryan Lochte, plan to compete into their 30s. Financial motivation is unlikely to be a factor; Phelps has already earned significant endorsement income and remains a marketable figure. Ultimately, Phelps’ possible return is likely driven by his passion for competition and the sport itself. As he put it, 'There are a lot of things that motivate me. But I swam for 20 years—that's going to be hard to top.'
